Squaring instead of cubing ($10^4\text{ cm}^3$ per m³) gives 25 L; stopping at $2.5 \times 10^6\text{ cm}^3$ and calling it liters gives 2 500 000 L; treating 1 m³ as 1 L gives 2.5 L.

questions.stem: A dart player's throws all land within 1 cm of each other, but 10 cm left of the bullseye. The throws are
questions.explanation: Precision is how tightly results cluster (very tight here); accuracy is closeness to the true target (they all miss by 10 cm). A systematic error like this produces precise but inaccurate results.

questions.stem: A student derives $v = \sqrt{2 g h^2}$ for the speed of an object dropped from height $h$. What does dimensional analysis say?
choices: It is wrong only by a numerical factor
It is wrong: the units come out $\text{m}^{3/2}/\text{s}$
questions.explanation: $[g h^2] = \tfrac{L}{T^2}L^2 = L^3/T^2$, whose square root is $L^{3/2}/T$, not a speed. The correct result is $v = \sqrt{2gh}$, where $[gh] = L^2/T^2$.

questions.stem: Write $0.000\,0372\text{ s}$ in scientific notation and with a prefix.
questions.explanation: Move the decimal 5 places right: $3.72 \times 10^{-5}$ s. Since 1 μs $= 10^{-6}$ s, this is $37.2 \times 10^{-6}$ s $= 37.2$ μs.

questions.stem: A vector has magnitude 10 m and points $60^\circ$ above the $+x$ axis. Its components are
questions.explanation: $A_x = 10\cos 60^\circ = 5.0$ m and $A_y = 10\sin 60^\circ = 8.66$ m. Swapping sine and cosine gives $A_x = 8.7$ m, $A_y = 5.0$ m.

questions.stem: Which of these is a vector quantity?
questions.explanation: Acceleration has a direction (it points the way velocity is changing). Mass, energy and temperature are scalars: one number and a unit describe them fully.

questions.stem: You walk 6 m east and then 8 m north. What is the magnitude of your displacement?
questions.explanation: The legs are perpendicular, so $\sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{100} = 10$ m. 14 m is the distance walked (adding magnitudes), not the displacement.

questions.stem: A vector has components $A_x = -3$ and $A_y = 3$. What angle does it make with the $+x$ axis (counterclockwise)?
questions.explanation: $\tan^{-1}(3/(-3)) = -45^\circ$ on a calculator, but the vector is in the second quadrant ($A_x < 0$, $A_y > 0$), so add $180^\circ$: $135^\circ$.

questions.stem: Given $\vec A = 2\hat\imath + 5\hat\jmath$ and $\vec B = 4\hat\imath - 1\hat\jmath$, find $\vec A - \vec B$.
questions.explanation: Subtract components: $(2-4)\hat\imath + (5-(-1))\hat\jmath = -2\hat\imath + 6\hat\jmath$. The choice $-2\hat\imath + 4\hat\jmath$ comes from $5 - 1$, a sign slip.

questions.stem: Two forces of 3 N and 4 N act on an object. Which total force magnitude is impossible?
questions.explanation: The resultant of two vectors ranges from $|A - B| = 1$ N (opposite directions) to $A + B = 7$ N (same direction). 5 N occurs when they are perpendicular. 8 N exceeds the maximum.

questions.stem: Compute $\vec A \cdot \vec B$ for $\vec A = 3\hat\imath - 2\hat\jmath + \hat k$ and $\vec B = 4\hat\imath + 5\hat\jmath - 2\hat k$.
questions.explanation: $3(4) + (-2)(5) + 1(-2) = 12 - 10 - 2 = 0$. A zero dot product means the vectors are perpendicular. Dropping every minus sign gives 24, dropping only the sign of the last product gives 4, and using only the $x$ components gives 12.

questions.stem: What is $\hat\imath \times \hat\jmath$?
questions.explanation: By the right-hand rule, fingers along $+x$ curled toward $+y$ put the thumb along $+z$: $\hat\imath \times \hat\jmath = \hat k$. (The dot product $\hat\imath\cdot\hat\jmath$ is 0, and $\hat\jmath\times\hat\imath = -\hat k$.)

questions.stem: Two vectors of magnitudes 4 and 5 make a $30^\circ$ angle. What is the magnitude of their cross product?
questions.explanation: $|\vec A\times\vec B| = AB\sin\phi = 4(5)\sin 30^\circ = 10$. Using cosine gives 17.3, which is the dot product.

questions.stem: If $\vec A \times \vec B = 2\hat\imath - 3\hat k$, what is $\vec B \times \vec A$?
questions.explanation: The cross product is anticommutative: $\vec B\times\vec A = -(\vec A\times\vec B) = -2\hat\imath + 3\hat k$.

questions.stem: A block sits on a ramp inclined at $25^\circ$. To simplify a force problem, the most useful choice of axes is
choices: $x$ along the ramp, $y$ perpendicular to it
questions.explanation: With $x$ along the ramp, the acceleration has only an $x$ component and the normal force only a $y$ component; only gravity needs to be split into components. Any axes give the same physics, but these give the least algebra.

questions.stem: A displacement of 12 m points $40^\circ$ south of west. Its components ($+x$ east, $+y$ north) are
questions.explanation: The angle is measured from the west ($-x$) direction toward south. The west component is $12\cos 40^\circ = 9.19$ m and the south component is $12\sin 40^\circ = 7.71$ m, so $(A_x, A_y) = (-9.19, -7.71)$ m. Both components are negative in the third quadrant.

questions.stem: A runner completes exactly two laps of a 400 m track in 160 s, finishing where she started. Her average speed and average velocity are
questions.explanation: Average speed = distance/time = 800 m / 160 s = 5.0 m/s. Average velocity = displacement/time, and the displacement is zero because she ends at the start, so the average velocity is 0.

questions.stem: A car moving in the $-x$ direction is slowing down. The signs of its velocity and acceleration are
questions.explanation: Moving in $-x$ means $v < 0$. Slowing down means $a$ is opposite to $v$, so $a > 0$. "Negative acceleration means slowing down" is only true when $v > 0$.

questions.stem: On a position–time graph, the instantaneous velocity at a moment is
choices: the slope of the tangent line at that moment
the height of the graph at that moment
the area under the graph up to that moment
the curvature of the graph at that moment
questions.explanation: Velocity is the rate of change of position, which is the slope of the $x$–$t$ graph (for a curve, the slope of the tangent line). The height is the position itself; area under a $v$–$t$ (not $x$–$t$) graph gives displacement; curvature relates to acceleration.

questions.stem: A velocity–time graph is a straight line from $(0\text{ s}, 10\text{ m/s})$ to $(8\text{ s}, 30\text{ m/s})$. What are the acceleration and the displacement over the 8 s?
questions.explanation: Slope: $(30 - 10)/8 = 2.5$ m/s². Displacement is the area under the line, a trapezoid: $\tfrac12(10 + 30)(8) = 160$ m. 240 m would use the final speed for the whole time; 80 m is only the triangle part.

questions.stem: On a velocity–time graph, a segment lies below the $t$ axis between 4 s and 6 s. During that interval the object
questions.explanation: Below the axis means $v < 0$, motion in the $-x$ direction. That says nothing about where the object is (position), and whether it slows depends on the slope, not the sign of $v$.

questions.stem: A cyclist rides 10 km at 20 km/h and then 10 km at 10 km/h. What is her average speed for the trip?
questions.explanation: The legs take $10/20 = 0.5$ h and $10/10 = 1.0$ h. Average speed $= 20\text{ km}/1.5\text{ h} = 13.3$ km/h. Averaging the speeds (15 km/h) is wrong because she spends more time at the slower speed.

questions.stem: A position–time graph is a straight line from $(0\text{ s}, 12\text{ m})$ to $(4.0\text{ s}, 0\text{ m})$. What is the object's velocity?
questions.explanation: Velocity is the slope: $\dfrac{0 - 12}{4.0 - 0} = -3.0$ m/s. The object moves in the $-x$ direction at a steady 3.0 m/s. Dropping the sign gives 3.0 m/s; run over rise gives $-0.33$ m/s; reaching $x = 0$ doesn't mean the velocity is zero.

questions.stem: On a curved position–time graph, the tangent line drawn at $t = 4$ s passes through $(2\text{ s}, 1\text{ m})$ and $(6\text{ s}, 13\text{ m})$. What is the instantaneous velocity at 4 s?
questions.explanation: The instantaneous velocity is the slope of the tangent: $\dfrac{13 - 1}{6 - 2} = \dfrac{12}{4} = 3.0$ m/s. Dividing one point's height by its time ($13/6 = 2.2$) is not a slope; $0.33$ is run over rise; 12 is the rise alone.

questions.stem: An acceleration–time graph shows a constant 3 m/s² from 0 to 4 s. If $v(0) = 2$ m/s, what is $v(4)$?
questions.explanation: The area under the $a$–$t$ graph is $\Delta v = 3 \times 4 = 12$ m/s, so $v(4) = 2 + 12 = 14$ m/s. 12 m/s forgets the initial velocity.

questions.stem: Which statement about a ball at the very top of its vertical flight is true?
choices: Its velocity and acceleration are both zero
Its velocity is zero and its acceleration is less than 9.8 m/s²
Its velocity is zero and its acceleration is 9.8 m/s² downward
Its velocity is 9.8 m/s and its acceleration is zero
questions.explanation: Momentarily $v = 0$, but gravity still acts with full strength, so $a = 9.8$ m/s² downward, the same as at every other point of the flight. If the acceleration were zero, the ball would stay at the top forever.

questions.stem: A velocity–time graph shows $v = +4.0$ m/s from 0 to 3.0 s, then $v = -2.0$ m/s from 3.0 s to 5.0 s. What are the displacement and the distance traveled over the 5.0 s?
questions.explanation: Areas: $+4.0 \times 3.0 = +12$ m, then $-2.0 \times 2.0 = -4.0$ m. Displacement is the signed sum, $12 - 4.0 = 8.0$ m. Distance counts every area as positive: $12 + 4.0 = 16$ m. Treating the area below the axis as positive in the displacement gives 16 m.

questions.stem: An object's position–time graph is a straight line sloping downward. The object
choices: is slowing down to a stop
moves in the $+x$ direction while slowing
moves in the $-x$ direction at constant speed
questions.explanation: A straight line has constant slope, so the velocity is constant; a downward slope means that velocity is negative. Constant velocity means zero acceleration. Reading the falling height of the line as "slowing down" confuses position with speed.

questions.stem: A car traveling at 20 m/s brakes at a constant 4.0 m/s². How far does it travel before stopping?
questions.explanation: $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x$: $0 = 400 + 2(-4.0)\Delta x$, so $\Delta x = 50$ m. Forgetting the 2 gives 100 m.

questions.stem: If a car's speed doubles, its braking distance (same deceleration) becomes
questions.explanation: From $0 = v_0^2 - 2a d$, $d = v_0^2/(2a)$. Distance is proportional to $v_0^2$, so doubling $v_0$ quadruples $d$.

questions.stem: A jet starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 3.0 m/s² down a runway. How long must the runway be for it to reach 24 m/s?
questions.explanation: $v^2 = 2a\Delta x$ gives $\Delta x = 24^2/(2 \times 3.0) = 576/6 = 96$ m. (It takes 8 s; 192 m drops the factor of 2.)

questions.stem: A rock is dropped from a 45 m cliff. How long does it take to reach the bottom? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: $45 = \tfrac12(9.8)t^2 \Rightarrow t^2 = 9.18$, $t = 3.0$ s. 4.6 s comes from $t = 45/9.8$ (forgetting the square).

questions.stem: A ball is thrown straight up at 19.6 m/s. How long is it in the air before returning to the launch height? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: It takes $19.6/9.8 = 2.0$ s to reach the top and the same time to fall back, so 4.0 s total. 2.0 s is only the trip up.

questions.stem: Ignoring air resistance, a 10 kg bowling ball and a 1 kg ball are dropped together from the same height. Which lands first?
questions.explanation: In free fall every object has the same acceleration $g$, regardless of mass, so with the same start they land together.

questions.stem: Which kinematic equation should you use if you know $v_0$, $a$ and $\Delta x$, and want $v$, with no time given?
questions.explanation: Pick the equation that omits the quantity you don't know and don't need: here that's $t$, and $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x$ is the time-free equation.

questions.stem: A student writes $y = v_0t - \tfrac12(-9.8)t^2$ for a ball thrown upward with up positive. What is wrong?
choices: The sign of gravity is counted twice, so the ball would accelerate upward
questions.explanation: With up positive, $a = -g = -9.8$ m/s², so $y = v_0t + \tfrac12(-9.8)t^2 = v_0t - 4.9t^2$. Writing $-\tfrac12(-9.8)$ makes the gravity term positive, an upward acceleration.

questions.stem: A train speeds up uniformly from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 20 s. How far does it travel in that time?
questions.explanation: $\Delta x = \tfrac12(v_0 + v)t = \tfrac12(10 + 30)(20) = 400$ m. 600 m uses the final speed only; 200 m uses the initial speed only.

questions.stem: A ball thrown upward at 15 m/s from a balcony lands on the ground below. With up positive and the origin at the balcony, the ball's final displacement $\Delta y$ is
questions.explanation: Displacement is final minus initial position. The ground is below the balcony, so $\Delta y < 0$, even though the ball went up first. Using a positive $\Delta y$ is a common error.

questions.stem: Substituting $t = (v - v_0)/a$ from $v = v_0 + at$ into $\Delta x = \tfrac12(v_0 + v)t$ gives
questions.explanation: $\Delta x = \tfrac12(v_0 + v)\dfrac{v - v_0}{a} = \dfrac{v^2 - v_0^2}{2a}$, and multiplying by $2a$ gives $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x$, the time-free equation. The other choices still contain $t$, which the substitution removed.

questions.stem: A cart starts from rest, accelerates at 3.0 m/s² for 4.0 s, then coasts at constant velocity for 5.0 s more. How far does it travel in total?
questions.explanation: Phase 1: $\Delta x = \tfrac12(3.0)(4.0)^2 = 24$ m, ending at $v = 12$ m/s. Phase 2: $12 \times 5.0 = 60$ m. Total 84 m. Using 12 m/s for all 9.0 s gives 108 m; using the average speed of phase 1 (6 m/s) for the whole 9.0 s gives 54 m; 60 m is phase 2 alone.

questions.stem: A ball is launched horizontally from a table. Ignoring air resistance, which quantity stays constant during its flight?
questions.explanation: Gravity acts only vertically, so $v_x$ never changes. $v_y$ grows downward, which changes both the speed and the direction.

questions.stem: A package is dropped from a plane flying horizontally at 60 m/s at a height of 490 m. How far ahead of the drop point does it land? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: Fall time: $490 = 4.9t^2$, so $t = 10$ s. The package keeps the plane's horizontal speed: $x = 60 \times 10 = 600$ m.

questions.stem: A ball is kicked at 25 m/s at $40^\circ$ above level ground. What is its range? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: $R = \dfrac{v_0^2\sin 2\theta}{g} = \dfrac{625\sin 80^\circ}{9.8} = 62.8$ m. 41.0 m uses $\sin 40^\circ$ instead of $\sin 80^\circ$; 63.8 m is $v_0^2/g$ (the 45° maximum); 13.2 m is the maximum height.

questions.stem: At the highest point of a projectile's path (launched at $30^\circ$), its velocity is
questions.explanation: At the top $v_y = 0$, but $v_x = v_0\cos\theta$ is unchanged, so the velocity is horizontal with magnitude $v_0\cos 30^\circ$.

questions.stem: Two balls are launched from level ground with the same speed, one at $25^\circ$ and one at $65^\circ$. Compared with the $25^\circ$ ball, the $65^\circ$ ball
choices: lands at the same distance but stays up longer
lands at the same distance and same time
questions.explanation: Complementary angles give equal ranges because $\sin 50^\circ = \sin 130^\circ$. The steeper launch has a larger $v_{0y}$, so it rises higher and its flight time $2v_0\sin\theta/g$ is longer.

questions.stem: A ball rolls off a 19.6 m high cliff at 12 m/s. How far from the base does it land? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: Fall time: $19.6 = 4.9t^2$, so $t = 2.0$ s. Horizontal distance $= 12 \times 2.0 = 24$ m.

questions.stem: Ignoring air resistance, what launch angle maximizes the range on level ground, and why?
choices: $90^\circ$, because the ball stays up longest
$30^\circ$, because the horizontal speed is large
questions.explanation: $R = v_0^2\sin 2\theta/g$, and $\sin 2\theta$ reaches its maximum of 1 at $2\theta = 90^\circ$, i.e. $\theta = 45^\circ$. A $90^\circ$ launch has zero horizontal speed and lands where it started.

questions.stem: A projectile is launched at 20 m/s at $30^\circ$ above horizontal from a 15 m high platform. Why can't you use $R = v_0^2\sin 2\theta/g$ to find where it lands?
choices: Because it lands below its launch height, and the formula assumes equal heights
Because the formula only works for horizontal launches
questions.explanation: The range formula comes from setting $y = 0$ at landing, i.e. landing at launch height. From a platform, solve $-15 = v_{0y}t - 4.9t^2$ for $t$ and then use $x = v_{0x}t$.

questions.stem: A ball is thrown at 10 m/s at $53^\circ$ above horizontal ($\sin 53^\circ \approx 0.80$, $\cos 53^\circ \approx 0.60$). What is its velocity 0.50 s later? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
Eliminating time from the projectile equations shows that the path $y(x)$ is
questions.explanation: $y = x\tan\theta - \dfrac{g}{2v_0^2\cos^2\theta}x^2$ is quadratic in $x$, so the path is a parabola (without air resistance).

questions.stem: A ball is launched from level ground and lands 15 m away. It is launched again at the same angle with twice the speed. Ignoring air resistance, it now lands
questions.explanation: $R = v_0^2\sin 2\theta/g$ is proportional to $v_0^2$, so doubling the speed multiplies the range by 4: 60 m. Both the horizontal speed and the flight time double, and range is their product. 30 m doubles only one of them.

questions.stem: A river flows east at 3 m/s. A boat heads due north at 4 m/s relative to the water. What is the boat's speed relative to the shore?
questions.explanation: $\vec v_{BG} = \vec v_{BW} + \vec v_{WG} = (3, 4)$ m/s, magnitude $\sqrt{9 + 16} = 5$ m/s. Adding magnitudes (7 m/s) ignores the directions.

questions.stem: A river is 60 m wide and flows at 2.0 m/s. A swimmer swims at 3.0 m/s relative to the water, heading straight across. How long does she take to cross, and how far downstream does she land?
questions.explanation: Only the across component matters for the crossing time: $60/3.0 = 20$ s. Meanwhile the current carries her $2.0 \times 20 = 40$ m downstream. 26.8 s is the time if she aims upstream to land directly opposite.

questions.stem: Same river (60 m wide, current 2.0 m/s), swimmer 3.0 m/s relative to the water. At what angle upstream from straight across must she head to land directly opposite?
questions.explanation: The upstream component of her velocity must cancel the current: $3.0\sin\alpha = 2.0$, so $\alpha = \sin^{-1}(2/3) = 41.8^\circ$. $33.7^\circ$ is $\tan^{-1}(2/3)$, the wrong trig function.

questions.stem: A car drives around a circular track at a constant 25 m/s. Is it accelerating?
choices: Yes, because the direction of its velocity changes
No, because its speed is constant
Only if the track is banked
questions.explanation: Acceleration is the rate of change of the velocity vector. Turning changes the vector's direction, so there is a (centripetal) acceleration even at constant speed.

questions.stem: Car A drives north at 25 m/s and car B drives south at 20 m/s. What is the velocity of A relative to B?
questions.explanation: With north positive, $v_{AB} = v_{AG} + v_{GB} = v_{AG} - v_{BG} = 25 - (-20) = +45$ m/s, i.e. 45 m/s north.

questions.stem: If $\vec v_{AB} = 4\hat\imath - 2\hat\jmath$ m/s, then $\vec v_{BA}$ is
questions.explanation: Reversing the observer reverses the relative velocity: $\vec v_{BA} = -\vec v_{AB}$.

questions.stem: A drone flies from the origin to the point $(12\text{ m}, -9.0\text{ m})$ in 3.0 s. What is the magnitude of its average velocity?
questions.explanation: The displacement has magnitude $\sqrt{12^2 + 9.0^2} = 15$ m, so $v_{\text{avg}} = 15/3.0 = 5.0$ m/s. Adding the component sizes ($21/3.0 = 7.0$) or subtracting them ($3.0/3.0 = 1.0$) ignores how vectors combine; 15 m/s forgets to divide by the time.

questions.stem: A plane with airspeed 300 km/h heads due north while a 40 km/h wind blows toward the east. What is its ground speed?
questions.explanation: $\vec v_{PG} = (40, 300)$ km/h, magnitude $\sqrt{40^2 + 300^2} = 302.7 \approx 303$ km/h, drifting $7.6^\circ$ east of north. 297 km/h would be the ground speed if it instead headed into the wind to fly due north.

questions.stem: An object's velocity changes from $(3, 0)$ m/s to $(0, 4)$ m/s in 2.0 s. What is the magnitude of its average acceleration?
questions.explanation: $\Delta\vec v = (0 - 3, 4 - 0) = (-3, 4)$ m/s, magnitude 5 m/s. Divided by 2.0 s: 2.5 m/s². Subtracting speeds ($4 - 3 = 1$ m/s, giving 0.5 m/s²) ignores the change in direction.

questions.stem: Observers in two frames moving at constant velocity relative to each other measure a ball's motion. They agree on its
questions.explanation: Their velocities for the ball differ by the constant relative velocity of the frames, $\vec v_{AC} = \vec v_{AB} + \vec v_{BC}$. A constant term doesn't change, so both see the same change in velocity over any interval, and hence the same acceleration. Velocities (and so kinetic energies) and positions differ between the frames.

questions.stem: A passenger on a train moving east at constant velocity drops a ball. Ignoring air resistance, how does someone standing beside the track see the ball move?
choices: Along a parabola, moving east as it falls
Along a parabola, curving west as it falls
Along a straight line slanting east
questions.explanation: To the passenger the ball falls straight down. Relative to the ground it starts with the train's eastward velocity, which stays constant while gravity speeds up its fall: a projectile launched horizontally, so a parabola moving east. It doesn't drift west because nothing slows its horizontal motion.

questions.stem: A spacecraft far from any planet coasts with its engines off. According to Newton's first law, it
questions.explanation: With no net force there is no acceleration, so the velocity (speed and direction) stays constant. A force is needed to change motion, not to maintain it.

questions.stem: A 10 kg box is pushed across a floor by a 50 N horizontal force while kinetic friction of 29.4 N opposes it. What is its acceleration?
questions.explanation: Net force $= 50 - 29.4 = 20.6$ N, so $a = 20.6/10 = 2.06$ m/s². Ignoring friction gives 5.0 m/s²; 7.9 m/s² adds the forces instead of subtracting.

questions.stem: A book rests on a table. What is the third-law partner of the gravitational force Earth exerts on the book?
choices: The normal force of the table on the book
The force of the book on the table
The gravitational force of the book on Earth
The normal force of the floor on the table
questions.explanation: Third-law pairs are the same type of force between the same two objects, acting on each other. Earth pulls the book down gravitationally, so the book pulls Earth up gravitationally. The normal force on the book is equal and opposite to its weight here, but it acts on the same object and is a different interaction.

questions.stem: A 70 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator that is accelerating downward at 1.5 m/s². What does the scale read? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: Up positive: $n - mg = ma$ with $a = -1.5$ m/s², so $n = m(g + a) = 70(9.8 - 1.5) = 581$ N. 791 N would be for upward acceleration; 686 N is the true weight.

questions.stem: An elevator moves upward at a constant 3 m/s. Compared with the passenger's weight, the normal force from the floor is
questions.explanation: Constant velocity means $a = 0$, so the net force is zero and $n = mg$. Only acceleration, not velocity, changes the apparent weight.

questions.stem: An astronaut has a mass of 80 kg on Earth. On the Moon ($g = 1.62$ m/s²), her mass and weight are
questions.explanation: Mass is an intrinsic property and doesn't change: 80 kg. Weight is $mg = 80(1.62) = 130$ N on the Moon (784 N on Earth).

questions.stem: A 5.0 kg block on a frictionless floor is pulled by a 20 N force at $37^\circ$ above horizontal ($\cos 37^\circ \approx 0.80$, $\sin 37^\circ \approx 0.60$). What is the normal force on the block? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: Vertically $n + 20\sin 37^\circ - mg = 0$, so $n = 49 - 12 = 37$ N. The upward pull reduces the normal force; 61 N adds it instead.

questions.stem: Which of these belongs on the free-body diagram of a ball in flight after it leaves a pitcher's hand (no air resistance)?
choices: The force of the throw, along the velocity
Weight and the force of the throw
questions.explanation: Once released, nothing touches the ball, so the only force is gravity. The "force of the throw" acted only while the hand was in contact; the ball keeps moving because of inertia.

questions.stem: A net force $F$ gives an object of mass $m$ an acceleration $a$. If the net force is tripled and the mass is doubled, the new acceleration is
questions.explanation: $a_{\text{new}} = \dfrac{3F}{2m} = \tfrac32\cdot\dfrac{F}{m} = \tfrac32 a$. Multiplying the two factors gives $6a$, but a larger mass reduces the acceleration; $\tfrac23 a$ inverts the ratio.

questions.stem: Two blocks, 4.0 kg and 2.0 kg, sit side by side on a frictionless floor. A 30 N horizontal push on the 4.0 kg block moves both. What force does the 4.0 kg block exert on the 2.0 kg block?
questions.explanation: Whole system: $a = 30/6.0 = 5.0$ m/s². The 2.0 kg block's only horizontal force is the contact force, so $F = 2.0(5.0) = 10$ N.

questions.stem: A 1200 kg car speeds up uniformly from 10 m/s to 25 m/s in 5.0 s. What net force acts on it?
questions.explanation: $a = \Delta v/\Delta t = (25 - 10)/5.0 = 3.0$ m/s², so $F_{\text{net}} = ma = 1200(3.0) = 3600$ N. Using the final speed alone ($25/5.0$) gives 6000 N, the initial speed alone gives 2400 N, and adding the speeds gives 8400 N.

questions.stem: A crate with $\mu_s n = 50$ N rests on the floor. You push it horizontally with 20 N and it doesn't move. The static friction force is
questions.explanation: Static friction adjusts to prevent sliding: it equals 20 N to balance your push. $\mu_s n = 50$ N is only the maximum it could supply.

questions.stem: Why is it usually harder to start a heavy box sliding than to keep it sliding?
choices: Because the normal force decreases once it moves
Because kinetic friction increases with speed
Because inertia vanishes once it moves
questions.explanation: The maximum static friction $\mu_s n$ is usually larger than kinetic friction $\mu_k n$. The normal force doesn't change, and kinetic friction is roughly independent of speed.

questions.stem: A block slides down a frictionless $30^\circ$ incline. What is its acceleration? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: Along the slope only $mg\sin\theta$ acts, so $a = g\sin 30^\circ = 4.9$ m/s². 8.5 m/s² uses cosine by mistake.

questions.stem: A block slides down a $30^\circ$ incline with $\mu_k = 0.20$. What is its acceleration? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta) = 9.8(0.500 - 0.20 \times 0.866) = 3.2$ m/s². 6.6 m/s² adds friction instead of subtracting it.

questions.stem: On an incline at angle $\theta$ with no other perpendicular forces, the normal force on a block of mass $m$ is
questions.explanation: Perpendicular to the slope there's no acceleration: $n - mg\cos\theta = 0$. Check: on a flat surface ($\theta = 0$) it gives $mg$; on a vertical wall it gives 0.

questions.stem: A coin on a book starts to slide when the book is tilted to $31^\circ$. What is the coefficient of static friction?
questions.explanation: At the verge of slipping, $mg\sin\theta = \mu_s mg\cos\theta$, so $\mu_s = \tan 31^\circ = 0.60$. 0.52 is $\sin 31^\circ$; 0.86 is $\cos 31^\circ$.

questions.stem: You pull a sled with a rope angled upward instead of horizontally (same rope tension). Compared with a horizontal pull, the kinetic friction on the sled is
choices: larger, because the force is at an angle
smaller, because the normal force is smaller
questions.explanation: The upward component of the pull reduces the normal force ($n = mg - T\sin\theta$), and $f_k = \mu_k n$, so friction drops.

questions.stem: A 20 kg box slides across a floor with $\mu_k = 0.40$ and no applied force. How quickly does it slow down? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: Only friction acts horizontally: $\mu_k mg = ma$, so $a = \mu_k g = 0.40(9.8) = 3.92$ m/s². The mass cancels. 78 is the friction force in newtons, not the acceleration.

questions.stem: A block is pushed up a ramp and released while still moving up. While it slides up, the friction force points
choices: nowhere; friction only acts on the way down
questions.explanation: Kinetic friction opposes the sliding velocity. Moving up the slope, friction points down the slope, adding to $mg\sin\theta$: $a = -g(\sin\theta + \mu_k\cos\theta)$.

questions.stem: An object of mass $m$ falls through a fluid that exerts a drag force $bv$ proportional to its speed. Its terminal speed is
questions.explanation: At terminal speed the acceleration is zero, so drag balances weight: $bv_T = mg$ and $v_T = mg/b$. The square root belongs to drag proportional to $v^2$, not $v$; $b/(mg)$ inverts the ratio.

questions.stem: A skydiver is falling straight down at her terminal velocity. Which statement is true?
choices: Drag is smaller than her weight, so she is still speeding up
The net force on her and her acceleration are both zero
Drag is larger than her weight, so she is slowing down
questions.explanation: Terminal velocity is the constant speed reached when drag has grown to equal her weight. The forces balance, so the net force is zero and, by the second law, so is her acceleration. She accelerates at $g$ only at the instant she starts falling, when drag is zero.

questions.stem: In an Atwood machine with $m_1 = 4.0$ kg and $m_2 = 2.0$ kg on an ideal pulley, what is the acceleration? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: $a = \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}g = \dfrac{2.0}{6.0}(9.8) = 3.27$ m/s². 4.9 m/s² divides by $m_1$ alone.

questions.stem: In the same Atwood machine (4.0 kg and 2.0 kg), what is the rope tension?
questions.explanation: $T = \dfrac{2m_1m_2}{m_1 + m_2}g = \dfrac{2(4.0)(2.0)}{6.0}(9.8) = 26.1$ N. Check: it lies between the weights 19.6 N and 39.2 N, as it must.

questions.stem: A 10 kg lamp hangs at rest from two cables, each $30^\circ$ above horizontal. What is the tension in each cable? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: $2T\sin 30^\circ = mg = 98$ N, so $T = 98/(2 \times 0.5) = 98$ N. Each cable carries the full weight because shallow cables need large tension to supply the vertical support.

questions.stem: A 5.0 kg block on a table ($\mu_k = 0.25$) is connected over an ideal pulley to a hanging 3.0 kg mass. What is the acceleration? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: $a = \dfrac{m_2 - \mu_k m_1}{m_1 + m_2}g = \dfrac{3.0 - 1.25}{8.0}(9.8) = 2.14$ m/s². 3.7 m/s² ignores friction.

questions.stem: A mass hangs from a rope in an elevator that accelerates upward. The rope tension is
questions.explanation: $T - mg = ma$ with $a > 0$, so $T = m(g + a) > mg$. Tension equals the weight only when the mass isn't accelerating.

questions.stem: When you treat two blocks joined by a rope as a single system to find their common acceleration, why can you ignore the rope tension?
choices: It is an internal force; its pulls on the two blocks cancel in the system's net force
The rope is massless, so it has no tension
Tension acts only when the system is at rest
questions.explanation: The rope pulls block A toward B and block B toward A with equal magnitude. Within the system these cancel, so only external forces determine the system's acceleration.

questions.stem: A 200 N load hangs from a movable pulley supported by two strands of the same rope. In equilibrium, what force must you pull with, and how far must you pull to raise the load 1 m?
questions.explanation: Two strands support the load, so $2T = 200$ N and $T = 100$ N. Raising the load 1 m shortens each strand by 1 m, so you pull 2 m of rope. Force is halved, distance doubled, work unchanged.

questions.stem: An Atwood machine has equal masses on both sides and is given a push so it moves. What happens next?
choices: It keeps moving at constant speed
questions.explanation: With $m_1 = m_2$, $a = 0$: the net force on each mass is zero, so they keep the velocity they were given (Newton's first law).

questions.stem: A uniform rope of mass 2.0 kg and length 4.0 m hangs vertically from a ceiling. What is the tension at its midpoint? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: The midpoint supports the rope below it: half the rope, 1.0 kg, weighing 9.8 N. Tension in a massive rope grows toward the top (19.6 N at the ceiling, 0 at the bottom).

questions.stem: A load hangs from a movable pulley supported by two strands of rope. You pull the free end of the rope upward at a steady 0.60 m/s. How fast does the load rise?
questions.explanation: Pulling 0.60 m of rope shortens each of the two supporting strands by 0.30 m, so the load rises half as far in the same time: 0.30 m/s. Half the force needed comes at the cost of twice the rope pulled, not twice the speed of the load.

questions.stem: Block A on a frictionless table is tied over a pulley to a hanging block B. Taking "A moves toward the pulley" and "B moves down" as positive, the correct equations are
questions.explanation: Only tension acts horizontally on A (toward the pulley, positive). On B, weight acts down (positive) and tension up (negative). Adding gives $a = m_Bg/(m_A + m_B)$.

questions.stem: A car moves at 10 m/s around a circle of radius 5.0 m. What is its centripetal acceleration?
questions.explanation: $a_c = v^2/r = 100/5.0 = 20$ m/s², directed toward the center. 2.0 m/s² is $v/r$ (that's the angular speed in rad/s).

questions.stem: A ball whirled in a horizontal circle on a string is released when it is at the north side of the circle, moving east. Immediately after release it moves
questions.explanation: With the string's inward force gone, there's no horizontal force, so the ball continues with the velocity it had: east, tangent to the circle. It doesn't fly radially outward.

questions.stem: What is the maximum speed for a car on a flat curve of radius 80 m if $\mu_s = 0.50$? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: Static friction supplies the inward force: $\mu_s mg = mv^2/r$, so $v = \sqrt{\mu_s g r} = \sqrt{0.50(9.8)(80)} = \sqrt{392} = 19.8$ m/s.

questions.stem: At what angle should a curve of radius 80 m be banked so that cars at 20 m/s need no friction? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: $\tan\theta = v^2/(rg) = 400/784 = 0.510$, so $\theta = 27.0^\circ$. 63° inverts the ratio.

questions.stem: What is the minimum speed at the top of a vertical loop of radius 10 m for a roller coaster car to stay on the track? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: At the minimum, the normal force is zero and gravity alone provides the inward force: $mg = mv^2/r$, so $v = \sqrt{gr} = \sqrt{98} = 9.9$ m/s.

questions.stem: At the bottom of a vertical loop, the normal force on a rider is
questions.explanation: The net force must point up (toward the center): $n - mg = mv^2/r$, so $n = mg + mv^2/r > mg$. That's why riders feel heavy at the bottom.

questions.stem: If a car takes the same curve at twice the speed, the inward force needed becomes
questions.explanation: $F = mv^2/r$ depends on $v^2$, so doubling $v$ quadruples the required force.

questions.stem: An object moves in a circle of radius 2.0 m with a period of 4.0 s. What is its speed?
A 0.50 kg puck on frictionless ice moves in a circle of radius 0.80 m at 4.0 m/s, held by a horizontal string. What is the tension?
questions.explanation: The string alone provides the inward force: $T = mv^2/r = 0.50(16)/0.80 = 10$ N.

questions.stem: A wheel of radius 0.30 m spins at 600 rpm. What is the speed of a point on its rim?
questions.explanation: $f = 600/60 = 10$ rev/s, so $v = 2\pi rf = 2\pi(0.30)(10) = 18.8$ m/s. Using 600 rev/s (forgetting to divide by 60) gives 1130 m/s; leaving out $2\pi$ gives 3.0 m/s, and leaving out only $\pi$ gives 6.0 m/s.

questions.stem: Which statement about "centripetal force" is correct?
choices: It is an extra force that appears whenever objects move in circles
It points outward from the center
It exists only on banked curves
It is the name for the net inward force supplied by real forces such as tension, friction or gravity
questions.explanation: Centripetal force is a role played by real forces. You never add a separate centripetal arrow to a free-body diagram; you set the net inward force equal to $mv^2/r$.

questions.stem: A 40 N force pulls a wagon 10 m along level ground. The force is directed $60^\circ$ above the horizontal. How much work does it do?
questions.explanation: $W = Fd\cos\theta = 40(10)\cos 60^\circ = 200$ J. Only the horizontal component (20 N) acts along the displacement. 346 J uses $\sin 60^\circ$. 400 J ignores the angle.

questions.stem: A ball on a string moves in a horizontal circle at constant speed. How much work does the string tension do during one revolution?
choices: Zero, because the tension is perpendicular to the motion
Positive, because the tension pulls the ball
Negative, because the tension points inward
questions.explanation: The tension is always perpendicular to the velocity ($\cos 90^\circ = 0$), so it does no work, consistent with the speed (and kinetic energy) staying constant.

questions.stem: A 1000 kg car moves at 20 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?
questions.explanation: $K = \tfrac12mv^2 = \tfrac12(1000)(20)^2 = 200\,000$ J $= 200$ kJ. Forgetting the $\tfrac12$ gives 400 kJ; forgetting to square gives 10 kJ.

questions.stem: A 2.0 kg box at rest has 100 J of net work done on it. What is its final speed?
questions.explanation: $W_{\text{net}} = \tfrac12mv^2$: $100 = \tfrac12(2.0)v^2$, so $v^2 = 100$ and $v = 10$ m/s. 7.1 m/s forgets the $\tfrac12$. 100 m/s forgets the square root; 50 m/s is $W/m$.

questions.stem: If an object's speed triples, its kinetic energy
questions.explanation: $K \propto v^2$, so tripling $v$ multiplies $K$ by $3^2 = 9$.

questions.stem: How much work is needed to stretch a spring with $k = 200$ N/m by 0.15 m from its natural length?
questions.explanation: $W = \tfrac12kx^2 = \tfrac12(200)(0.15)^2 = 2.25$ J. Using $kx^2$ gives 4.5 J; $kx = 30$ N is the final force, not the work.

questions.stem: A box slides across a rough floor and comes to rest. The work done on it by kinetic friction is
choices: equal to its weight times the distance
questions.explanation: Friction points opposite the displacement ($\theta = 180^\circ$), so $W = -f_kd < 0$. That negative net work is what removes the kinetic energy.

questions.stem: The force on a cart, along its motion, rises steadily from 0 at $x = 0$ to 30 N at $x = 4.0$ m. How much work does the force do over those 4.0 m?
questions.explanation: The work is the area under the $F$–$x$ graph, here a triangle: $\tfrac12(4.0)(30) = 60$ J. 120 J uses the final force for the whole distance; 7.5 N/m is the slope of the graph, not an area; 15 J is the average force (15 N) without multiplying by the distance.

questions.stem: On a graph of force versus position, the work done by the force between two positions equals
choices: the force at the final position times the distance
the area under the graph between them
the average of the two forces
questions.explanation: Work is force times distance, which on an $F$–$x$ graph is an area. For a constant force it's a rectangle, $Fd$; for a spring it's a triangle, $\tfrac12kx^2$. The slope has units of N/m, not joules.

questions.stem: A weightlifter holds a 100 kg barbell motionless overhead for 5 s. How much work does she do on the barbell during that time?
questions.explanation: Work requires a displacement. The barbell doesn't move, so $W = 0$ even though she exerts 980 N and her muscles use chemical energy.

questions.stem: A car brakes to a stop with a constant friction force. If it had been going twice as fast, with the same braking force, its stopping distance would
questions.explanation: Work–energy theorem: $-fd = 0 - \tfrac12mv^2$, so $d = \dfrac{mv^2}{2f} \propto v^2$. Doubling $v$ multiplies $d$ by $2^2 = 4$. Doubling would be true only if $d$ were proportional to $v$.

questions.stem: A spring with $k = 300$ N/m is already stretched 0.10 m. How much work is needed to stretch it further, to 0.20 m?
questions.explanation: $W = \tfrac12kx_2^2 - \tfrac12kx_1^2 = 150(0.040 - 0.010) = 4.5$ J, the trapezoid area under the $F$–$x$ line. 1.5 J uses $\tfrac12k(\Delta x)^2$, as if the spring started unstretched; 6.0 J is the work from 0 to 0.20 m; 30 N is the extra force, $k\Delta x$, not a work.

questions.stem: A sled starts from rest at the top of a frictionless hill 5.0 m high. What is its speed at the bottom? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: $mgh = \tfrac12mv^2$, so $v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{98} = 9.9$ m/s. 7.0 m/s is $\sqrt{gh}$, missing the 2. The mass and the hill's shape don't matter. 98 is $2gh$ before taking the square root, and 49 is $gh$.

questions.stem: Two identical balls are released from the same height: one slides down a steep frictionless ramp, the other down a gentle frictionless ramp. At the bottom,
questions.explanation: Gravity's work depends only on the height drop and the normal force does no work, so both reach $v = \sqrt{2gh}$. The steep ramp just gets there sooner.

questions.stem: A pendulum bob is released from rest 0.80 m above its lowest point. Ignoring air resistance, how fast does it move at the bottom? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: The string tension is perpendicular to the motion and does no work, so $v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2(9.8)(0.80)} = 3.96$ m/s. 2.8 m/s is $\sqrt{gh}$ (missing the 2); 15.7 is $2gh$, which is $v^2$, not $v$.

questions.stem: A 3.0 kg block slides down a 2.0 m high ramp from rest and reaches the bottom at 5.0 m/s. How much work did friction do? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: $U_i = 3.0(9.8)(2.0) = 58.8$ J and $K_f = \tfrac12(3.0)(25) = 37.5$ J. $W_{\text{nc}} = K_f - U_i = -21.3$ J. Friction removes mechanical energy, so its work is negative. −37.5 J is just $K_f$ and −58.8 J just $U_i$; +21.3 J has the wrong sign.

questions.stem: Which force is nonconservative?
choices: The force of an ideal spring
questions.explanation: The work done by kinetic friction depends on the path length (longer path, more negative work), so no potential energy can be defined for it. Gravity, springs and electrostatic forces are conservative.

questions.stem: A 60 kg student runs up stairs that rise 5.0 m in 10 s. What average power does she deliver against gravity? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: $P = \dfrac{mgh}{t} = \dfrac{60(9.8)(5.0)}{10} = 294$ W, about 0.4 hp. 30 W leaves out $g$; 2940 J is the work, not divided by the time; 588 N is her weight.

questions.stem: A car's engine delivers 15 kW while the car moves at a steady 30 m/s. What is the total resistive force on the car?
questions.explanation: At constant speed the driving force equals the resistive force, and $P = Fv$: $F = 15\,000/30 = 500$ N. 450 kN multiplies instead of dividing; 0.50 N forgets to convert kW to W; 2.0 N divides the speed by the power in kW.

questions.stem: A household bill charges for kilowatt-hours. A kilowatt-hour is a unit of
questions.explanation: 1 kWh is the energy used at 1000 W for 3600 s: $3.6\times10^6$ J. It's an energy unit, not a power.

questions.stem: On a particle's potential energy graph, $U$ rises steadily from 2.0 J at $x = 0$ to 8.0 J at $x = 3.0$ m. What force acts on the particle in that region?
questions.explanation: The force is the negative of the graph's slope. Slope $= (8.0 - 2.0)/3.0 = 2.0$ J/m $= 2.0$ N, so $F = -2.0$ N: 2.0 N toward $-x$, downhill on the graph. The $+x$ answer forgets the minus sign; 6.0 N is the change in $U$ without dividing by the distance.

questions.stem: A 0.50 kg ball is launched straight up by a spring ($k = 400$ N/m) compressed 0.20 m. How high above the release point does it rise? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: $\tfrac12kx^2 = \tfrac12(400)(0.04) = 8.0$ J $= mgh$, so $h = 8.0/(0.50 \times 9.8) = 1.63$ m. 3.3 m drops the $\tfrac12$ in the spring energy; 16 m leaves out $g$; 0.82 m leaves out the mass.

questions.stem: On a potential energy diagram, a particle with total energy $E$ has a turning point where
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy is $E - U(x)$; at a turning point the particle stops, so $K = 0$ and $U = E$. Minima of $U$ (and other flat spots on the graph) are equilibrium points, where the force is zero, not turning points.

questions.stem: Motor A lifts a crate to a shelf in 10 s. Motor B lifts an identical crate to the same shelf in 5.0 s, at constant speed in both cases. Compared with motor A, motor B does
choices: the same work at twice the power
twice the work at the same power
twice the work at twice the power
the same work at half the power
questions.explanation: The work against gravity, $mgh$, is the same for both. Power is work divided by time, $P = W/\Delta t$, so doing it in half the time takes twice the power. Confusing power with energy leads to the "twice the work" choices.

questions.stem: A spring launcher fires a ball straight up. If the spring is compressed twice as far, how high does the ball rise compared with before? (Ignore air resistance and the small height change during launch.)
questions.explanation: All the spring energy $\tfrac12kx^2$ becomes $mgh$, so $h \propto x^2$. Doubling $x$ gives $2^2 = 4$ times the height. "Twice as high" treats the stored energy as proportional to $x$, like the force.

questions.stem: A 0.50 kg ball moving at 8.0 m/s hits a wall and rebounds at 6.0 m/s. What is the magnitude of the impulse from the wall?
questions.explanation: Taking the rebound direction as positive, $\Delta p = 0.50(6.0 - (-8.0)) = 7.0$ N·s. Ignoring the change of direction gives $0.50(8.0 - 6.0) = 1.0$ N·s.

questions.stem: Air bags reduce injuries in a crash mainly because they
choices: reduce the passenger's change in momentum
increase the time over which the passenger stops, reducing the average force
questions.explanation: The passenger's $\Delta p$ is fixed by the initial speed. Impulse $F_{\text{avg}}\Delta t = \Delta p$, so a longer stopping time means a smaller average force.

questions.stem: A 4.0 kg rifle fires a 20 g bullet at 400 m/s. What is the rifle's recoil speed?
questions.explanation: Total momentum stays zero: $0.020(400) = 4.0\,v$, so $v = 2.0$ m/s backward. 20 m/s and 0.20 m/s come from converting 20 g to kilograms wrongly; 8.0 is the bullet's momentum in kg·m/s, not a speed.

questions.stem: A 1.0 kg mass is at $x = 0$ and a 3.0 kg mass is at $x = 4.0$ m. Where is the center of mass?
questions.explanation: $x_{\text{cm}} = \dfrac{1.0(0) + 3.0(4.0)}{4.0} = 3.0$ m, closer to the heavier mass. 1.0 m weights the positions the wrong way round.

questions.stem: Under what condition is the total momentum of a system conserved?
choices: When the net external force on the system is zero
questions.explanation: Internal forces cancel in third-law pairs, so only a net external force can change total momentum. Kinetic energy conservation is a separate condition.

questions.stem: A truck and a bicycle have the same momentum. Which has more kinetic energy?
choices: They have the same kinetic energy
questions.explanation: $K = p^2/(2m)$. With the same $p$, the smaller mass has the larger kinetic energy (it must be moving much faster).

questions.stem: A firework shell moving along a parabolic path explodes into many fragments in midair. Until any fragment lands, the center of mass of the fragments
questions.explanation: The explosion forces are internal. The only external force is gravity, so $\vec F_{\text{ext}} = M\vec a_{\text{cm}}$ gives $\vec a_{\text{cm}} = \vec g$, exactly as before the explosion.

questions.stem: During a kick, the force on a ball rises steadily from 0 to 800 N in 2.0 ms, then falls steadily back to 0 in another 2.0 ms. What impulse does the ball receive?
questions.explanation: Impulse is the area under the $F$–$t$ graph, a triangle: $\tfrac12(4.0\times10^{-3}\text{ s})(800\text{ N}) = 1.6$ N·s. 3.2 N·s uses the peak force for the whole 4.0 ms; 0.80 N·s counts only the rising half; 1600 N·s leaves the time in milliseconds.

questions.stem: A 0.15 kg ball is caught: it goes from 30 m/s to rest in 0.050 s. What is the average force on the catcher's glove?
questions.explanation: $F_{\text{avg}} = \Delta p/\Delta t = 0.15(30)/0.050 = 90$ N. (4.5 kg·m/s is the momentum change, not the force.) 600 N ignores the mass ($v/\Delta t$); 1350 N divides the kinetic energy by the time.

questions.stem: A uniform 2.0 m rod of mass 3.0 kg has a small 1.0 kg ball fixed to one end. How far from the other (bare) end is the center of mass of the rod and ball?
questions.explanation: Treat the rod as 3.0 kg at its midpoint (1.0 m from the bare end) and the ball as 1.0 kg at 2.0 m: $x_{\text{cm}} = \dfrac{3.0(1.0) + 1.0(2.0)}{4.0} = 1.25$ m. 1.0 m ignores the ball; 1.5 m averages the two positions without weighting by mass; 0.75 m is the distance from the ball's end.

questions.stem: A 2.0 kg cart moving at 3.0 m/s collides with a 1.0 kg cart at rest, and they stick together. What is their final speed?
questions.explanation: $2.0(3.0) = 3.0\,v_f$, so $v_f = 2.0$ m/s. Momentum is conserved in every collision. 3.0 m/s ignores the second cart; 1.0 m/s divides by the wrong mass.

questions.stem: In the previous collision (2.0 kg at 3.0 m/s sticking to 1.0 kg at rest), how much kinetic energy is lost?
questions.explanation: $K_i = \tfrac12(2.0)(9.0) = 9.0$ J; $K_f = \tfrac12(3.0)(4.0) = 6.0$ J. Lost: 3.0 J, turned into heat and deformation. 9.0 J and 6.0 J are the kinetic energies before and after, not the loss.

questions.stem: Which quantity is conserved in an elastic collision but not in a perfectly inelastic one?
questions.explanation: Momentum (and total energy, and mass) is conserved in both. Only in an elastic collision is kinetic energy also conserved.

questions.stem: A 2.0 kg ball moving at 6.0 m/s collides elastically head-on with a 1.0 kg ball at rest. What are the final velocities?
questions.explanation: $v_{1f} = \dfrac{2 - 1}{3}(6.0) = 2.0$ m/s; $v_{2f} = \dfrac{2(2)}{3}(6.0) = 8.0$ m/s. Check: relative velocity 6.0 before, $8.0 - 2.0 = 6.0$ after. 4.0 m/s each would be the perfectly inelastic result.

questions.stem: Two identical billiard balls collide elastically head-on; one was at rest. Afterward,
choices: both move at half the original speed
the moving ball stops and the other moves off with its velocity
questions.explanation: With $m_1 = m_2$: $v_{1f} = 0$ and $v_{2f} = v_{1i}$. Equal masses exchange velocities in a head-on elastic collision.

questions.stem: In a ballistic pendulum problem, why can't you use conservation of mechanical energy from the instant before the bullet hits until the block reaches its highest point?
choices: Because momentum is not conserved during the swing
Because gravity does work during the collision
Because the collision is perfectly inelastic and converts much kinetic energy to heat
Because the strings do work on the block
questions.explanation: Use momentum conservation for the collision (where kinetic energy is lost) and energy conservation only for the swing afterward.

questions.stem: An 8.0 g bullet embeds in a 1.992 kg block hanging as a pendulum, which then rises 5.0 cm. What was the bullet's speed? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: Swing: $V = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2(9.8)(0.050)} = 0.990$ m/s. Collision: $v = \dfrac{m + M}{m}V = \dfrac{2.000}{0.008}(0.990) = 248$ m/s. 0.99 m/s is the block's speed, not the bullet's; 15.7 m/s wrongly applies energy conservation through the collision, $\tfrac12mv^2 = (m + M)gh$.

questions.stem: A 5.0 kg object moving east at 2.0 m/s collides with a 3.0 kg object moving north at 4.0 m/s, and they stick. How fast does the wreckage move?
questions.explanation: $p_x = 5.0(2.0) = 10$ kg·m/s and $p_y = 3.0(4.0) = 12$ kg·m/s, so $p = \sqrt{100 + 144} = 15.6$ kg·m/s. Dividing by the total mass, 8.0 kg: $v = 1.95$ m/s. Adding the momenta as scalars gives $22/8 = 2.75$ m/s; dividing by only 5.0 kg gives 3.12 m/s; 15.6 is the momentum, not the speed.

questions.stem: A tennis ball (light) hits a stationary bowling ball (heavy) head-on elastically. The tennis ball
choices: continues forward at about the same speed
moves forward at twice its speed
bounces back with nearly its original speed
questions.explanation: With $m_1 \ll m_2$, $v_{1f} = \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}v_{1i} \approx -v_{1i}$: the light ball rebounds, and the heavy ball barely moves.

questions.stem: For an elastic head-on collision, the relative velocity of the two objects
choices: is reversed, with the same magnitude
questions.explanation: Combining momentum and kinetic energy conservation gives $v_{1i} - v_{2i} = -(v_{1f} - v_{2f})$: they separate as fast as they approached (coefficient of restitution 1).

questions.stem: In the center-of-mass frame, which part of the kinetic energy can be lost in a collision?
choices: Only the kinetic energy of motion relative to the CM
questions.explanation: $v_{\text{cm}}$ can't change (momentum is conserved), so $\tfrac12Mv_{\text{cm}}^2$ must remain. Only the relative kinetic energy can be converted; a perfectly inelastic collision converts all of it.

questions.stem: A wheel turns at 120 rpm. What is its angular velocity in rad/s?
questions.explanation: $120\,\tfrac{\text{rev}}{\text{min}} \times \tfrac{2\pi\text{ rad}}{1\text{ rev}} \times \tfrac{1\text{ min}}{60\text{ s}} = 4\pi = 12.6$ rad/s. 2.0 is rev/s; 720 is degrees per second.

questions.stem: A wheel speeds up uniformly from rest to 20 rad/s in 5.0 s. How many revolutions does it make?
questions.explanation: $\Delta\theta = \tfrac12(\omega_0 + \omega)t = \tfrac12(0 + 20)(5.0) = 50$ rad $= 50/2\pi = 7.96 \approx 8.0$ rev. 50 is the answer in radians, not revolutions. 4.0 is the angular acceleration in rad/s²; 16 divides by $\pi$ instead of $2\pi$.

questions.stem: A disk of radius 0.40 m spins at 10 rad/s. What are the speed and centripetal acceleration of a point on its rim?
questions.explanation: $v = r\omega = 0.40(10) = 4.0$ m/s; $a_c = r\omega^2 = 0.40(100) = 40$ m/s² (equivalently $v^2/r$). 25 m/s divides by $r$ instead of multiplying; 40 m/s and 4.0 m/s² swaps the two values.

questions.stem: A hoop and a solid disk have the same mass and radius. About their central axes, which has the larger moment of inertia, and why?
choices: The disk, because it has more material
They are equal, because $I$ depends only on mass and radius
The disk, because its mass is spread over a larger area
The hoop, because all its mass is at the maximum distance from the axis
questions.explanation: $I = \sum mr^2$ weights mass by the square of its distance from the axis. The hoop has $I = MR^2$; the disk, with much of its mass nearer the center, has $\tfrac12MR^2$.

questions.stem: A uniform rod of mass 3.0 kg and length 2.0 m rotates about one end. Use the parallel-axis theorem to find its moment of inertia.
questions.explanation: $I_{\text{cm}} = \tfrac1{12}ML^2 = 1.0$ kg·m². Shifting by $d = 1.0$ m: $I = 1.0 + 3.0(1.0)^2 = 4.0$ kg·m², matching $\tfrac13ML^2$. 1.0 kg·m² is $I_{\text{cm}}$ without the shift; 3.0 kg·m² is only the $Md^2$ term; 12 kg·m² treats all the mass as sitting at the far end.

questions.stem: Two 2.0 kg masses are fixed to the ends of a light 2.0 m rod. What is the moment of inertia about the rod's center?
questions.explanation: Each mass is 1.0 m from the center: $I = 2(2.0)(1.0)^2 = 4.0$ kg·m². Using the full rod length (2.0 m) as the distance gives 16 kg·m².

questions.stem: A 5.0 kg solid disk of radius 0.20 m spins at 20 rad/s. What is its rotational kinetic energy?
questions.explanation: $I = \tfrac12(5.0)(0.20)^2 = 0.10$ kg·m²; $K = \tfrac12I\omega^2 = \tfrac12(0.10)(400) = 20$ J. Using $I = MR^2$ gives 40 J.

questions.stem: Which quantity is the same for every point on a rigid wheel rotating about a fixed axle?
questions.explanation: Every point turns through the same angle in the same time, so $\omega$ (and $\theta$, $\alpha$) are shared. Linear speed $r\omega$ and centripetal acceleration $r\omega^2$ grow with distance from the axis.

questions.stem: A wheel's angular velocity rises steadily from 0 to 8.0 rad/s in 4.0 s. Through what angle does it turn in that time?
questions.explanation: The angle is the area under the $\omega$–$t$ graph, a triangle: $\tfrac12(4.0)(8.0) = 16$ rad. 32 rad uses the final angular velocity for the whole time; 2.0 is the slope (the angular acceleration in rad/s²); 2.5 is the number of revolutions ($16/2\pi$), not radians.

questions.stem: A wheel speeds up uniformly from 10 rad/s to 30 rad/s while turning through 100 rad. What is its angular acceleration?
questions.explanation: $\omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha\Delta\theta$: $900 = 100 + 2\alpha(100)$, so $\alpha = 800/200 = 4.0$ rad/s². 8.0 forgets the 2; 4.5 drops the $\omega_0^2$ term; 0.20 divides the change in $\omega$ by the angle, which has the wrong units.

questions.stem: A flywheel's angular speed is doubled. Its rotational kinetic energy
questions.explanation: $K = \tfrac12I\omega^2$ with $I$ fixed (same object, same axis), so $K \propto \omega^2$ and doubling $\omega$ gives $2^2 = 4$ times the energy.

questions.stem: A 50 N force is applied at the end of a 0.25 m wrench, at $30^\circ$ to the handle. What torque does it produce?
questions.explanation: $\tau = rF\sin\theta = 0.25(50)\sin 30^\circ = 6.25$ N·m. Only the perpendicular component (25 N) turns the wrench; using cosine gives 10.8 N·m.

questions.stem: Where and in what direction should you push a door to open it with the least force?
choices: Near the hinges, perpendicular to the door
At the edge far from the hinges, perpendicular to the door
At the far edge, pushing toward the hinges
questions.explanation: Torque $= rF\sin\theta$ is largest for the largest $r$ and $\theta = 90^\circ$. Pushing toward the hinges gives zero torque.

questions.stem: A 2.0 kg solid disk of radius 0.50 m on a frictionless axle has a 10 N force applied tangentially to its rim. What is its angular acceleration?
questions.explanation: $\tau = 0.50(10) = 5.0$ N·m; $I = \tfrac12(2.0)(0.50)^2 = 0.25$ kg·m²; $\alpha = \tau/I = 20$ rad/s². Using $I = MR^2$ gives 10 rad/s². 5.0 is the torque in N·m, not $\alpha$.

questions.stem: A 1.0 kg bucket hangs from a rope wound on a 2.0 kg solid cylinder (frictionless axle). What is the bucket's acceleration? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: $a = \dfrac{mg}{m + \tfrac12M} = \dfrac{9.8}{1.0 + 1.0} = 4.9$ m/s². 3.3 m/s² uses $m + M$, which would be right only for a hoop ($I = MR^2$), not a solid cylinder. 9.8 m/s² ignores the cylinder's inertia altogether.

questions.stem: Why are the rope tensions on the two sides of a pulley with mass different when the system accelerates?
choices: A net torque is needed to give the pulley angular acceleration
Friction in the rope changes the tension
The rope stretches more on one side
They are always equal; the difference is an approximation
questions.explanation: $(T_1 - T_2)R = I\alpha$. With $I > 0$ and $\alpha \ne 0$, the tensions must differ. Only a massless pulley has equal tensions.

questions.stem: An engine produces 250 N·m of torque at 3000 rpm. What power is that?
questions.explanation: $\omega = 3000(2\pi/60) = 314$ rad/s; $P = \tau\omega = 250(314) = 78.5$ kW. Using rpm directly gives 750 kW. 12.5 kW forgets the $2\pi$ in converting rpm.

questions.stem: A force $\vec F = 2\hat\imath + 5\hat\jmath$ N acts at $\vec r = 3\hat\imath + 1\hat\jmath$ m from an axis along $z$. What is $\tau_z$?
questions.explanation: $\tau_z = xF_y - yF_x = 3(5) - 1(2) = 13$ N·m (counterclockwise). 17 adds the terms instead of subtracting.

questions.stem: Which equation is the rotational analog of $\sum F = ma$?
questions.explanation: Net torque produces angular acceleration in proportion to the moment of inertia: $\sum\tau = I\alpha$. $L = I\omega$ is the analog of $p = mv$.

questions.stem: A constant 4.0 N·m torque turns a flywheel through 25 rad from rest. How much rotational kinetic energy does the flywheel gain (no friction)?
questions.explanation: $W = \tau\Delta\theta = 4.0(25) = 100$ J, and by the rotational work–energy theorem that all becomes $\tfrac12I\omega^2$. 50 J adds a stray $\tfrac12$; 6.25 divides the angle by the torque.

questions.stem: By the right-hand rule, a wheel spinning counterclockwise when viewed from above has a torque or angular velocity vector pointing
questions.explanation: Curl the fingers of your right hand counterclockwise (seen from above): your thumb points up. Counterclockwise in the $xy$ plane corresponds to $+\hat k$.

questions.stem: A solid sphere, a solid cylinder and a hoop roll without slipping from rest down the same incline. In what order do they reach the bottom?
questions.explanation: $v = \sqrt{2gh/(1 + c)}$ with $c = 0.4$ (sphere), $0.5$ (cylinder), $1$ (hoop). The smaller the fraction of energy tied up in rotation, the faster. Mass and radius don't matter.

questions.stem: A solid cylinder rolls without slipping from rest down a ramp 2.0 m high. What is its speed at the bottom? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: $Mgh = \tfrac12(1 + \tfrac12)Mv^2$, so $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2gh}{1.5}} = \sqrt{26.1} = 5.1$ m/s. 6.3 m/s ignores rotation; 4.4 m/s uses the hoop's $c = 1$; 5.3 m/s uses the solid sphere's $c = 0.4$.

questions.stem: A car tire rolls without slipping at 20 m/s. How fast is the top of the tire moving relative to the road?
questions.explanation: The top moves at $v_{\text{cm}} + R\omega = 2v_{\text{cm}} = 40$ m/s; the contact point is momentarily at rest.

questions.stem: For a ball rolling without slipping down a ramp, the work done by static friction is
choices: zero, because the contact point does not slide
questions.explanation: Static friction acts at the contact point, which is instantaneously at rest, so it does no work. It redistributes energy between translation and rotation, and mechanical energy is conserved.

questions.stem: A skater spinning at 3.0 rev/s with $I = 5.0$ kg·m² pulls in her arms, reducing $I$ to 1.5 kg·m². Her new spin rate is
questions.explanation: No external torque, so $I_i\omega_i = I_f\omega_f$: $\omega_f = (5.0/1.5)(3.0) = 10$ rev/s. 0.9 rev/s inverts the ratio.

questions.stem: When the skater above pulls her arms in, her rotational kinetic energy
choices: stays the same, because angular momentum is conserved
increases, because her muscles do work
questions.explanation: $K = L^2/(2I)$. With $L$ fixed and $I$ smaller, $K$ increases (here by a factor of 3.3). The energy comes from the work her arms do pulling mass inward.

questions.stem: A disk with $I = 0.020$ kg·m² spinning at 40 rad/s has an identical non-spinning disk dropped onto it; they spin together. What is the final angular speed?
questions.explanation: $I\omega = 2I\omega_f$, so $\omega_f = 20$ rad/s. (28 rad/s would conserve kinetic energy instead, which this "rotational sticking collision" doesn't.)

questions.stem: Kepler's second law (equal areas in equal times) follows from conservation of
questions.explanation: Gravity points toward the Sun, so it exerts no torque about the Sun. The planet's angular momentum $L = mvr_\perp$ is constant, and the area swept per unit time is $L/(2m)$.

questions.stem: A spinning gyroscope supported at one end of its axle doesn't fall; its axle slowly circles horizontally. This happens because gravity's torque
choices: is zero for a spinning object
is balanced by a centrifugal force
is perpendicular to $\vec L$, so it changes the direction of $\vec L$ rather than its size
questions.explanation: Torque changes angular momentum: $\Delta\vec L = \vec\tau\,\Delta t$. Gravity's torque about the support is horizontal, perpendicular to $\vec L$, so it swings $\vec L$ (and the axle) sideways instead of tipping it down: precession. There is no centrifugal force to balance it, and the torque is not zero.

questions.stem: What fraction of a rolling solid sphere's kinetic energy is rotational?
questions.explanation: $K_{\text{rot}} = \tfrac12\cdot\tfrac25MR^2\omega^2 = \tfrac15Mv^2$ and $K_{\text{total}} = \tfrac12(1.4)Mv^2 = 0.7Mv^2$. Ratio: $0.2/0.7 = 2/7$. 2/5 is the ratio $I/(MR^2)$, not an energy fraction; 5/7 is the translational fraction.

questions.stem: A 25 kg child sits 2.0 m from the center pivot of a uniform seesaw. Where must a 40 kg child sit to balance it?
questions.explanation: Equal torques: $25g(2.0) = 40g\,x$, so $x = 1.25$ m. The heavier child sits closer. 3.2 m inverts the mass ratio; 2.0 m balances weights instead of torques.

questions.stem: Which conditions must hold for an extended rigid object to be in static equilibrium?
choices: Zero net force and zero net torque
questions.explanation: Zero net force prevents translational acceleration and zero net torque prevents angular acceleration. Both are needed (two equal, opposite forces at different points give zero net force but a nonzero torque).

questions.stem: A uniform 4.0 m, 100 N beam rests on supports at its ends. A 600 N load sits 1.0 m from the left end. What force does the right support exert?
questions.explanation: Torques about the left end: $F_R(4.0) = 100(2.0) + 600(1.0)$, so $F_R = 200$ N. Then $F_L = 700 - 200 = 500$ N. The support nearer the load carries more. 350 N splits the total load evenly, ignoring where the crate sits.

questions.stem: When solving for support forces, why is it smart to take torques about a point where an unknown force acts?
choices: Because that point is the center of mass
Because that force then has zero lever arm and drops out of the torque equation
Because torques are only zero about that point
Because forces there are always zero
questions.explanation: In equilibrium the net torque is zero about every point, so you may choose any pivot. Choosing one where an unknown acts eliminates it from that equation.

questions.stem: A box on a ramp is about to tip over (rather than slide). At that moment its center of gravity is
choices: directly above the lower edge of its base
directly above the center of its base
above the upper edge of its base
questions.explanation: An object tips when gravity's line of action passes beyond the edge of its base. At the tipping point it passes exactly through the lower edge, so gravity's torque about that edge is zero.

questions.stem: A uniform horizontal beam of weight $W$ is hinged at the wall and held by a cable from its far end at angle $\theta$ above the beam. The cable tension is
questions.explanation: Torques about the hinge with beam length $L$: $T\sin\theta\cdot L = W\cdot\tfrac L2$, so $T = \dfrac{W}{2\sin\theta}$. The beam's weight acts at its center, not its end.

questions.stem: In a hinged-beam problem, which forces can the hinge exert on the beam?
choices: Only a force along the beam
No force; it only allows rotation
questions.explanation: A hinge (pin) can push or pull in any direction in the plane, so treat its force as two unknown components. It exerts no torque about its own axis.

questions.stem: A uniform 2.0 m board of mass 10 kg sticks out horizontally over a ledge with 0.50 m overhanging. How far past the edge can a 20 kg child walk before the board tips?
questions.explanation: The board's center is 0.50 m behind the edge (1.0 m from either end, the edge at 1.5 m from the back end). Tipping about the edge: $20g\,x = 10g(0.50)$, so $x = 0.25$ m past the edge.

questions.stem: A beam carries a load that increases linearly from zero at one end to $w_0$ (N/m) at the other, over length $L$. The total load and where it effectively acts are
questions.explanation: The total load is the area under the load-per-meter graph, a triangle: $\tfrac12w_0L$. It acts at the triangle's centroid, $\tfrac23L$ from the zero end, toward the heavier end. $w_0L$ treats the whole beam as carrying the maximum load; $L/2$ would be right only for a uniform load.

questions.stem: Why are racing cars built low and wide?
choices: To keep the center of gravity well inside the base so they resist tipping
questions.explanation: A low center of gravity and a wide base mean the car must tilt much farther before the center of gravity passes beyond the wheels' contact line, so cornering forces are less likely to roll it over.

questions.stem: A steel wire 2.0 mm in diameter supports a 500 N load. What is the tensile stress in the wire?
questions.explanation: The radius is 1.0 mm, so $A = \pi(1.0\times10^{-3})^2 = 3.14\times10^{-6}$ m² and the stress is $500/(3.14\times10^{-6}) = 1.6\times10^{8}$ Pa. Using the diameter as the radius makes the area 4 times too big and gives $4.0\times10^{7}$ Pa. Taking the area as $d^2$ (no $\pi/4$) gives $1.3\times10^{8}$ Pa. Leaving the area in mm² (3.14 mm²) gives 160 Pa.

questions.stem: A 3.0 m aluminum rod ($Y = 7.0\times10^{10}$ Pa) is under a tensile stress of $1.4\times10^{7}$ Pa. How much does it stretch?
questions.explanation: Strain $= 1.4\times10^{7}/7.0\times10^{10} = 2.0\times10^{-4}$, so $\Delta L = (2.0\times10^{-4})(3.0\text{ m}) = 6.0\times10^{-4}$ m $= 0.60$ mm. Reading the strain itself as the stretch in meters gives 0.20 mm (the length was never multiplied in). Dividing by the length instead of multiplying gives 0.067 mm. Dividing $Y$ by the stress (upside down) gives the absurd 15 km.

questions.stem: The Young's modulus of a metal rod depends on
choices: the cross-sectional area of the rod
the size of the load, as long as it is small
only the material the rod is made of
questions.explanation: Stress divides out the area and strain divides out the length, so $Y = (F/A)/(\Delta L/L_0)$ is a property of the material alone. A longer or thinner rod does stretch more, but that shows up in $\Delta L = FL_0/(YA)$, not in $Y$. Within the linear range the ratio is the same for every small load.

questions.stem: What is the elastic limit of a material?
choices: The stress at which the material breaks
The largest stress after which the material still returns fully to its original shape
The stress at which the strain reaches 1
The stress at which Young's modulus drops to zero
questions.explanation: Below the elastic limit the deformation is elastic: remove the load and the object springs back. Beyond it the deformation is partly permanent (plastic). Breaking happens later, at or after the ultimate strength, so confusing the two is the usual mistake. A strain of 1 (doubling in length) is far beyond what metals reach, and the modulus is the slope of the straight part, not something that drops to zero at a particular stress.

questions.stem: Wires A and B are made of the same metal and carry the same load. Wire B is twice as long as A and has twice the diameter. How does B's stretch compare with A's?
questions.explanation: $\Delta L = FL_0/(YA)$ with $A \propto d^2$. Doubling $L_0$ doubles the stretch; doubling $d$ quadruples $A$, quartering it. Net: $2/4 = \tfrac12$. Ignoring the area change gives 2 times; treating doubled diameter as doubled area gives the same stretch; ignoring the doubled length gives one quarter.

questions.stem: A rubber block 3.0 cm thick has a square top face 10 cm on a side and a shear modulus of $6.0\times10^{5}$ Pa. Its bottom is glued down, and a 120 N force acts along its top face. How far does the top shift sideways?
questions.explanation: The force lies along the top face, $A = (0.10)^2 = 0.010$ m². $\Delta x = FL_0/(SA) = (120)(0.030)/[(6.0\times10^{5})(0.010)] = 6.0\times10^{-4}$ m $= 0.60$ mm. Using the side face ($0.10\times0.030$ m²) as the area gives 2.0 mm. Leaving out $L_0$ gives the strain 0.020, misread as 2.0 cm. Converting 3.0 cm as 0.30 m gives 6.0 mm.

questions.stem: Water has a bulk modulus of $2.2\times10^{9}$ Pa. What increase in pressure compresses a sample of water by 1.0% of its volume?
questions.explanation: $\Delta P = B\,|\Delta V|/V_0 = (2.2\times10^{9})(0.010) = 2.2\times10^{7}$ Pa, about 220 atmospheres. Giving $B$ itself forgets to multiply by the fractional change. Using 0.0001 (treating 1.0% as 0.01%) gives $2.2\times10^{5}$ Pa, and dividing by 0.010 instead of multiplying gives $2.2\times10^{11}$ Pa.

questions.stem: Which statement about a liquid such as water is correct?
choices: It has a large shear modulus, so it resists sideways forces
It has no bulk modulus, so it is easy to compress
It has a bulk modulus but no shear modulus, so it flows under a sideways force
It has about the same shear modulus as steel
questions.explanation: A liquid resists being squeezed (water's bulk modulus is $2.2\times10^{9}$ Pa, so it is hard to compress), but it can't hold a sideways shear: it just flows. Having no shear modulus is what makes something a fluid.

questions.stem: A steel wire ($Y = 2.0\times10^{11}$ Pa) is 2.0 m long with a cross-sectional area of $1.0\times10^{-6}$ m². Treated as a spring, what is its spring constant?
questions.explanation: From $F = (YA/L_0)\Delta L$, $k = YA/L_0 = (2.0\times10^{11})(1.0\times10^{-6})/2.0 = 1.0\times10^{5}$ N/m. Multiplying by the length instead of dividing gives $4.0\times10^{5}$. Leaving out the area gives $1.0\times10^{11}$, and inverting the whole expression gives $1.0\times10^{-5}$.

questions.stem: In the straight part of a metal's stress–strain graph, a stress of $1.5\times10^{8}$ Pa produces a strain of 0.075%. What is the metal's Young's modulus?
questions.explanation: A strain of 0.075% is $7.5\times10^{-4}$. $Y = \text{stress}/\text{strain} = 1.5\times10^{8}/7.5\times10^{-4} = 2.0\times10^{11}$ Pa (steel). Using 0.075 without converting the percent gives $2.0\times10^{9}$. Dividing strain by stress gives $5.0\times10^{-12}$, and multiplying them gives $1.1\times10^{5}$.

questions.stem: A steel rod 1.0 cm in diameter has an elastic limit of $2.5\times10^{8}$ Pa. What is the largest tension it can carry without being permanently stretched?
questions.explanation: $A = \pi(0.0050)^2 = 7.85\times10^{-5}$ m², so $F = (2.5\times10^{8})(7.85\times10^{-5}) = 2.0\times10^{4}$ N. Using the diameter as the radius gives $7.9\times10^{4}$ N; using $d^2$ as the area gives $2.5\times10^{4}$ N. Dividing by $g$ gives about $2.0\times10^{3}$, which is a mass in kilograms, not a force.

questions.stem: Concrete beams are usually built with steel rods cast inside them, mainly because concrete is
choices: strong in compression but weak in tension
weak in compression but strong in tension
questions.explanation: Concrete holds up well when squeezed but cracks easily when pulled. In a loaded beam the bottom side is stretched, so steel rods there carry the tension. Concrete is less stiff than steel ($3\times10^{10}$ Pa against $2.0\times10^{11}$ Pa), and as a solid it does resist shear.

questions.stem: If the distance between two masses is tripled, the gravitational force between them becomes
questions.explanation: $F \propto 1/r^2$, so tripling $r$ divides $F$ by $3^2 = 9$.

questions.stem: What is $g$ at a height above Earth's surface equal to one Earth radius? (Surface $g = 9.8$ m/s².)
questions.explanation: The distance from Earth's center doubles ($R \to 2R$), so $g$ falls by $2^2$: $9.8/4 = 2.45$ m/s². 4.9 m/s² divides by 2 instead of $2^2$, as if gravity fell off as $1/r$; 1.1 m/s² divides by $3^2$, as if the distance from the center had tripled.

questions.stem: Astronauts on the International Space Station float because
choices: there is no gravity in space
gravity there is about 1% of its surface value
the station's walls shield them from gravity
they and the station are in free fall together
questions.explanation: At 400 km, $g$ is still about 89% of its surface value. Everything in the station falls around Earth with the same acceleration, so nothing presses on the floor: apparent weightlessness.

questions.stem: What is the orbital speed of a satellite in a circular orbit of radius $1.27\times10^7$ m (two Earth radii) around Earth? ($GM_E = 3.98\times10^{14}$ m³/s²)
questions.explanation: $v = \sqrt{GM/r} = \sqrt{3.98\times10^{14}/1.27\times10^7} = \sqrt{3.13\times10^7} = 5.6\times10^3$ m/s. 7.9 km/s is the speed for an orbit at Earth's surface radius.

questions.stem: Planet B orbits a star at 4 times the orbital radius of planet A. How do their periods compare?
questions.explanation: Kepler's third law: $T^2 \propto r^3$, so $T_B/T_A = 4^{3/2} = 8$. $T_B = 16T_A$ uses $T \propto r^2$; $T_B = 4T_A$ uses $T \propto r$; $T_B = 2T_A$ uses $T \propto \sqrt r$.

questions.stem: Two satellites orbit Earth at the same radius; one has twice the mass of the other. Compared with the lighter one, the heavier satellite's orbital speed is
questions.explanation: $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$ depends only on the central mass and the radius; the satellite's mass cancels.

questions.stem: Find the escape speed from the Moon ($M = 7.35\times10^{22}$ kg, $R = 1.74\times10^6$ m, $G = 6.67\times10^{-11}$ N·m²/kg²).
questions.explanation: $v_{\text{esc}} = \sqrt{2GM/R} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2(6.67\times10^{-11})(7.35\times10^{22})}{1.74\times10^6}} = 2.37$ km/s. 1.68 km/s omits the 2 (that's the low-orbit speed).

questions.stem: According to Kepler's second law, a planet in an elliptical orbit moves fastest
questions.explanation: Equal areas in equal times means that near the Sun, where the radius is short, the planet must cover more arc per unit time. Equivalently $mvr_\perp$ is constant, so smaller $r$ means larger $v$.

questions.stem: Gravitational potential energy $U = -GMm/r$ is negative because
choices: the zero is chosen at infinite separation, and work must be done to separate the masses
it is measured below the surface
questions.explanation: With $U(\infty) = 0$, bringing masses together releases energy (gravity does positive work as they approach), so $U$ is lower, negative, at any finite separation. Weakness of gravity has nothing to do with the sign.

questions.stem: The total mechanical energy of a satellite in a circular orbit of radius $r$ is
questions.explanation: $K = \tfrac12mv^2 = \dfrac{GMm}{2r}$ and $U = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$, so $E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$: negative, meaning the satellite is bound.

questions.stem: What is the gravitational force between two 1000 kg masses whose centers are 1.0 m apart? ($G = 6.67\times10^{-11}$ N·m²/kg²)
questions.explanation: $F = Gm_1m_2/r^2 = (6.67\times10^{-11})(10^6)/1 = 6.67\times10^{-5}$ N, about the weight of a few grains of sand.

questions.stem: A 2.0 kg mass on a spring with $k = 50$ N/m oscillates. What is its period?
questions.explanation: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k} = 2\pi\sqrt{2.0/50} = 2\pi(0.20) = 1.26$ s. Inverting the ratio, $2\pi\sqrt{k/m}$, gives 31 s.

questions.stem: A mass on a spring oscillates with amplitude 5 cm. If the amplitude is increased to 10 cm, the period
questions.explanation: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$ has no amplitude in it. Twice the distance is covered with twice the force (and twice the speed), in the same time.

questions.stem: Where in its cycle does a mass in SHM have its maximum speed and where its maximum acceleration?
choices: Maximum speed at the endpoints, maximum acceleration at equilibrium
Maximum speed at equilibrium, maximum acceleration at the endpoints
questions.explanation: At equilibrium the spring force is zero (so $a = 0$) and all the energy is kinetic (maximum speed). At the endpoints the speed is zero and the restoring force, hence the acceleration, is largest.

questions.stem: What is the period of a simple pendulum 1.0 m long? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g} = 2\pi\sqrt{1.0/9.8} = 2.0$ s. 0.32 s leaves out the $2\pi$; 6.3 s leaves out $g$.

questions.stem: To double the period of a simple pendulum, you should
choices: double the mass of the bob
questions.explanation: $T \propto \sqrt{L}$, so doubling $T$ needs $4L$. The bob's mass and (small) amplitude don't affect the period.

questions.stem: A 2.0 kg mass on a spring ($k = 800$ N/m) oscillates with amplitude 0.050 m. What is its maximum speed?
