questions.explanation: $\omega = \sqrt{800/2.0} = 20$ rad/s, so $v_{\max} = A\omega = 0.050(20) = 1.0$ m/s. 20 m/s² is the maximum acceleration $A\omega^2$, not the speed.

questions.stem: A spring with $k = 100$ N/m oscillates with amplitude 0.20 m. What is the total mechanical energy?
questions.explanation: $E = \tfrac12kA^2 = \tfrac12(100)(0.20)^2 = 2.0$ J. It's all spring energy at the turning points and all kinetic at equilibrium. 20 is $kA$, a force in N; 4.0 J forgets the $\tfrac12$; 10 J uses $\tfrac12kA$ without squaring.

questions.stem: A child on a swing is pushed once per swing, exactly in step with its natural motion, and swings higher and higher. This is an example of
questions.explanation: Driving an oscillator at its natural frequency feeds in energy each cycle, building up a large amplitude: resonance.

questions.stem: An oscillator's acceleration is related to its displacement by $a = -36x$ (SI units). What is its period?
questions.explanation: Matching $a = -\omega^2x$ gives $\omega^2 = 36$, so $\omega = 6.0$ rad/s and $T = 2\pi/6.0 = 1.05$ s. 6.0 is $\omega$, not the period; 0.17 s is $1/6.0$, forgetting the $2\pi$.

questions.stem: A pendulum clock that keeps perfect time on Earth is taken to the Moon, where $g$ is about 1/6 as large. Its period becomes
questions.explanation: $T \propto 1/\sqrt g$, so with $g$ six times smaller the period is $\sqrt6 \approx 2.45$ times longer; the clock runs slow.

questions.stem: For $x(t) = 0.30\cos(4t)$ m, what is the maximum acceleration?
questions.explanation: Here $A = 0.30$ m and $\omega = 4$ rad/s, so $a_{\max} = A\omega^2 = 0.30(16) = 4.8$ m/s². 1.2 is $A\omega$, the maximum speed in m/s; 0.075 divides by $\omega$ instead of multiplying.

questions.stem: A sound wave in air (speed 340 m/s) has frequency 170 Hz. What is its wavelength?
questions.explanation: $\lambda = v/f = 340/170 = 2.0$ m. 0.50 m inverts the ratio.

questions.stem: A wave passes from a light rope into a heavy rope tied to it. Which property stays the same?
questions.explanation: Frequency is set by the source: each point of the junction must oscillate in step on both sides. The speed (and so the wavelength) changes with the medium.

questions.stem: In a longitudinal wave, the particles of the medium move
choices: parallel to the direction the wave travels
perpendicular to the direction the wave travels
along with the wave to the far end
questions.explanation: Longitudinal waves (like sound) consist of compressions and rarefactions along the direction of travel. Transverse waves (like waves on a string) move the medium perpendicular to the travel.

questions.stem: A string has linear mass density 0.010 kg/m and tension 100 N. What is the speed of waves on it?
questions.explanation: $v = \sqrt{F_T/\mu} = \sqrt{100/0.010} = \sqrt{10\,000} = 100$ m/s. 10 000 m/s forgets the square root; 1.0 m/s multiplies $F_T\mu$.

questions.stem: If the tension in a string is quadrupled, the wave speed
questions.explanation: $v = \sqrt{F_T/\mu}$, so $v \propto \sqrt{F_T}$: four times the tension gives twice the speed.

questions.stem: A 0.50 m string fixed at both ends carries waves at 100 m/s. What is its fundamental frequency?
questions.explanation: $f_1 = v/(2L) = 100/1.0 = 100$ Hz. Using $v/L$ gives 200 Hz; using $v/(4L)$ gives 50 Hz (that's for a closed pipe).

questions.stem: In a standing wave, the distance between adjacent nodes is
questions.explanation: Nodes of $\sin(kx)$ occur every $\pi/k = \lambda/2$. A node and the next antinode are $\lambda/4$ apart.

questions.stem: Two waves of amplitude 3 cm meet crest to trough at a point. The resulting displacement there is
questions.explanation: By superposition, $+3 + (-3) = 0$: complete destructive interference. Each wave continues unchanged afterward.

questions.stem: A wave is described by $y = 0.02\sin(4\pi x - 20\pi t)$ (SI units). What is its speed?
questions.explanation: $v = \omega/k = 20\pi/4\pi = 5.0$ m/s. (Here $\lambda = 2\pi/k = 0.5$ m and $f = \omega/2\pi = 10$ Hz; $f\lambda = 5.0$ ✓.)

questions.stem: If the amplitude of a wave is doubled (same frequency and medium), the power it carries
questions.explanation: Wave energy and power are proportional to amplitude squared, so $2^2 = 4$ times the power.

questions.stem: The third harmonic of a string fixed at both ends has how many nodes, counting the ends?
questions.explanation: The $n$th harmonic fits $n$ half-wavelengths, giving $n$ antinodes and $n + 1$ nodes. For $n = 3$: 4 nodes.

questions.stem: A sound has intensity $10^{-5}$ W/m². What is its intensity level? ($I_0 = 10^{-12}$ W/m²)
questions.explanation: $\beta = 10\log_{10}(10^{-5}/10^{-12}) = 10\log_{10}(10^7) = 70$ dB. Forgetting the factor 10 gives 7 dB.

questions.stem: Two identical machines each produce 70 dB at a certain spot. With both running, the level is
questions.explanation: Intensities add, not decibels: twice the intensity adds $10\log 2 = 3$ dB, giving 73 dB. 80 dB would need ten machines.

questions.stem: You move three times farther from a small speaker that produces 90 dB where you started. The new level is about
questions.explanation: Intensity falls as $1/r^2$: one-ninth. The level drops by $10\log 9 = 9.5$ dB, to about 80 dB. 87 dB subtracts only 3 dB; 30 dB divides the decibel level by 3, but decibels aren't proportional to intensity.

questions.stem: A pipe 0.50 m long is closed at one end. What is its fundamental frequency? ($v = 343$ m/s)
questions.explanation: Closed at one end: $f_1 = v/(4L) = 343/2.0 = 171.5$ Hz. 343 Hz would be the fundamental if both ends were open. 686 Hz is $v/L$; 85.8 Hz is $v/(8L)$.

questions.stem: Which harmonics can a pipe closed at one end produce?
choices: Only odd multiples of the fundamental
questions.explanation: A node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end require an odd number of quarter-wavelengths: $f_n = nv/(4L)$, $n = 1, 3, 5, \ldots$

questions.stem: A car horn emits 500 Hz. The car moves toward a stationary listener at 20 m/s. What frequency does the listener hear? ($v = 343$ m/s)
questions.explanation: Source approaching: $f' = f\dfrac{v}{v - v_s} = 500\dfrac{343}{323} = 531$ Hz. 529 Hz is the formula for a moving observer; 472 Hz uses $v + v_s$ (receding).

questions.stem: As a train passes you blowing its whistle at constant speed, the pitch you hear
choices: is higher while it approaches and drops as it moves away
is lower while it approaches and rises as it moves away
stays the same, only the loudness changes
questions.explanation: Approaching sources sound higher, receding ones lower. At constant speed each pitch is steady, with a quick drop as it passes.

questions.stem: A guitar string and a 440 Hz tuning fork sound together and produce 4 beats per second. The string's frequency is
questions.explanation: $f_{\text{beat}} = |f_1 - f_2| = 4$ Hz, so the string is 4 Hz away from 440 in an unknown direction. Tightening it slightly and listening to whether the beats speed up or slow down tells which.

questions.stem: The speed of sound in air increases with temperature because
choices: faster-moving molecules pass the disturbance along more quickly
questions.explanation: Sound is passed on by molecular collisions; higher temperature means faster molecules, so the wave travels faster ($v \approx 331 + 0.6\,T_C$ m/s).

questions.stem: A jet flies at Mach 2. What is the half-angle of its shock-wave cone?
questions.explanation: $\sin\theta = v/v_s = 1/2$, so $\theta = 30^\circ$. $60^\circ$ uses cosine instead of sine.

questions.stem: At the closed end of an organ pipe, the air's displacement and pressure variation are
choices: a displacement node and a pressure antinode
a displacement antinode and a pressure node
questions.explanation: The air can't move into the wall, so displacement is zero there; that's where compressions build up the largest pressure swings. Pressure and displacement waves are a quarter-cycle out of step.

questions.stem: What is the absolute pressure 20 m below the surface of fresh water? ($P_{\text{atm}} = 1.013\times10^5$ Pa, $g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: $P = P_{\text{atm}} + \rho gh = 1.013\times10^5 + 1000(9.8)(20) = 2.97\times10^5$ Pa (about 3 atm). $1.96\times10^5$ Pa is the gauge pressure only.

questions.stem: Three containers of different shapes are filled with water to the same depth. The pressure at the bottom is
choices: greatest in the one holding the most water
questions.explanation: Pressure in a static fluid depends only on depth: $P = P_0 + \rho gh$. Shape and total volume don't matter.

questions.stem: A hydraulic lift has a small piston of radius 5.0 cm and a large piston of radius 50 cm. A 100 N force on the small piston can support
questions.explanation: $F_2 = F_1(A_2/A_1) = 100(50/5.0)^2 = 100(100) = 10\,000$ N. Area scales with radius squared; using the radius ratio alone gives 1000 N.

questions.stem: A 50 N object with volume $2.0\times10^{-3}$ m³ is fully submerged in water. What is its apparent weight? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: $F_B = \rho_{\text{water}}Vg = 1000(2.0\times10^{-3})(9.8) = 19.6$ N up. Apparent weight $= 50 - 19.6 = 30.4$ N. 19.6 N is the buoyant force itself.

questions.stem: A block of wood with density 800 kg/m³ floats in water. What fraction of its volume is under water?
questions.explanation: A floating object displaces its own weight: $\rho_{\text{obj}}V = \rho_{\text{water}}V_{\text{sub}}$, so $V_{\text{sub}}/V = 800/1000 = 0.80$.

questions.stem: The buoyant force on a fully submerged object depends on
choices: the depth at which it is submerged
the volume of fluid it displaces and the fluid's density
questions.explanation: Archimedes: $F_B = \rho_{\text{fluid}}V_{\text{disp}}g$. A lead block and an aluminum block of the same volume feel the same buoyant force; depth doesn't matter for an incompressible fluid.

questions.stem: A tire gauge reads 220 kPa. The absolute pressure in the tire is about
questions.explanation: Gauges read pressure above atmospheric: absolute $= 220 + 101 = 321$ kPa.

questions.stem: Why does a mercury barometer stand about 760 mm tall at sea level, while a water barometer would need about 10.3 m?
choices: Mercury is about 13.6 times denser, so a shorter column has the same weight per area
Atmospheric pressure pushes harder on mercury
questions.explanation: The column height satisfies $P_{\text{atm}} = \rho gh$, so $h \propto 1/\rho$. Mercury (13 600 kg/m³) needs a column 13.6 times shorter than water.

questions.stem: The gauge pressure at the bottom of a tank of water is 30 kPa. Water is added until the depth is doubled. What is the absolute pressure at the bottom now? (Take $P_{\text{atm}} = 101$ kPa.)
questions.explanation: Gauge pressure is $\rho gh$, proportional to depth, so doubling the depth doubles it to 60 kPa. Absolute pressure adds the atmosphere: $101 + 60 = 161$ kPa. 60 kPa is the new gauge pressure alone; 262 kPa doubles the atmospheric part too, though the air above hasn't changed; 131 kPa is the absolute pressure before the water was added.

questions.stem: A steel ship floats even though steel is about 8 times denser than water because
choices: steel becomes less dense in salt water
the ship's average density, including the air inside its hull, is less than water's
the buoyant force on steel is larger than on other metals
questions.explanation: What matters is the average density of everything inside the hull's outline. A hull encloses a large volume of air, so it can displace its own weight of water before sinking too deep.

questions.stem: A pool's end wall is 4.0 m wide and the water against it is 2.5 m deep. What is the total force of the water on the wall, counting gauge pressure only? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: Gauge pressure rises steadily from 0 at the surface to $\rho gD = 1000(9.8)(2.5) = 24\,500$ Pa at the bottom, so the average is 12 250 Pa. Force $=$ average pressure $\times$ area $= 12\,250(4.0)(2.5) = 1.2\times10^5$ N. Using the bottom pressure over the whole wall gives $2.5\times10^5$ N; multiplying by the width alone instead of the area gives $4.9\times10^4$ N; adding atmospheric pressure (which pushes equally on the other side) gives about $1.1\times10^6$ N.

questions.stem: Water flows at 2.0 m/s through a pipe of diameter 3.0 cm, which narrows to 1.0 cm. What is the speed in the narrow part?
questions.explanation: Continuity: $v_2 = v_1(A_1/A_2) = 2.0(3.0/1.0)^2 = 18$ m/s. Using the diameter ratio without squaring gives 6.0 m/s.

questions.stem: In a horizontal pipe, where the flow speeds up through a constriction, the pressure
questions.explanation: Bernoulli: $P + \tfrac12\rho v^2$ is constant at the same height. Higher $v$ means lower $P$; the pressure difference is what accelerates the fluid into the constriction.

questions.stem: Water in a horizontal pipe has pressure $3.0\times10^5$ Pa where its speed is 2.0 m/s. What is the pressure where the speed is 8.0 m/s?
questions.explanation: $P_2 = P_1 + \tfrac12\rho(v_1^2 - v_2^2) = 3.0\times10^5 + 500(4 - 64) = 2.7\times10^5$ Pa. Adding instead of subtracting gives $3.3\times10^5$.

questions.stem: Water leaks from a small hole 5.0 m below the open surface of a large tank. How fast does it come out? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: Torricelli: $v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{98} = 9.9$ m/s, the same as free fall from the surface. 7.0 m/s omits the 2.

questions.stem: Which assumption is NOT part of the ideal fluid model used for Bernoulli's equation?
questions.explanation: The ideal fluid is incompressible, nonviscous, steady and irrotational. Turbulence is exactly what it excludes.

questions.stem: Strong wind blows over a house with closed windows during a storm. The roof may lift off because
choices: pressure above the roof is lower than the still air inside
the wind pushes up under the eaves only
pressure above the roof is higher than inside
the house is buoyant in air
questions.explanation: Fast-moving air above the roof has lower pressure (Bernoulli); the still air inside is at normal pressure, so the net force on the roof is upward.

questions.stem: A garden hose delivers 0.50 L/s through a nozzle of area 0.50 cm². How fast does the water leave the nozzle?
Bernoulli's equation is a statement of conservation of
questions.explanation: Each term is energy per unit volume: pressure work, kinetic energy ($\tfrac12\rho v^2$) and gravitational energy ($\rho gy$). Conservation of mass gives the continuity equation.

questions.stem: By Poiseuille's law ($Q \propto R^4$ for viscous flow), if a pipe's radius is halved with the same pressure difference, the flow rate becomes
questions.explanation: $(1/2)^4 = 1/16$. Viscous flow is extremely sensitive to radius, which is why narrowed arteries matter so much.

questions.stem: A horizontal water main narrows. Bernoulli's equation predicts a negative absolute pressure in the narrow section. What does this mean physically?
choices: The assumed flow is impossible; the water would cavitate (form vapor bubbles) first
The water speeds up even more
questions.explanation: Absolute pressure can't go below zero in a liquid. Before that, the liquid boils into vapor (cavitation), so the assumed steady flow can't occur.

questions.stem: Water flows steadily up a pipe of constant diameter, rising 5.0 m. The pressure at the bottom is $2.0\times10^5$ Pa. What is the pressure at the top? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: Constant diameter means constant speed (continuity), so the $\tfrac12\rho v^2$ terms cancel and only height matters: $P_2 = P_1 - \rho g\Delta y = 2.0\times10^5 - 1000(9.8)(5.0) = 1.51\times10^5$ Pa. Adding the $\rho gh$ term gives $2.5\times10^5$ Pa; ignoring the climb gives $2.0\times10^5$ Pa; $4.9\times10^4$ Pa is just the pressure change itself.

questions.stem: How much heat raises the temperature of 2.0 kg of water by 30°C? ($c = 4186$ J/(kg·K))
questions.explanation: $Q = mc\Delta T = 2.0(4186)(30) = 251\,160$ J $\approx 251$ kJ. (A change of 30°C is a change of 30 K.)

questions.stem: Room temperature, 25°C, is what in kelvins and in °F?
How much heat is needed to melt 0.50 kg of ice already at 0°C? ($L_f = 3.34\times10^5$ J/kg)
choices: 0 J, since its temperature doesn't change
questions.explanation: $Q = mL_f = 0.50(3.34\times10^5) = 1.67\times10^5$ J. Heat goes into breaking bonds, not raising temperature, during a phase change.

questions.stem: A 0.10 kg copper block at 100°C ($c = 385$ J/(kg·K)) is placed in 0.40 kg of water at 20°C. Ignoring the container, what is the final temperature?
questions.explanation: $0.10(385)(T - 100) + 0.40(4186)(T - 20) = 0 \Rightarrow 38.5T - 3850 + 1674.4T - 33\,488 = 0$, so $T = 37\,338/1712.9 = 21.8$°C. Averaging the temperatures (60°C) ignores the very different heat capacities.

questions.stem: A 2.0 m aluminum rod ($\alpha = 23\times10^{-6}$ K⁻¹) is heated by 50 K. How much longer does it get?
Why do coastal cities have milder temperature swings than inland cities?
choices: Water has a low specific heat
Water has a high specific heat, so the ocean changes temperature slowly
Sea breezes carry away all heat
questions.explanation: Water's specific heat (4186 J/(kg·K)) is several times that of soil or rock, so the ocean absorbs and releases large amounts of heat with small temperature changes.

questions.stem: A burn from 100°C steam is usually worse than one from the same mass of 100°C water because the steam
choices: releases its large latent heat of vaporization as it condenses on the skin
questions.explanation: Condensing releases $L_v = 2.26\times10^6$ J/kg before the water even starts cooling, far more energy than cooling 100°C water to skin temperature.

questions.stem: Lakes freeze from the top down because
choices: water is densest near 4°C, so colder water stays near the top
questions.explanation: Below 4°C water expands as it cools, so the coldest water floats; ice (less dense still) forms on top and insulates the water below.

questions.stem: Which mode of heat transfer can carry energy across a vacuum?
questions.explanation: Radiation is carried by electromagnetic waves and needs no medium; it's how sunlight reaches Earth. Conduction and convection need matter.

questions.stem: Heat conducts through a wall at 400 W. If the wall is replaced by one of the same material that is twice as thick, and the temperature difference across it is also doubled, the rate of heat flow becomes
questions.explanation: $Q/t = kA\Delta T/L$. Doubling $\Delta T$ doubles the rate and doubling $L$ halves it, so the two changes cancel: still 400 W. 800 W counts only the temperature change; 200 W only the thickness change.

questions.stem: A mug of coffee at 70°C sits in a 20°C room and is losing heat at 10 W. Assuming the rate of heat loss is proportional to the temperature difference with the room, about how fast is it losing heat when it has cooled to 45°C?
questions.explanation: The temperature difference falls from $70 - 20 = 50$ K to $45 - 20 = 25$ K, half as much, so the rate halves to 5.0 W. 6.4 W comes from the ratio of the temperatures $45/70$ instead of the differences; the rate doesn't stay at 10 W because the driving difference has shrunk.

questions.stem: What is the pressure of 2.0 mol of an ideal gas at 300 K in a 50 L container? ($R = 8.314$ J/(mol·K))
questions.explanation: $P = nRT/V = 2.0(8.314)(300)/0.050 = 9.98\times10^4 \approx 1.0\times10^5$ Pa (about 1 atm). Using $V = 50$ instead of 0.050 m³ gives 99.8 Pa; leaving out $n = 2.0$ gives $5.0\times10^4$ Pa.

questions.stem: A sealed rigid container of gas is heated from 27°C to 327°C. Its pressure
questions.explanation: At constant volume $P \propto T$ in kelvins: $300\text{ K} \to 600$ K doubles the pressure. Using Celsius ($327/27$) gives the bogus factor of 12.

questions.stem: A gas at 1.0 atm occupies 6.0 L. At constant temperature it is compressed to 2.0 L. The new pressure is
The absolute temperature of a gas is doubled. The rms speed of its molecules
questions.explanation: $v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{3RT/M} \propto \sqrt T$, so doubling $T$ multiplies $v_{\text{rms}}$ by $\sqrt2 \approx 1.41$. It's the average kinetic energy that doubles.

questions.stem: Helium and oxygen are mixed at the same temperature. Compared with oxygen molecules, helium atoms have
choices: the same average kinetic energy but higher rms speed
higher average kinetic energy and higher speed
questions.explanation: Average translational KE is $\tfrac32k_BT$, the same for any gas at the same $T$. With less mass, helium must move faster: $v_{\text{rms}} \propto 1/\sqrt M$.

questions.stem: What is the rms speed of O₂ molecules ($M = 0.032$ kg/mol) at 300 K?
questions.explanation: $v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{3RT/M} = \sqrt{3(8.314)(300)/0.032} = 484$ m/s. Using $M = 32$ (g/mol, not kg/mol) gives 15.3 m/s.

questions.stem: What is the average translational kinetic energy of a gas molecule at 600 K? ($k_B = 1.38\times10^{-23}$ J/K)
The internal energy of a fixed amount of ideal gas depends only on its
questions.explanation: For an ideal gas the molecules don't interact, so internal energy is just their kinetic energy, $\tfrac32nRT$ for a monatomic gas: a function of $T$ alone.

questions.stem: A gas is heated from 300 K to 900 K. How does the graph of its molecular speed distribution change?
choices: The peak moves to higher speed and the curve becomes lower and broader
The peak moves to higher speed and the curve becomes taller and narrower
The peak stays at the same speed but the curve grows taller
The peak moves to lower speed and the curve becomes broader
questions.explanation: Hotter molecules move faster on average, so the peak shifts to higher speed, and the speeds spread over a wider range. The area under the curve represents all the molecules and can't change, so a wider curve must also be lower. A taller, narrower curve would describe a colder gas (or heavier molecules).

questions.stem: A balloon holds 3.0 L of gas at 300 K and 1.0 atm. It is taken to where the pressure is 0.50 atm and the temperature 250 K. Its new volume is
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{P_1V_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{P_2V_2}{T_2}$: $V_2 = 3.0\cdot\dfrac{1.0}{0.50}\cdot\dfrac{250}{300} = 5.0$ L. Inverting the temperature ratio gives 7.2 L; inverting the pressure ratio gives 1.25 L.

questions.stem: The absolute temperature of a sample of monatomic ideal gas rises from 300 K to 450 K. By what factor does its internal energy change?
choices: It depends on whether the volume or the pressure is held fixed
questions.explanation: $E_{\text{int}} = \tfrac32nRT$ is proportional to $T$ in kelvins, so it changes by $450/300 = 1.5$, whatever the process. 1.22 is $\sqrt{1.5}$, the factor for the rms speed; 2.25 squares the temperature ratio.

questions.stem: A gas absorbs 800 J of heat and does 300 J of work on its surroundings. Its internal energy
questions.explanation: $\Delta E_{\text{int}} = Q - W = 800 - 300 = +500$ J. Adding gives 1100 J, which would be the case if 300 J of work were done on the gas instead of by it.

questions.stem: In an isothermal process for an ideal gas,
choices: the internal energy doesn't change, so $Q = W$
questions.explanation: Constant $T$ means constant $E_{\text{int}}$ for an ideal gas, so the heat absorbed equals the work done. "No heat flow" describes an adiabatic process.

questions.stem: A gas expands at a constant pressure of $2.0\times10^5$ Pa from 1.0 L to 4.0 L. How much work does it do?
questions.explanation: $W = P\Delta V = (2.0\times10^5)(3.0\times10^{-3}) = 600$ J. Forgetting to convert liters to m³ gives $6.0\times10^5$ J.

questions.stem: In an adiabatic expansion of an ideal gas, the gas
choices: warms up, because it does work
absorbs heat equal to the work it does
cools, because it does work with no heat coming in
questions.explanation: $Q = 0$, so $\Delta E_{\text{int}} = -W < 0$ for an expansion: internal energy and temperature drop. This is why rising air cools.

questions.stem: On a PV diagram, the work done by a gas during a process equals
choices: the product of the final $P$ and $V$
questions.explanation: At constant pressure $W = P\Delta V$, the area of the rectangle under the path; for a changing pressure, add the areas of many thin strips. The slope of the curve is not work. Different paths between the same two states enclose different areas, so work is path-dependent.

questions.stem: One mole of ideal gas at 400 K expands isothermally to twice its volume. How much work does it do? ($R = 8.314$ J/(mol·K))
questions.explanation: $W = nRT\ln(V_f/V_i) = 8.314(400)\ln 2 = 2305$ J. 3326 J is $nRT$ without the logarithm.

questions.stem: Why is the molar specific heat at constant pressure larger than at constant volume for a gas?
choices: At constant pressure some of the heat goes into work as the gas expands
Pressure adds kinetic energy to molecules
The gas has more molecules at constant pressure
questions.explanation: At constant volume all heat raises $E_{\text{int}}$. At constant pressure the gas also expands and does work $nR\Delta T$, so $C_P = C_V + R$.

questions.stem: Over one complete cycle of a heat engine's working gas, which is zero?
questions.explanation: The gas returns to its initial state, and internal energy is a state variable, so $\Delta E_{\text{int}} = 0$. Hence $Q_{\text{net}} = W_{\text{net}}$, the area enclosed by the cycle.

questions.stem: Three moles of a monatomic ideal gas are heated at constant volume, raising the temperature by 50 K. How much heat is added?
questions.explanation: $Q = nC_V\Delta T = 3(\tfrac32)(8.314)(50) = 1871$ J; no work is done at constant volume. 3118 J uses $C_P$.

questions.stem: A monatomic gas ($\gamma = 5/3$) is compressed adiabatically to 1/8 of its volume. Its absolute temperature
questions.explanation: $TV^{\gamma - 1}$ is constant, so $T_f = T_i(8)^{2/3} = 4T_i$. Adiabatic compression heats a gas strongly (diesel ignition).

questions.stem: A gas expands along a straight line on a PV diagram from 2.0 L at 400 kPa to 6.0 L at 200 kPa. How much work does the gas do?
questions.explanation: The area under the line is a trapezoid: average pressure $300$ kPa times $\Delta V = 4.0\times10^{-3}$ m³ gives $1200$ J. Using only the final pressure gives 800 J and only the initial pressure 1600 J; forgetting to convert liters to m³ gives $1.2\times10^6$ J.

questions.stem: What is the maximum possible efficiency of an engine working between 600 K and 300 K?
An engine takes in 1500 J of heat per cycle and exhausts 1050 J. What is its efficiency?
A Carnot engine runs between 127°C and 7°C. Its efficiency is
questions.explanation: In kelvins: 400 K and 280 K. $e = 1 - 280/400 = 0.30$. Using Celsius ($1 - 7/127$) gives the impossible-looking 94%.

questions.stem: Which statement is a form of the second law of thermodynamics?
choices: No cyclic engine can convert heat entirely into work
The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature
questions.explanation: That's the Kelvin–Planck statement; some heat must always be rejected to a colder reservoir. Energy conservation is the first law.

questions.stem: A refrigerator removes 300 J of heat from its interior using 100 J of work. What is its coefficient of performance, and how much heat goes to the kitchen?
questions.explanation: $K = Q_C/W = 300/100 = 3.0$. Energy conservation: $Q_H = Q_C + W = 400$ J delivered to the kitchen.

questions.stem: A reservoir at 400 K absorbs 2000 J of heat. What is its entropy change?
questions.explanation: $\Delta S = Q/T = 2000/400 = +5.0$ J/K (positive because heat flows in).

questions.stem: When heat flows from a hot object to a cold object, the total entropy of the two
questions.explanation: The hot object loses $Q/T_H$, the cold one gains $Q/T_C$, and since $T_C < T_H$ the gain is larger. Irreversible processes always raise total entropy.

questions.stem: What is the entropy change of 0.20 kg of ice melting at 0°C? ($L_f = 3.34\times10^5$ J/kg)
questions.explanation: $\Delta S = mL_f/T = 0.20(3.34\times10^5)/273 = +245$ J/K. Using $T = 0$ (Celsius) would make it undefined; always use kelvins.

questions.stem: A heat pump delivers 4 J of heat to a house for each 1 J of electrical work. Does this violate energy conservation?
choices: No: it moves 3 J of heat from outdoors plus the 1 J of work indoors
Yes, unless it is a Carnot engine
No, because heat is not energy
questions.explanation: $Q_H = Q_C + W$: 3 J extracted from the cold outdoors plus 1 J of work. A coefficient of performance above 1 is allowed; an efficiency above 1 is not.

questions.stem: 1.0 kg of ice melts at 0°C (273 K), taking its heat from a room at 20°C (293 K). What is the total entropy change of the ice and the room? ($L_f = 3.34\times10^5$ J/kg)
choices: Zero, because the heat lost equals the heat gained
questions.explanation: Ice: $+3.34\times10^5/273 = +1223.4$ J/K. Room: $-3.34\times10^5/293 = -1139.9$ J/K. Total: $+83.5 \approx +84$ J/K (keep extra digits when subtracting nearly equal numbers). The heat amounts are equal, but the room gives it up at a higher temperature, so its entropy loss is smaller than the ice's gain. Adding the two magnitudes gives 2363 J/K; reversing the signs gives $-84$ J/K.

questions.stem: A Carnot engine absorbs 900 J per cycle from a reservoir at 450 K and rejects heat to a reservoir at 300 K. How much heat does it reject per cycle?
questions.explanation: For a reversible engine $Q_H/T_H = Q_C/T_C$, so $Q_C = 900(300/450) = 600$ J, and the work is $900 - 600 = 300$ J (efficiency $1/3$). 300 J is the work, not the rejected heat; 1350 J inverts the temperature ratio; zero would be a perfect engine, which the second law forbids.

questions.stem: Two point charges, $+2.0$ μC and $+3.0$ μC, are 0.30 m apart. What is the force between them? ($k = 8.99\times10^9$ N·m²/C²)
questions.explanation: $F = k\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r^2} = (8.99\times10^9)\dfrac{(2.0\times10^{-6})(3.0\times10^{-6})}{0.090} = 0.60$ N. Like charges repel. Forgetting to square $r$ gives 0.18 N; forgetting the μ conversion gives an absurd $6\times10^5$ N.

questions.stem: If the distance between two charges is doubled, the electric force between them
questions.explanation: Coulomb's law is an inverse-square law: $F \propto 1/r^2$, so doubling $r$ gives $F/4$.

questions.stem: How many excess electrons give an object a charge of $-1.0$ μC?
questions.explanation: $n = q/e = (1.0\times10^{-6})/(1.602\times10^{-19}) = 6.2\times10^{12}$ electrons. $6.2\times10^{18}$ is the number in a full coulomb.

questions.stem: A negatively charged rod is brought near (not touching) a small neutral piece of paper. The paper
choices: feels no force because it is neutral
is attracted, because it becomes polarized
questions.explanation: The rod pushes the paper's electrons slightly away, leaving the near side slightly positive. The nearer positive side is attracted more strongly than the farther negative side is repelled, so there's a net attraction.

questions.stem: When a glass rod is rubbed with silk and becomes positively charged, what has happened?
choices: Protons moved from the silk to the glass
Electrons moved from the glass to the silk
Positive charge was created in the glass
questions.explanation: Charge is conserved and only electrons move easily in ordinary materials. The glass lost electrons (becoming positive) and the silk gained the same number (becoming equally negative).

questions.stem: Charges $+q$ at $x = 0$ and $+q$ at $x = 2d$. Where on the line between them is the net force on a third charge zero?
questions.explanation: At the midpoint the two equal repulsions (or attractions) have equal size and opposite directions, so they cancel, whatever the sign of the third charge.

questions.stem: Charges $+4.0$ μC at $x = 0$ and $-2.0$ μC at $x = 0.30$ m. What is the direction of the net force on a $+1.0$ μC charge at $x = 0.10$ m?
questions.explanation: The $+4.0$ μC charge repels it in $+x$, and the $-2.0$ μC charge attracts it toward itself, also $+x$. Both forces point the same way (3.60 N + 0.45 N = 4.05 N).

questions.stem: Compared with the gravitational attraction between two protons, their electric repulsion is
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{ke^2}{Gm_p^2} \approx 1.2\times10^{36}$. Gravity dominates large-scale structure only because matter is almost perfectly neutral.

questions.stem: Which statement about electric charge is correct?
choices: Charge is conserved only in conductors
Charge is quantized in multiples of $e$ and conserved
questions.explanation: Free charges come in multiples of $e = 1.602\times10^{-19}$ C, and total charge never changes. Neutral objects contain equal positive and negative charge.

questions.stem: Two point charges exert a force $F$ on each other. Both charges are doubled, and the distance between them is also doubled. The force becomes
questions.explanation: $F \propto q_1q_2/r^2$. Doubling both charges multiplies $F$ by 4; doubling $r$ divides it by $2^2 = 4$. Net factor: $4/4 = 1$. $4F$ forgets the distance change; $2F$ treats the distance as $1/r$ instead of $1/r^2$.

questions.stem: A $+9.0$ μC charge is at $x = 0$ and a $+1.0$ μC charge is at $x = 0.40$ m. At what point between them is the net electric force on a third charge zero?
questions.explanation: The forces balance when $9.0/x^2 = 1.0/(0.40 - x)^2$. Taking square roots, $3/x = 1/(0.40 - x)$, so $1.20 - 3x = x$ and $x = 0.30$ m, closer to the smaller charge. The midpoint (0.20 m) would only work for equal charges; 0.36 m divides the distance in the ratio 9 : 1, forgetting that force depends on $1/r^2$; 0.10 m is on the wrong side, near the larger charge.

questions.stem: What is the electric field 0.30 m from a $+4.0$ nC point charge? ($k = 8.99\times10^9$ N·m²/C²)
questions.explanation: $E = kq/r^2 = (8.99\times10^9)(4.0\times10^{-9})/0.090 = 400$ N/C, pointing away from a positive charge. 120 N/C forgets to square $r$.

questions.stem: A $-3.0$ μC charge sits where the electric field is 500 N/C pointing east. The force on it is
questions.explanation: $F = |q|E = (3.0\times10^{-6})(500) = 1.5\times10^{-3}$ N. A negative charge is pushed opposite to $\vec E$: west.

questions.stem: Which statement about electric field lines is false?
choices: They start on positive charges and end on negative charges
Their density shows the field strength
They can cross where two fields overlap
They are tangent to the field direction
questions.explanation: The field has a single direction at each point, so field lines never cross. The other statements are the rules for drawing them.

questions.stem: A proton is placed in a uniform field of 1000 N/C. What is its acceleration? ($m_p = 1.67\times10^{-27}$ kg, $e = 1.60\times10^{-19}$ C)
questions.explanation: $a = eE/m_p = (1.60\times10^{-19})(1000)/(1.67\times10^{-27}) = 9.6\times10^{10}$ m/s². $1.6\times10^{-16}$ is the force in newtons. $1.8\times10^{14}$ uses the electron's mass.

questions.stem: Two equal positive charges are a distance $d$ apart. The electric field at the midpoint is
choices: twice the field of one charge
directed toward one of the charges
perpendicular to the line joining them
questions.explanation: Each charge's field at the midpoint has the same magnitude and points away from it, so the two fields are opposite and cancel.

questions.stem: For an electric dipole ($+q$ and $-q$), the field at the midpoint between the charges points
questions.explanation: The $+q$ field points away from $+q$ (toward $-q$) and the $-q$ field points toward $-q$: both point toward the negative charge, so they add.

questions.stem: In electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field inside the material of a conductor is
questions.explanation: If there were a field inside, free electrons would move; equilibrium means they have rearranged until the internal field vanishes. Excess charge sits on the surface.

questions.stem: An electron moves horizontally into the uniform field between two horizontal deflection plates. Its path between the plates is
questions.explanation: The field gives a constant acceleration perpendicular to the initial velocity, just like gravity on a horizontally launched projectile, so the path is parabolic.

questions.stem: An electron and a proton are released from rest in the same uniform electric field. Compared with the proton, the electron experiences
choices: a force of the same size in the opposite direction, and a much larger acceleration
a larger force in the same direction
the same force and the same acceleration
a smaller force and a smaller acceleration
questions.explanation: Both have charge of size $e$, so $F = eE$ is the same size, but the electron's negative charge pushes it opposite to $\vec E$. With about 1/1800 of the proton's mass, the electron accelerates about 1800 times more ($a = F/m$).

questions.stem: Why are you relatively safe inside a car during a lightning strike?
choices: Rubber tires insulate the car from the ground
The metal body acts as a Faraday cage; charge stays on the outside and the field inside stays near zero
questions.explanation: Charge on a conductor resides on its outer surface and the field inside a closed conducting shell is shielded. The tires have nothing to do with it; lightning easily jumps a few centimeters of rubber.

questions.stem: An electron enters the uniform field between two deflection plates moving parallel to them, and it is deflected 4.0 mm by the time it leaves. If it enters at twice the speed (same field), its deflection is
questions.explanation: The deflection is $\tfrac12at^2$ with the same acceleration. At twice the speed it spends half as long between the plates, and $(1/2)^2 = 1/4$, so the deflection is 1.0 mm. 2.0 mm forgets to square the time.

questions.stem: A closed surface surrounds a $+2.0$ μC charge. What is the net electric flux through it? ($\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}$ C²/(N·m²))
choices: It depends on the shape of the surface
questions.explanation: Gauss: $\Phi_E = Q_{\text{enc}}/\varepsilon_0 = (2.0\times10^{-6})/(8.85\times10^{-12}) = 2.26\times10^5$ N·m²/C, for any closed surface around the charge.

questions.stem: A closed surface encloses no charge, but a charge sits just outside it. The net flux through the surface is
questions.explanation: Every field line from the outside charge that enters the surface also leaves it. The field on the surface isn't zero, but the net flux is.

questions.stem: A uniform field of 100 N/C passes through a flat 0.50 m² surface whose normal makes $60^\circ$ with the field. What is the flux?
questions.explanation: $\Phi = EA\cos\theta = 100(0.50)\cos 60^\circ = 25$ N·m²/C. 43 uses $\sin 60^\circ$.

questions.stem: What is the electric field inside a thin, uniformly charged spherical shell?
questions.explanation: A Gaussian sphere inside the shell encloses no charge, and by symmetry the field must be radial and uniform on it, so $E = 0$.

questions.stem: A long straight wire carries 2.0 nC/m. What is the field 5.0 cm away? ($k = 8.99\times10^9$ N·m²/C²)
questions.explanation: $E = 2k\lambda/r = 2(8.99\times10^9)(2.0\times10^{-9})/0.050 = 719$ N/C. Forgetting the factor 2 gives 360 N/C.

questions.stem: Inside a uniformly charged solid insulating sphere, the field at distance $r$ from the center is proportional to
questions.explanation: The enclosed charge grows as $r^3$ and the Gaussian area as $r^2$, so $E = kQr/R^3 \propto r$.

questions.stem: For an infinite charged sheet, how does the field depend on distance from the sheet?
questions.explanation: The pillbox argument gives $E = \sigma/(2\varepsilon_0)$ with no distance in it. That's why the field between large parallel plates is uniform.

questions.stem: Gauss's law is always true, but it gives the field directly only when
choices: symmetry makes $E$ constant and perpendicular (or parallel) over a chosen surface
questions.explanation: The total flux reduces to $E$ times an area only with spherical, cylindrical or planar symmetry. Otherwise Gauss's law still holds but doesn't isolate $E$.

questions.stem: A point charge $+q$ sits inside a cavity in a neutral conducting block. What charge appears on the cavity wall and on the outer surface?
choices: $-q$ on the wall, $+q$ on the outer surface
questions.explanation: A Gaussian surface inside the metal (where $E = 0$) must enclose zero net charge, so the wall carries $-q$. The block is neutral, so $+q$ appears on its outer surface.

questions.stem: The field just outside the surface of a conductor with surface charge density $\sigma$ is
questions.explanation: A pillbox straddling the surface has flux only through its outer cap (the field inside the metal is zero): $EA = \sigma A/\varepsilon_0$.

questions.stem: A $+4.0$ nC point charge sits at the center of a closed cube. What is the electric flux through one face of the cube? ($\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}$ C²/(N·m²))
questions.explanation: Total flux: $Q/\varepsilon_0 = (4.0\times10^{-9})/(8.85\times10^{-12}) = 452$ N·m²/C. By symmetry the six faces share it equally: $452/6 = 75$ N·m²/C. 452 is the total through all faces; 113 divides by 4 instead of 6; $2.7\times10^3$ multiplies by 6.

questions.stem: What is the electric potential 0.30 m from a $+2.0$ nC charge (zero at infinity)? ($k = 8.99\times10^9$ N·m²/C²)
Charges $+4.0$ nC and $-4.0$ nC are 0.20 m apart. What is the potential at the midpoint?
questions.explanation: Potentials add as scalars with signs: $k(4.0\times10^{-9})/0.10 + k(-4.0\times10^{-9})/0.10 = 0$. (The field there is not zero, though.)

questions.stem: A proton is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 100 V. How much kinetic energy does it gain?
Two parallel plates 3.0 mm apart are connected to a 9.0 V battery. What is the field between them?
questions.explanation: $E = \Delta V/d = 9.0/0.0030 = 3000$ V/m. Forgetting to convert mm to m gives 3.0 V/m.

questions.stem: What is the potential energy of a $+2.0$ μC charge and a $-3.0$ μC charge 0.20 m apart?
questions.explanation: $U = kq_1q_2/r = (8.99\times10^9)(2.0\times10^{-6})(-3.0\times10^{-6})/0.20 = -0.27$ J. Negative: the pair is bound. $-1.35$ J divides by $r^2$.

questions.stem: An electron released from rest in an electric field moves toward
questions.explanation: Its potential energy $U = qV = -eV$ decreases as $V$ increases, so the electron "falls" toward higher potential. Positive charges move toward lower potential.

questions.stem: How much work does the electric field do on a charge moved along an equipotential surface?
questions.explanation: $W = -q\Delta V$ and $\Delta V = 0$ along an equipotential. Equivalently, the field is perpendicular to equipotentials, so it does no work along them.

questions.stem: Along the $x$ axis, the potential falls steadily from 60 V at $x = 0$ to 0 V at $x = 0.30$ m. What is the electric field in this region?
questions.explanation: $E_x = -\Delta V/\Delta x = -(0 - 60)/0.30 = +200$ V/m. The field points toward lower potential, in $+x$. Pointing it toward higher potential gives $-x$; 18 V/m multiplies $V$ by distance instead of dividing; the value of $V$ at a point says nothing about the field there, only its rate of change does.

questions.stem: An electron volt (eV) is a unit of
questions.explanation: It's the kinetic energy gained by charge $e$ crossing 1 V: $1.602\times10^{-19}$ J.

questions.stem: Electric field lines and equipotential surfaces are
questions.explanation: No work is done moving along an equipotential, so the field has no component along it: field lines cross equipotentials at right angles, pointing toward lower potential.

questions.stem: On a graph of potential versus position, one region is a horizontal line at $V = 25$ V. In that region the electric field is
choices: impossible to find without the charges
questions.explanation: The field is the negative slope of the $V$-versus-$x$ graph. A horizontal line has zero slope, so $E = 0$ there, even though $V$ is 25 V. A constant nonzero potential is like a flat plateau: high up, but with no downhill direction.

questions.stem: A parallel-plate capacitor has plates of area 0.020 m² separated by 0.50 mm of air. What is its capacitance? ($\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}$ F/m)
If the plate separation of a parallel-plate capacitor is doubled (same area), its capacitance
questions.explanation: $C = \varepsilon_0A/d$, so $C \propto 1/d$: doubling $d$ halves $C$.

questions.stem: A 4.0 μF and a 12 μF capacitor are connected in series. Their equivalent capacitance is
questions.explanation: $1/C = 1/4.0 + 1/12 = 4/12$, so $C = 3.0$ μF, smaller than either. 16 μF is the parallel combination.

questions.stem: How much energy is stored in a 10 μF capacitor charged to 100 V?
questions.explanation: $U = \tfrac12CV^2 = \tfrac12(10\times10^{-6})(100)^2 = 0.050$ J. $CV^2 = 0.10$ J forgets the $\tfrac12$.

questions.stem: Capacitors in series all have the same
questions.explanation: In a single path, the charge pushed onto one plate induces an equal charge on each successive plate, so every series capacitor carries the same $Q$. The voltages divide, with the smallest capacitor taking the largest share.

questions.stem: A capacitor is connected to a battery, then a dielectric with $\kappa = 3$ is slid between the plates while the battery stays connected. The charge on the plates
questions.explanation: $C$ triples and the battery holds $V$ fixed, so $Q = CV$ triples (the battery supplies the extra charge).

questions.stem: The energy stored in a capacitor is located
choices: in the battery that charged it
in the electric field between the plates
in the metal of the plates
questions.explanation: The energy is stored in the field, with density $u = \tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2$; multiplying by the volume $Ad$ between the plates gives back $\tfrac12CV^2$.

questions.stem: Three 6.0 μF capacitors are connected in parallel across a 10 V source. What is the total charge stored?
questions.explanation: Parallel: $C_{\text{eq}} = 18$ μF; $Q = 18(10) = 180$ μC (60 μC on each). 20 μC would be the series result.

questions.stem: A capacitor is charged from zero to charge $Q$ and voltage $V$. On a graph of its voltage against its charge, the stored energy equals
choices: the triangular area under the line, $\tfrac12QV$
questions.explanation: Adding a small charge $\Delta q$ at voltage $V$ takes work $V\Delta q$, a thin strip under the line. The strips fill a triangle of base $Q$ and height $V$, area $\tfrac12QV$. The rectangle $QV$ would be right only if every bit of charge were moved against the final voltage.

questions.stem: The capacitance of an isolated conducting sphere of radius $R$ is
questions.explanation: $V = kQ/R$, so $C = Q/V = R/k = 4\pi\varepsilon_0R$. Larger spheres hold more charge per volt.

questions.stem: A capacitor is charged to 20 V and then disconnected from the battery. A dielectric with $\kappa = 2.0$ is slid between its plates. The voltage across the capacitor becomes
questions.explanation: Disconnected, the charge $Q$ can't change. The dielectric doubles $C$, so $V = Q/C$ halves to 10 V. 20 V would be right only if the battery were still connected; 40 V multiplies by $\kappa$ instead of dividing.

questions.stem: A current of 0.50 A flows in a wire for 1.0 minute. How much charge passes a point in the wire?
questions.explanation: $Q = It = 0.50(60) = 30$ C. Using 1.0 (minutes) instead of 60 s gives 0.50 C.

questions.stem: A 120 V source drives 2.0 A through a resistor. What is the resistance?
questions.explanation: $R = V/I = 120/2.0 = 60$ Ω. Multiplying gives 240 (that's the power in watts).

questions.stem: A wire's length is doubled and its diameter is doubled. Its resistance
questions.explanation: $R = \rho L/A$. Doubling $L$ doubles $R$; doubling the diameter quadruples $A$, dividing $R$ by 4. Net: $2/4 = 1/2$.

questions.stem: A 1500 W hair dryer runs on 120 V. What current does it draw, and what is its resistance?
What is the resistance of a 100 m copper wire of diameter 1.0 mm? ($\rho = 1.7\times10^{-8}$ Ω·m)
questions.explanation: $A = \pi(0.50\times10^{-3})^2 = 7.85\times10^{-7}$ m². $R = (1.7\times10^{-8})(100)/(7.85\times10^{-7}) = 2.2$ Ω. Using the diameter as the radius gives 0.54 Ω.

questions.stem: Power companies transmit electricity at very high voltage mainly because
choices: for the same power, the current is smaller, reducing $I^2R$ losses in the lines
questions.explanation: $P = IV$: at higher $V$ the same power needs less $I$, and the heat lost in the lines is $I^2R$, so losses drop with the square of the current.

questions.stem: A 1500 W heater runs 4.0 hours. At \$0.12 per kWh, what does it cost?
questions.explanation: Energy $= 1.5\text{ kW} \times 4.0\text{ h} = 6.0$ kWh; cost $= 6.0 \times 0.12 =$ \$0.72. Forgetting to convert W to kW gives \$720.

questions.stem: The drift velocity of electrons in a typical household wire is about
questions.explanation: $v_d = I/(nqA)$ is around $10^{-4}$ m/s. Lights still turn on instantly because the electric field spreads through the wire at nearly light speed, moving all the electrons at once.

questions.stem: A 10 Ω resistor carries 2.0 A. At what rate does it produce heat?
questions.explanation: $P = I^2R = (2.0)^2(10) = 40$ W. $IR = 20$ is the voltage, not the power.

questions.stem: The current in a wire rises steadily from 0 to 6.0 A over 4.0 s. How much charge passes through the wire during those 4.0 s?
questions.explanation: Charge is the area under the current–time graph, here a triangle: $\tfrac12(4.0\text{ s})(6.0\text{ A}) = 12$ C. 24 C uses the final current for the whole time; 1.5 C divides current by time.

questions.stem: An ohmic resistor dissipates 40 W when connected to 10 V. What power does it dissipate when connected to 20 V?
questions.explanation: With $R$ fixed, $P = V^2/R \propto V^2$: doubling the voltage quadruples the power, to 160 W. 80 W forgets that the current doubles too.

questions.stem: Resistors of 2.0 Ω, 4.0 Ω and 6.0 Ω are connected in parallel. Their equivalent resistance is
questions.explanation: $\dfrac1R = \dfrac12 + \dfrac14 + \dfrac16 = \dfrac{11}{12}$, so $R = 12/11 = 1.09$ Ω, less than the smallest. 12 Ω is the series total; 0.92 forgets to take the reciprocal.

questions.stem: Two resistors in series carry
choices: currents in inverse proportion to their resistances
questions.explanation: There's only one path, so the same current flows through both; the voltage divides in proportion to resistance.

questions.stem: A 6.0 Ω and a 3.0 Ω resistor are in parallel across 12 V. What is the current through the 3.0 Ω resistor and the total current?
questions.explanation: Each has the full 12 V: $12/3.0 = 4.0$ A and $12/6.0 = 2.0$ A, total 6.0 A (equivalent resistance 2.0 Ω). 1.3 A treats them as series.

questions.stem: A 12 V battery with internal resistance 1.0 Ω is connected to a 5.0 Ω resistor. What is the terminal voltage?
Kirchhoff's junction rule is a consequence of conservation of
questions.explanation: Charge can't accumulate at a junction, so what flows in must flow out. The loop rule expresses conservation of energy.

questions.stem: Going around a loop, you cross a resistor $R$ in the same direction as its current $I$. The potential change is
questions.explanation: Current flows from high to low potential through a resistor, so moving with the current you go downhill: $\Delta V = -IR$.

questions.stem: Solving a circuit with Kirchhoff's rules, you get $I_2 = -0.5$ A. This means
choices: current flows opposite to the direction you assumed for $I_2$
the battery is reversed in the diagram
questions.explanation: Assumed directions are guesses; a negative result simply means 0.5 A flows the other way.

questions.stem: Three currents meet at a junction: 3.0 A flows in, 1.2 A flows out. The third current is
questions.explanation: Junction rule: in = out, so $3.0 = 1.2 + I_3$ and $I_3 = 1.8$ A flowing out.

questions.stem: How should a voltmeter be connected, and what resistance should it have?
questions.explanation: A voltmeter measures the potential difference across a component, so it goes in parallel, and its high resistance keeps it from drawing current and disturbing the circuit. Ammeters go in series with low resistance.

questions.stem: More appliances are plugged into parallel outlets on one household circuit. The total current drawn from the circuit
choices: increases, because the equivalent resistance decreases
questions.explanation: Each new parallel path lowers $R_{\text{eq}}$ while the voltage stays 120 V, so total current rises, which is why circuit breakers are needed.

questions.stem: A source has emf 10 V and internal resistance 5.0 Ω. Which of these load resistances receives the most power?
questions.explanation: $P = I^2R = \mathcal{E}^2R/(R + r)^2$ gives 4.4 W for 2.5 Ω, 5.0 W for 5.0 Ω, 4.4 W for 10 Ω and 3.2 W for 20 Ω. The maximum is at $R = r = 5.0$ Ω (impedance matching): smaller loads have little voltage across them, larger ones draw little current.

questions.stem: Three identical bulbs are connected to an ideal battery: bulb A is in series with a parallel pair, B and C. A wire is then connected directly across bulb B. What happens to bulbs A and C?
choices: A gets dimmer and C gets brighter
A stays the same and C goes out
A gets brighter and C goes out
questions.explanation: The wire has almost no resistance, so it carries all the current that used to split between B and C: both B and C go out (C is in parallel with the wire too). Only A's resistance is left, so the battery current rises from $\mathcal{E}/(1.5R)$ to $\mathcal{E}/R$ and A gets brighter.

questions.stem: What is the time constant of a 10 kΩ resistor in series with a 100 μF capacitor?
A capacitor charging through a resistor reaches what fraction of its final charge after two time constants?
questions.explanation: $1 - e^{-2} = 0.865$. After one time constant it's 63%, after three 95%.

questions.stem: At the instant the switch is closed in a series circuit with a battery, a resistor and an uncharged capacitor, the current is
questions.explanation: An uncharged capacitor has no voltage across it, so the whole emf appears across $R$: $I_0 = \mathcal{E}/R$. The current then decays exponentially.

questions.stem: A capacitor charged to 20 V discharges through a resistor. After one time constant, its voltage is about
questions.explanation: Discharging: $V = V_0e^{-t/RC} = 20e^{-1} = 7.36$ V. 12.6 V would be the charging value $20(1 - e^{-1})$.

questions.stem: Long after the switch is closed in a DC circuit, a capacitor behaves like
questions.explanation: Once fully charged, no more current flows into it, so it acts as a break in that branch.

questions.stem: A 2.0 μF capacitor discharges through a 1.0 MΩ resistor. How long until its charge halves?
When a capacitor is charged to $\mathcal{E}$ through a resistor, what fraction of the energy supplied by the battery ends up stored in the capacitor?
questions.explanation: The battery supplies $C\mathcal{E}^2$; the capacitor stores $\tfrac12C\mathcal{E}^2$; the rest, $\tfrac12C\mathcal{E}^2$, heats the resistor, independent of $R$.

questions.stem: Which change makes an RC circuit charge faster?
questions.explanation: The timing depends only on $\tau = RC$. Smaller $R$ (or $C$) shortens it. A larger emf changes the final charge, not the time to reach a given fraction.

questions.stem: A capacitor is charging through a resistor from a battery. At the instant the capacitor's voltage is 75% of the battery's emf, the current is
questions.explanation: Loop rule: $I = (\mathcal{E} - V_C)/R$. The resistor gets only the 25% of the emf the capacitor hasn't taken, so the current is 25% of its starting value $\mathcal{E}/R$. The current reaches zero only when the capacitor is fully charged.

questions.stem: What are the units of the product $RC$?
choices: ohm-farads, which are not a time
questions.explanation: $\Omega\cdot F = \dfrac{V}{A}\cdot\dfrac{C}{V} = \dfrac{C}{A} = \dfrac{C}{C/s} = s$. That's why $RC$ is called the time constant.

questions.stem: A 12 V battery and a 3.0 kΩ resistor are in series with a parallel pair: a 6.0 kΩ resistor and an uncharged capacitor. Long after the switch is closed, what is the voltage across the capacitor?
questions.explanation: Fully charged, the capacitor carries no current, so the two resistors are in series: $I = 12$ V / 9.0 kΩ = 1.33 mA. The capacitor shares the 6.0 kΩ resistor's voltage, $IR = 8.0$ V. 12 V ignores the drop across the 3.0 kΩ resistor; 4.0 V is that drop; 0 V is the value just after the switch closes.

questions.stem: A proton moves at $2.0\times10^6$ m/s perpendicular to a 0.50 T magnetic field. What force acts on it? ($e = 1.6\times10^{-19}$ C)
A charged particle moves parallel to a uniform magnetic field. The magnetic force on it is
questions.explanation: $F = qvB\sin\theta$ with $\theta = 0$ gives zero. Only the velocity component perpendicular to $\vec B$ feels a force.

questions.stem: Why does a magnetic field never change the speed of a charged particle?
choices: The force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work
Magnetic fields only act on stationary charges
The force is parallel to the velocity
questions.explanation: The force is perpendicular to the velocity, so over any short step it acts at $90^\circ$ to the displacement and does work $Fd\cos 90^\circ = 0$. With no work done, kinetic energy and speed stay constant; only the direction changes.

questions.stem: An electron moves at $1.0\times10^7$ m/s perpendicular to a 0.010 T field. What is the radius of its circular path? ($m_e = 9.11\times10^{-31}$ kg, $e = 1.6\times10^{-19}$ C)
A wire carries current east in a magnetic field pointing up. With $x$ east, $y$ north and $z$ up, the force on the wire points
questions.explanation: $\vec F = I\vec L\times\vec B \propto \hat\imath\times\hat k = -\hat\jmath$: south. Check with the right hand: fingers east, curl toward up, thumb points south.

questions.stem: A 0.40 m wire carrying 5.0 A lies perpendicular to a 0.20 T field. What force acts on it?
The period of a charged particle circling in a uniform magnetic field
questions.explanation: $r = mv/(qB)$ grows with $v$, so the circumference grows as fast as the speed: $T = 2\pi m/(qB)$ has no $v$. This makes the cyclotron possible.

questions.stem: In a velocity selector with crossed fields $E = 2.0\times10^4$ V/m and $B = 0.10$ T, which particles pass straight through?
choices: Those with $v = 2.0\times10^5$ m/s, of either sign
questions.explanation: Undeflected when $qE = qvB$: $v = E/B = 2.0\times10^5$ m/s. The charge cancels, so the sign and size of $q$ don't matter.

questions.stem: A current loop in a uniform magnetic field experiences
choices: a net force but no torque
a torque that tends to align its normal with the field, and zero net force
questions.explanation: Forces on opposite sides cancel in a uniform field, but they form a couple: $\tau = NIAB\sin\phi$. That torque drives electric motors.

questions.stem: In a mass spectrometer, singly charged ions with the same speed enter a magnetic field. A heavier isotope
questions.explanation: $r = mv/(qB)$: at the same speed and charge, radius is proportional to mass, so heavier ions curve less and land farther away.

questions.stem: A velocity selector is set so that ions moving at speed $v_0$ pass straight through. An ion moving faster than $v_0$ is
choices: deflected in the direction of the electric force
deflected in the direction of the magnetic force
not deflected, because the forces still balance
slowed down until its speed is $v_0$
questions.explanation: The electric force $qE$ doesn't depend on speed, but the magnetic force $qvB$ grows with $v$. For a faster ion the magnetic force wins, so it bends toward the magnetic force's side. The magnetic force does no work, so the ion isn't slowed to $v_0$.

questions.stem: A proton moves in a circle in a uniform magnetic field. If its speed is doubled, its radius and its period become
questions.explanation: $r = \dfrac{mv}{|q|B}$ is proportional to $v$, so the radius doubles. The period $T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v} = \dfrac{2\pi m}{|q|B}$ has no $v$: twice the circumference at twice the speed takes the same time. Doubling the period too would assume the speed stayed the same around a bigger circle.

questions.stem: A long straight wire carries 10 A. What is the magnetic field 2.0 cm away? ($\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A)
questions.explanation: $B = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi r} = \dfrac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(10)}{2\pi(0.020)} = 1.0\times10^{-4}$ T. Using the loop-center formula $\mu_0I/(2r)$ by mistake gives $3.1\times10^{-4}$ T.

questions.stem: Doubling the distance from a long straight current-carrying wire changes its field by a factor of
questions.explanation: $B \propto 1/r$ for a straight wire, so doubling $r$ halves $B$. (The $1/r^2$ law is for point sources.)

questions.stem: A solenoid has 1000 turns per meter and carries 2.0 A. What is the field inside? ($\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A)
questions.explanation: $B = \mu_0nI = (4\pi\times10^{-7})(1000)(2.0) = 2.5\times10^{-3}$ T, uniform across the interior.

questions.stem: Two long parallel wires carry currents in the same direction. They
choices: exert no force on each other
questions.explanation: Each wire sits in the other's circular field; the right-hand rules give a force toward the other wire. Like currents attract and opposite currents repel, the reverse of electric charges.

questions.stem: Two parallel wires 10 cm apart each carry 5.0 A. What is the force per meter between them?
Current flows counterclockwise in a horizontal loop as seen from above. At the loop's center the field points
questions.explanation: Curl right-hand fingers counterclockwise (seen from above): the thumb points up. The loop's upper face acts as a north pole.

questions.stem: What is the field at the center of a single circular loop of radius 10 cm carrying 5.0 A? ($\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A)
questions.explanation: $B = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{2R} = \dfrac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(5.0)}{0.20} = 3.1\times10^{-5}$ T. $1.0\times10^{-5}$ is the straight-wire formula at 10 cm.

questions.stem: For a path along which the field is constant and points along the path, Ampère's law says $B\times(\text{path length}) = \mu_0I_{\text{enc}}$. Applied to a circle of radius $r$ centered on a long straight wire, it gives
questions.explanation: By symmetry $B$ is the same all the way around the circle and points along it. The path length is $2\pi r$, so $B(2\pi r) = \mu_0I$. $\mu_0I/(2r)$ is the field at the center of a loop, and $\mu_0nI$ is a solenoid's.

questions.stem: Inserting an iron core into a current-carrying solenoid greatly increases the field because
choices: the magnetic domains in the iron align with the field and add their own
iron increases the number of turns
questions.explanation: Iron is ferromagnetic: its domains line up with the applied field, contributing a much larger field of their own. That's the principle of the electromagnet.

questions.stem: Two long parallel wires 10 cm apart each carry 20 A out of the page. What is the magnetic field at the point midway between them? ($\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A)
questions.explanation: Each wire alone gives $B = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi r} = \dfrac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(20)}{2\pi(0.050)} = 8.0\times10^{-5}$ T at 5.0 cm. Both fields circle counterclockwise, so at the midpoint one points up the page and the other down: they cancel. Adding them gives $1.6\times10^{-4}$ T, which is the answer only if the currents are opposite; $4.0\times10^{-5}$ T uses the full 10 cm as the distance.

questions.stem: A solenoid's number of turns is doubled and its length is halved, with the same current. The field inside becomes
questions.explanation: $B = \mu_0nI$ with $n = N/\ell$. Doubling $N$ and halving $\ell$ multiplies $n$ by $2 \times 2 = 4$, so $B$ is 4 times larger. Twice as large comes from noticing only one of the two changes.

questions.stem: A 100-turn coil of area 0.020 m² is perpendicular to a field that rises from 0.20 T to 0.60 T in 0.10 s. What emf is induced?
questions.explanation: $|\mathcal{E}| = N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t} = 100\dfrac{(0.40)(0.020)}{0.10} = 8.0$ V. Leaving out $N$ gives 0.080 V.

questions.stem: A strong magnet rests motionless inside a coil connected to a meter. The meter reads
questions.explanation: Only a changing flux induces an emf. A stationary magnet gives constant flux, so there's no induced current.

questions.stem: The north pole of a magnet is pushed toward a loop. By Lenz's law, the induced current makes the loop's near face act like
choices: a south pole, attracting the magnet
a north pole only if the loop is copper
a north pole, repelling the magnet
questions.explanation: The flux from the approaching north pole is increasing, so the induced current opposes it, making a north face that repels the magnet. You must do work to push it in, which becomes electrical energy.

questions.stem: A 0.50 m rod slides at 10 m/s along rails in a 2.0 T field perpendicular to the rails. What emf is induced?
questions.explanation: Motional emf $\mathcal{E} = BLv = 2.0(0.50)(10) = 10$ V.

questions.stem: Lenz's law is ultimately a consequence of conservation of
questions.explanation: If induced currents aided the change, a small push would produce runaway motion and energy from nothing. Opposing the change means work must be done to generate electrical energy.

questions.stem: A transformer has 50 primary turns and 500 secondary turns. With 120 V AC on the primary, the secondary voltage is
questions.explanation: $V_s = V_p(N_s/N_p) = 120(10) = 1200$ V. The current is stepped down by the same factor (ideal transformer).

questions.stem: Why won't a transformer work with a steady DC current in the primary?
choices: A steady current makes a constant flux, so no emf is induced in the secondary
questions.explanation: Faraday's law needs a changing flux. Steady DC produces a steady field, so the flux through the secondary doesn't change and no emf is induced. (DC does make a magnetic field; it just isn't changing.)

questions.stem: A generator coil rotates at angular speed $\omega$ in a uniform field. If $\omega$ is doubled, the peak emf
questions.explanation: $\mathcal{E}_{\max} = NBA\omega$: proportional to $\omega$ (and the frequency of the AC doubles too).

questions.stem: The flux through a single loop rises steadily from 0 to 0.060 Wb in 0.20 s, stays at 0.060 Wb for 0.50 s, then falls steadily to 0 in 0.10 s. When is the induced emf largest, and how large is it?
questions.explanation: The emf is the slope of the flux–time graph. Rise: $0.060/0.20 = 0.30$ V. Steady: slope zero, so no emf even though the flux is largest. Fall: $0.060/0.10 = 0.60$ V, the largest because the same change happens fastest. 0.060 V is the flux itself, not its rate of change.

questions.stem: Magnetic brakes on a roller coaster use fins passing between strong magnets. The braking force comes from
choices: eddy currents in the fins, whose fields oppose the motion
questions.explanation: The changing flux through the moving metal induces eddy currents; by Lenz's law their magnetic forces oppose the motion, converting kinetic energy to heat without contact.

questions.stem: A coil rotates steadily in a uniform magnetic field. At the instant the flux through the coil is at its maximum, the induced emf is
choices: zero, because the flux is momentarily not changing
at its maximum, because the flux is at its maximum
questions.explanation: The emf depends on the rate of change of flux, the slope of the flux–time graph. At a maximum of the cosine-shaped flux curve the graph is momentarily flat, so the emf is zero. The emf peaks a quarter turn later, when the flux passes through zero and changes fastest.

questions.stem: A 100-turn coil of area 0.020 m² rotates at 60 revolutions per second in a 0.50 T field. What is the peak emf?
questions.explanation: $\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi(60) = 377$ rad/s, so $\mathcal{E}_{\max} = NBA\omega = 100(0.50)(0.020)(377) = 377$ V. Using 60 in place of $\omega$ gives 60 V; leaving out $N$ gives 3.8 V.

questions.stem: What is the time constant of a circuit with a 0.50 H inductor in series with a 10 Ω resistor?
questions.explanation: $\tau = L/R = 0.50/10 = 0.050$ s. $LR = 5.0$ is not a time constant; that would be confusing it with $RC$-style multiplication.

questions.stem: How much energy is stored in a 2.0 H inductor carrying 0.30 A?
Immediately after the switch is closed in a series circuit of a battery, a resistor and an inductor, the current is
questions.explanation: An inductor prevents sudden changes in current, so the current starts at zero and rises toward $\mathcal{E}/R$ with time constant $L/R$.

questions.stem: An LC circuit has $L = 10$ mH and $C = 1.0$ μF. What is its oscillation frequency?
questions.explanation: $f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{(0.010)(1.0\times10^{-6})}} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi(10^{-4})} = 1.59$ kHz. $1/\sqrt{LC} = 10^4$ is $\omega$ in rad/s.

questions.stem: Household AC is rated 120 V (rms). What is the peak voltage?
questions.explanation: $V_0 = \sqrt2V_{\text{rms}} = 1.414(120) = 170$ V. Dividing instead of multiplying gives 85 V.

questions.stem: As the frequency of an AC source increases, the reactance of a capacitor
questions.explanation: $X_C = 1/(\omega C)$ falls as $\omega$ rises: capacitors pass high frequencies and block low ones (and block DC entirely). Inductors do the reverse, $X_L = \omega L$.

questions.stem: In a series RLC circuit driven at its resonant frequency,
questions.explanation: At $\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC}$, $X_L = X_C$, so $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + 0} = R$, its minimum, and the current is largest.

questions.stem: An inductor in a circuit opposes
choices: changes in the current through it
the battery's emf at all times
questions.explanation: $\mathcal{E}_L = -L\,\Delta I/\Delta t$: with a steady current, $\Delta I = 0$ and there's no induced emf, so the inductor acts like a plain wire. It's a kind of electrical inertia.

questions.stem: In the mechanical analogy for an LC circuit (mass on a spring), the inductance $L$ corresponds to
questions.explanation: Compare the energies. The inductor stores $\tfrac12LI^2$, like kinetic energy $\tfrac12mv^2$ with current playing velocity, so $L \leftrightarrow m$. The capacitor stores $\dfrac{q^2}{2C}$, like spring energy $\tfrac12kx^2$ with charge playing position, so $1/C \leftrightarrow k$. Like a mass resisting changes in velocity, an inductor resists changes in current.

questions.stem: What is the reactance of a 10 μF capacitor at 60 Hz?
questions.explanation: $X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi fC} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi(60)(10\times10^{-6})} = 265$ Ω. Forgetting the $2\pi$ gives 1670 Ω.

questions.stem: An inductor and resistor with time constant $L/R = 20$ ms are connected to a battery at $t = 0$. About what fraction of the final current flows at $t = 20$ ms?
questions.explanation: $I = I_{\text{final}}(1 - e^{-t/\tau})$ with $t = \tau$: $1 - e^{-1} = 0.63$. 37% is $e^{-1}$, the fraction that would remain in a decay; 50% would be a half-life, which is $0.69\tau$, not $\tau$.

questions.stem: A series circuit has $R = 40\ \Omega$, $X_L = 50\ \Omega$ and $X_C = 20\ \Omega$, driven by 100 V (rms). What is the rms current?
questions.explanation: $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2} = \sqrt{40^2 + 30^2} = 50\ \Omega$, so $I_{\text{rms}} = 100/50 = 2.0$ A. Adding all three as resistors ($110\ \Omega$) gives 0.91 A; ignoring the reactances gives 2.5 A; adding $X_L$ and $X_C$ inside the root instead of subtracting ($\sqrt{40^2 + 70^2} = 81\ \Omega$) gives 1.2 A.

questions.stem: What is the wavelength of light with frequency $5.0\times10^{14}$ Hz in vacuum?
questions.explanation: $\lambda = c/f = (3.00\times10^8)/(5.0\times10^{14}) = 6.0\times10^{-7}$ m $= 600$ nm (orange light).

questions.stem: Which statement about electromagnetic waves is correct?
choices: They need a medium to travel
Their electric and magnetic fields are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel
Radio waves travel faster than visible light in vacuum
questions.explanation: EM waves are transverse, with $\vec E \perp \vec B \perp$ direction of travel, and all travel at $c$ in vacuum, needing no medium.

questions.stem: Order these from longest to shortest wavelength: X-rays, microwaves, visible light, ultraviolet.
questions.explanation: The spectrum runs radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma in order of decreasing wavelength (increasing frequency).

questions.stem: Light passes from air into glass ($n = 1.50$) at $40^\circ$ to the normal. What is the angle of refraction?
questions.explanation: $\sin\theta_2 = \sin 40^\circ/1.50 = 0.429$, so $\theta_2 = 25.4^\circ$, bent toward the normal. 60° multiplies the angle by 1.5 instead of using sines.

questions.stem: When light passes from air into water, which quantity does not change?
questions.explanation: The frequency is set by the source. Speed drops to $c/n$ and wavelength to $\lambda/n$, and the direction bends unless the light hits head-on.

questions.stem: What is the critical angle for light going from water ($n = 1.33$) into air?
questions.explanation: $\sin\theta_c = n_2/n_1 = 1.00/1.33 = 0.752$, so $\theta_c = 48.8^\circ$. Beyond this, light is totally internally reflected. (41.8° is the value for glass with $n = 1.5$.)

questions.stem: Total internal reflection can occur when light travels
choices: from any medium into a mirror
questions.explanation: It requires going from higher to lower index, so the refracted ray bends away from the normal and can reach 90°. Going into a denser medium the light always refracts.

questions.stem: Unpolarized light of intensity $I_0$ passes through two polarizers whose axes are $60^\circ$ apart. The transmitted intensity is
questions.explanation: The first polarizer halves it: $0.5I_0$. Malus's law at the second: $0.5I_0\cos^2 60^\circ = 0.5I_0(0.25) = 0.125I_0$. Forgetting the first halving gives $0.25I_0$.

questions.stem: A prism spreads white light into a spectrum because
choices: different colors travel at different speeds in glass (dispersion)
different colors reflect at different angles
white light is polarized by the prism
questions.explanation: The index of refraction depends on wavelength (violet is slowed and bent more than red), so each color refracts by a different angle.

questions.stem: Light with a vacuum wavelength of 600 nm enters glass with $n = 1.50$. What are its wavelength and frequency inside the glass? ($c = 3.00\times10^8$ m/s)
questions.explanation: The frequency is fixed by the source: $f = c/\lambda = (3.00\times10^8)/(600\times10^{-9}) = 5.0\times10^{14}$ Hz, in air or glass. The speed drops to $c/n$, so the wavelength shrinks to $600/1.50 = 400$ nm. Multiplying by $n$ gives 900 nm; $3.3\times10^{14}$ Hz wrongly lets the frequency change with the speed.

questions.stem: Maxwell found the speed of electromagnetic waves to be $1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}$. Why was this result so important?
choices: It matched the measured speed of light, revealing light as an EM wave
It proved the existence of an ether
It showed EM waves are longitudinal
questions.explanation: The constants from electricity and magnetism gave $3.00\times10^8$ m/s, the speed of light, uniting optics with electromagnetism.

questions.stem: Unpolarized light of intensity $I_0$ meets two crossed polarizers (axes at $90^\circ$), so nothing gets through. A third polarizer is then slipped between them at $45^\circ$ to each. Now the transmitted intensity is
questions.explanation: First polarizer: $0.50I_0$. Middle one at $45^\circ$: $0.50I_0\cos^2 45^\circ = 0.25I_0$. Last one, at $45^\circ$ to the middle: $0.25I_0\cos^2 45^\circ = 0.125I_0$. Each polarizer re-polarizes the light along its own axis, so only the angle between neighbors matters. $0.25I_0$ stops after the middle polarizer.

questions.stem: An object is 60 cm from a converging lens of focal length 20 cm. Where is the image?
choices: 30 cm on the far side, real
questions.explanation: $\dfrac1{d_i} = \dfrac1{20} - \dfrac1{60} = \dfrac{2}{60}$, so $d_i = +30$ cm: real, on the far side, inverted, half size ($m = -0.5$).

questions.stem: An object is 10 cm from a converging lens of focal length 15 cm. The image is
choices: real, inverted, 30 cm from the lens
questions.explanation: $\dfrac1{d_i} = \dfrac1{15} - \dfrac1{10} = -\dfrac1{30}$: $d_i = -30$ cm (virtual). $m = -(-30)/10 = +3$: upright and 3 times larger. Inside $f$, a converging lens is a magnifier.

questions.stem: A concave mirror has a radius of curvature of 20 cm. An object is 30 cm away. Where is the image?
choices: 15 cm in front of the mirror, real
60 cm in front of the mirror
questions.explanation: $f = R/2 = 10$ cm. $\dfrac1{d_i} = \dfrac1{10} - \dfrac1{30}$, so $d_i = 15$ cm, positive: real, in front of the mirror. Using $f = R = 20$ cm gives 60 cm.

questions.stem: A convex mirror always produces an image that is
questions.explanation: With $f < 0$, the equation always gives $d_i < 0$ (virtual) and $0 < m < 1$ (upright, reduced). That's why convex mirrors give a wide field of view.

questions.stem: An image has magnification $m = -2.0$. It is
questions.explanation: A negative $m$ means inverted; $|m| = 2$ means twice the object's size.

questions.stem: A diverging lens has focal length $-10$ cm. An object is 10 cm away. Where is the image?
questions.explanation: $\dfrac1{d_i} = -\dfrac1{10} - \dfrac1{10} = -\dfrac{2}{10}$, so $d_i = -5.0$ cm: virtual, upright, half size. Using $f = +10$ cm gives "at infinity".

questions.stem: Where must an object be placed relative to a converging lens to form a real, enlarged image (as in a projector)?
questions.explanation: Between $f$ and $2f$ the image forms beyond $2f$ on the far side: real, inverted and enlarged. Beyond $2f$ it's reduced; inside $f$ it's virtual.

questions.stem: A nearsighted person's eyeglass prescription is $-2.5$ diopters. What kind of lens and focal length is that?
questions.explanation: $P = 1/f$: $f = 1/(-2.5) = -0.40$ m. Negative power means a diverging lens, which corrects nearsightedness.

questions.stem: Your image in a flat bathroom mirror is
choices: virtual, upright, the same size, and as far behind the mirror as you are in front
questions.explanation: Rays only appear to come from behind a plane mirror (virtual); the image is upright, unmagnified, and $d_i = -d_o$.

questions.stem: Two lenses are used in sequence; the first gives $m_1 = -4$ and the second $m_2 = -10$. The overall magnification is
questions.explanation: Magnifications multiply: $(-4)(-10) = +40$. The final image is upright relative to the object (inverted twice), as in some microscope arrangements.

questions.stem: By the lensmaker's equation, $1/f = (n - 1)(1/R_1 - 1/R_2)$, a lens immersed in water instead of air will have
questions.explanation: In water, the relevant index is $n_{\text{lens}}/n_{\text{water}}$, closer to 1, so $(n - 1)$ shrinks and $f$ grows: the lens bends light less. That's why your vision is blurry underwater.

questions.stem: An object starts far from a converging lens and moves toward it, stopping just outside the focal point. During this motion the real image
choices: moves toward the lens and shrinks
moves away from the lens and grows larger
questions.explanation: From $\dfrac{1}{d_i} = \dfrac1f - \dfrac{1}{d_o}$: as $d_o$ shrinks toward $f$, $\dfrac{1}{d_o}$ grows toward $\dfrac1f$, so $\dfrac{1}{d_i}$ shrinks toward zero and $d_i$ grows without limit. With $|m| = d_i/d_o$, the image also grows. It stays real while the object is outside $f$; only inside $f$ does it become virtual. The image is near the focal point only when the object is very far away.

questions.stem: An eye's near point is
choices: the farthest distance at which the eye can focus
the closest distance at which the eye can focus clearly
the focal length of the relaxed eye
the distance from the eye's lens to the retina
