questions.explanation: The near point is the closest an object can be and still be focused, by convention 25 cm for a young adult. The farthest such distance is the far point. The lens-to-retina distance (about 2.0 cm) is fixed and is not the near point, and the relaxed eye's focal length is also about 2.0 cm.

questions.stem: A nearsighted person's far point is 2.0 m. What contact-lens power lets them see distant objects clearly?
questions.explanation: The lens must image a distant object at the far point, on the object's side: $f = -2.0$ m, so $P = 1/f = -0.50$ D. A converging $+0.50$ D lens has the wrong sign (it makes myopia worse). $-2.0$ D uses $f$ instead of $1/f$, and $-0.0050$ D uses 200 cm instead of 2.0 m.

questions.stem: A farsighted person's near point is 50 cm. What lens power lets them read a page held 25 cm away? (Treat the lens as at the eye.)
questions.explanation: Object at $d_o = 25$ cm, virtual image at the near point, $d_i = -50$ cm: $1/f = 1/25 - 1/50 = 1/50$, so $f = 50$ cm $= 0.50$ m and $P = +2.0$ D. Taking $d_i = +50$ cm (forgetting the image is virtual) gives $+6.0$ D. A diverging lens ($-2.0$ D) is the correction for myopia, and $+0.020$ D comes from leaving $f$ in centimeters.

questions.stem: A magnifying glass has a focal length of 4.0 cm. What is its angular magnification when the image is at infinity (relaxed eye)? (Near point 25 cm.)
questions.explanation: With the object at the focal point, $M = 25\text{ cm}/f = 25/4.0 = 6.25 \approx 6.3$. The value 7.3 is $1 + 25/f$, which applies when the image is at the near point instead. 0.16 is the ratio upside down, and 100 multiplies 25 by 4.0.

questions.stem: Why does a magnifying glass make a small object look bigger?
choices: It lets the object sit closer than the near point while the eye still sees it in focus, so the object fills a larger angle
It forms a real, enlarged image that the eye looks at from 25 cm
It gathers more light, and brighter objects look bigger
It moves the image farther away, and farther images look bigger
questions.explanation: Apparent size is set by the angle an object subtends. Unaided, you can't bring the object closer than 25 cm and keep it sharp. The lens makes a virtual image you can focus on, so the object can sit just inside $f$, much closer, and fill a larger angle. The image of a magnifier is virtual, not real, and distance alone makes things look smaller, not bigger.

questions.stem: A microscope objective forms an image with magnification $-40$. The eyepiece has a focal length of 2.5 cm and is used with the final image at infinity. What is the overall magnification? (Near point 25 cm.)
questions.explanation: The eyepiece's angular magnification is $25/2.5 = 10$, and the stages multiply: $M = (-40)(10) = -400$. Adding them gives $-50$. Dividing $-40$ by the eyepiece focal length gives $-16$, and dividing by the eyepiece magnification gives $-4.0$.

questions.stem: A refracting telescope has an objective of focal length 120 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 3.0 cm. Find its angular magnification and its approximate length.
questions.explanation: $M = -f_o/f_e = -120/3.0 = -40$ (inverted), and the lenses sit $f_o + f_e = 123$ cm apart because they share a focal point. Multiplying the focal lengths gives $-360$, inverting the ratio gives $-0.025$, and subtracting the focal lengths gives 117 cm.

questions.stem: Astronomers build telescopes with very wide objectives mainly because a wider objective
choices: gathers more light and resolves finer detail
removes the need for an eyepiece
questions.explanation: Light collected grows with the objective's area, so fainter objects show up, and the smallest resolvable angle shrinks as $\lambda/D$. Magnification is $f_o/f_e$, set by focal lengths, not diameter. A wide objective doesn't shorten the tube or replace the eyepiece.

questions.stem: Model an eye as one lens 2.0 cm from the retina. By how much must its power increase to change focus from a very distant object to one 25 cm away?
questions.explanation: Distant object: $P = 1/0.020 = 50$ D. At 25 cm: $P = 1/0.25 + 1/0.020 = 54$ D. The increase is $54 - 50 = 4.0$ D. The values 54 D and 50 D are the two powers themselves, not the change, and 0.25 D uses the distance instead of its reciprocal.

questions.stem: What causes presbyopia, the need for reading glasses with age?
choices: The eye's lens stiffens, so accommodation decreases and the near point moves farther away
The eyeball grows longer, so the far point moves closer
The cornea becomes more strongly curved
The retina loses its sensitivity to red light
questions.explanation: With age the lens can't bulge as much, so the eye can't add enough power for close objects and the near point recedes. Converging reading glasses supply the missing power. An eye that focuses too strongly (a long eyeball or steep cornea) is myopia, a different problem; color sensitivity isn't involved.

questions.stem: The Moon (diameter $3.5\times10^{6}$ m, distance $3.8\times10^{8}$ m) is viewed through a telescope with angular magnification of magnitude 50. About what angle does its image fill?
questions.explanation: Unaided, $\theta_0 \approx h/d = 3.5\times10^{6}/3.8\times10^{8} = 0.0092$ rad. The telescope multiplies the angle by 50: $0.46$ rad (about 26°). 0.0092 rad forgets the telescope, 0.00018 rad divides by 50, and 26 rad mixes up degrees and radians.

questions.stem: In a compound microscope, the image formed by the objective lens is
questions.explanation: The specimen sits just outside the objective's focal point (between $f$ and $2f$), which gives a real, inverted, enlarged image inside the tube. The eyepiece then acts as a magnifier on that real image and produces the virtual image you see.

questions.stem: In a double-slit experiment, $\lambda = 500$ nm, $d = 0.50$ mm and the screen is 1.5 m away. What is the spacing between bright fringes?
If the slit spacing in a double-slit experiment is halved, the fringe spacing
questions.explanation: $\Delta y = \lambda L/d$, inversely proportional to $d$: closer slits spread the pattern out.

questions.stem: Why don't two ordinary light bulbs produce a visible interference pattern?
choices: They are not coherent; their phase relationship changes randomly
questions.explanation: A stable pattern requires a constant phase difference. Independent sources emit with randomly varying phases, so any fringes wash out instantly.

questions.stem: A grating with 600 lines/mm is lit with 500 nm light. At what angle is the first-order maximum?
questions.explanation: $d = 1/600$ mm $= 1.67\times10^{-6}$ m; $\sin\theta = \lambda/d = 0.30$, so $\theta = 17.5^\circ$.

questions.stem: In single-slit diffraction, the condition $a\sin\theta = m\lambda$ ($m = \pm1, \pm2, \ldots$) locates
choices: the edges of the slit's shadow
questions.explanation: For a single slit this is the condition for minima. (For double slits and gratings, $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ gives maxima: a common mix-up.)

questions.stem: Light of wavelength 600 nm passes through a slit 0.10 mm wide. What is the angle of the first dark fringe?
questions.explanation: $\sin\theta = \lambda/a = 600\times10^{-9}/1.0\times10^{-4} = 0.0060$, so $\theta = 0.34^\circ$. The central bright band spans twice this.

questions.stem: Why can a larger telescope mirror resolve finer detail?
choices: It has a shorter focal length
questions.explanation: Diffraction blurs point sources into disks of angular size about $1.22\lambda/D$. A larger aperture $D$ shrinks the blur, separating closer objects.

questions.stem: A soap film ($n = 1.33$) in air strongly reflects 532 nm light. What is its minimum thickness?
questions.explanation: One reflection (top surface) flips phase, so constructive reflection needs $2nt = \tfrac12\lambda$: $t = 532/(4 \times 1.33) = 100$ nm. Ignoring the phase flip gives 200 nm.

questions.stem: Compared with a double slit of the same spacing, a diffraction grating produces maxima that are
choices: at the same angles and equally broad
at the same angles but much sharper and brighter
questions.explanation: The maxima still satisfy $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$, but with $N$ slits their width shrinks as $1/N$ and peak intensity grows as $N^2$.

questions.stem: A grating has $d = 2.0$ μm. For 700 nm light, what is the highest order maximum that can appear?
questions.explanation: $\sin\theta = m\lambda/d \le 1$ requires $m \le 2.0/0.70 = 2.86$, so $m = 2$.

questions.stem: In a double-slit pattern, the first dark fringe on either side of the central bright fringe is where the path difference $d\sin\theta$ from the two slits equals
questions.explanation: Dark fringes need the two waves to arrive exactly out of step: a path difference of $(m + \tfrac12)\lambda$, the smallest being $\lambda/2$. A path difference of $\lambda$ gives the first-order bright fringe, and 0 is the central bright fringe.

questions.stem: A lens ($n = 1.52$) is coated with a film of $n = 1.38$ to cancel reflected 550 nm light. What is the minimum film thickness?
questions.explanation: Both reflections (air to film, film to glass) go to a higher index, so both flip and the flips cancel. Destructive interference then needs $2nt = \tfrac12\lambda$: $t = \dfrac{550}{4(1.38)} = 100$ nm. Using the one-flip soap-film condition, $2nt = \lambda$, gives 199 nm; 138 nm forgets that the wavelength in the film is $\lambda/n$.

questions.stem: A spaceship passes Earth at $0.80c$. A clock on board ticks 1.0 s between two events at the clock. How long between those events according to Earth observers?
questions.explanation: $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1 - 0.64} = 1.667$. The ship's clock measures proper time, so Earth measures $\Delta t = \gamma\Delta t_0 = 1.67$ s: moving clocks run slow. 0.60 s divides instead of multiplying.

questions.stem: Which statement is one of Einstein's postulates of special relativity?
choices: The speed of light in vacuum is the same in all inertial frames
Time passes at the same rate for all observers
Nothing can move faster than sound
questions.explanation: The two postulates are the principle of relativity and the constancy of $c$. Absolute time is exactly what relativity abandons.

questions.stem: A rod has proper length 50 m. How long is it measured by an observer it passes at $0.60c$ (moving along its length)?
questions.explanation: $\gamma = 1.25$; $L = L_0/\gamma = 50/1.25 = 40$ m. Multiplying by $\gamma$ (62.5 m) gets contraction backwards.

questions.stem: A ship moving at $0.50c$ fires a probe forward at $0.50c$ relative to the ship. What is the probe's speed relative to the ground?
questions.explanation: $u = \dfrac{0.50c + 0.50c}{1 + (0.50)(0.50)} = \dfrac{1.0c}{1.25} = 0.80c$. Classical addition would give $1.0c$, which relativity forbids for a massive object.

questions.stem: How much energy is equivalent to 1.0 g of mass? ($c = 3.0\times10^8$ m/s)
questions.explanation: $E = mc^2 = (1.0\times10^{-3}\text{ kg})(9.0\times10^{16}) = 9.0\times10^{13}$ J. Forgetting to convert grams to kilograms gives $9.0\times10^{16}$ J.

questions.stem: An electron ($mc^2 = 0.511$ MeV) moves at $0.60c$. What is its kinetic energy?
questions.explanation: $\gamma = 1.25$; $K = (\gamma - 1)mc^2 = 0.25(0.511) = 0.128$ MeV. The classical $\tfrac12mv^2 = 0.092$ MeV underestimates it; 0.639 MeV is the total energy.

questions.stem: Why can't a massive object be accelerated to the speed of light?
choices: Its momentum $\gamma mv$ and energy grow without limit as $v \to c$, requiring infinite work
Light would slow down to match it
questions.explanation: $\gamma \to \infty$ as $v \to c$, so the kinetic energy $(\gamma - 1)mc^2$ needed is infinite.

questions.stem: Muons from the upper atmosphere reach the ground in large numbers even though their rest-frame half-life would let them travel only a few hundred meters. In the muons' own frame, the explanation is
questions.explanation: From the ground, the muons' clocks run slow (time dilation). In the muons' frame their half-life is normal, but the atmosphere rushing past is contracted by $\gamma$. Both views agree on how many reach the ground.

questions.stem: For a photon, which relationship between energy and momentum holds?
questions.explanation: $E^2 = (pc)^2 + (mc^2)^2$ with $m = 0$ gives $E = pc$.

questions.stem: Two lightning strikes hit the ends of a moving train simultaneously according to an observer on the platform. An observer on the train sees them
choices: in reversed order only if the train moves faster than light
questions.explanation: Simultaneity is relative: events simultaneous in one frame generally aren't in another moving relative to it. (The train observer sees the front strike first.)

questions.stem: At what speed is a particle's kinetic energy equal to its rest energy?
questions.explanation: $K = (\gamma - 1)mc^2 = mc^2$ requires $\gamma = 2$, so $1 - v^2/c^2 = \tfrac14$ and $v = \sqrt{0.75}\,c = 0.866c$. Setting $\tfrac12mv^2 = mc^2$ gives $1.41c$, which is impossible; $0.707c$ comes from $\gamma^2 = 2$ instead of $\gamma = 2$.

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon of wavelength 620 nm? ($hc = 1240$ eV·nm)
questions.explanation: $E = hc/\lambda = 1240/620 = 2.0$ eV. Dividing the other way gives 0.50 eV.

questions.stem: In the photoelectric effect, making the light brighter (same frequency, above threshold)
choices: increases the number of ejected electrons, not their maximum energy
increases the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons
questions.explanation: Brighter light means more photons, so more electrons; each electron still absorbs one photon of the same energy, so $K_{\max} = hf - \phi$ is unchanged.

questions.stem: Light of 250 nm strikes a metal with work function 4.5 eV. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electrons?
What photon energy is emitted when a hydrogen electron drops from $n = 2$ to $n = 1$?
questions.explanation: $\Delta E = 13.6(1 - \tfrac14) = 10.2$ eV, an ultraviolet photon (122 nm). 3.4 eV is $|E_2|$.

questions.stem: Why does each element have its own unique line spectrum?
choices: Each element's atoms have a unique set of energy levels, and photons carry the differences
Each element absorbs all colors equally
The electrons move at different speeds
questions.explanation: Emitted photons have energies equal to differences between allowed levels, and those levels are set by the nucleus's charge and the electron arrangement, different for each element.

questions.stem: What is the de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving at $1.0\times10^6$ m/s? ($h = 6.63\times10^{-34}$ J·s, $m_e = 9.11\times10^{-31}$ kg)
questions.explanation: $\lambda = h/(mv) = 6.63\times10^{-34}/(9.11\times10^{-31}\times10^6) = 7.3\times10^{-10}$ m, comparable to atomic spacings.

questions.stem: Which experiment showed that electrons have wave properties?
questions.explanation: Electrons scattered from a nickel crystal produced a diffraction pattern matching $\lambda = h/p$. The photoelectric effect showed the particle nature of light.

questions.stem: Why don't red photons eject electrons from a metal with a work function of 2.3 eV, no matter how bright the light?
choices: Red light is not an electromagnetic wave
Each red photon has less energy (about 1.8 eV) than the work function
Red light is absorbed by air
questions.explanation: One photon frees one electron. A 700 nm photon carries $1240/700 = 1.8$ eV, short of the 2.3 eV needed, and electrons can't pool energy from several photons in ordinary light.

questions.stem: How much energy is needed to ionize a hydrogen atom from its ground state?
questions.explanation: Raising the electron from $E_1 = -13.6$ eV to $E_\infty = 0$ takes 13.6 eV.

questions.stem: A particle confined to a box of width $L$ has energies $E_n = n^2h^2/(8mL^2)$. If the box is made narrower, the energy levels
questions.explanation: $E_n \propto 1/L^2$, so tighter confinement raises every level and widens the spacing, a consequence of shorter allowed wavelengths (and the uncertainty principle).

questions.stem: On a graph of maximum photoelectron kinetic energy versus light frequency, the slope equals
questions.explanation: $K_{\max} = hf - \phi$ is a line with slope $h$ (the same for every metal) and intercept $-\phi$.

questions.stem: A star's spectrum peaks at 725 nm. Treating it as a blackbody, what is its surface temperature? (Wien constant $2.898\times10^{-3}$ m·K)
questions.explanation: $T = 2.898\times10^{-3}/\lambda_{\max} = 2.898\times10^{-3}/(725\times10^{-9}) = 4.0\times10^{3}$ K, a cool orange-red star. Leaving the wavelength in nm gives $4.0\times10^{-6}$ K, and multiplying instead of dividing gives $2.1\times10^{-9}$ K. Subtracting 273 gives $3.7\times10^{3}$, which is the temperature in °C, not kelvins.

questions.stem: A blackbody is heated to a higher temperature. What happens to its spectrum?
choices: The peak moves to shorter wavelengths and the total power increases
The peak moves to longer wavelengths and the total power increases
The peak stays put and only the total power increases
The peak moves to shorter wavelengths and the total power stays the same
questions.explanation: Wien's law, $\lambda_{\max}T = \text{constant}$, moves the peak to shorter wavelengths as $T$ rises (red, then orange, then white-hot), and the total power grows as $T^4$. The other combinations each miss one of these two effects or reverse the direction of the shift.

questions.stem: X-rays of wavelength 50.0 pm scatter off nearly free electrons. What is the wavelength of the X-rays scattered through 90°? ($h/(m_ec) = 2.43$ pm)
questions.explanation: $\Delta\lambda = (2.43\text{ pm})(1 - \cos 90^\circ) = 2.43$ pm, so $\lambda' = 50.0 + 2.43 = 52.4$ pm. The photon loses energy to the electron, so the wavelength gets longer; subtracting the shift gives 47.6 pm. 54.9 pm uses the 180° shift ($1 - \cos\theta = 2$), and 50.0 pm takes $\cos 90^\circ$ as 1, giving no shift.

questions.stem: Why is the Compton shift easy to see with X-rays but not with visible light?
choices: The shift is at most about 5 pm, a tiny fraction of a visible wavelength but a large fraction of an X-ray wavelength
Visible light behaves only as a wave and X-rays only as particles
questions.explanation: The shift $\dfrac{h}{m_ec}(1 - \cos\theta)$ is at most 4.86 pm whatever the wavelength. Against a 500 nm visible wavelength that is a change of one part in $10^{5}$; against a 50 pm X-ray it is about 10%. Visible photons do carry momentum $h/\lambda$ and do scatter from electrons, and both kinds of light show wave and particle behavior.

questions.stem: In Compton scattering, at what scattering angle does the photon lose the most energy to the electron?
questions.explanation: The wavelength shift $\dfrac{h}{m_ec}(1 - \cos\theta)$ is largest when $\cos\theta = -1$, at 180° (bounced straight back), where it equals $2h/(m_ec) = 4.86$ pm. A longer wavelength means a lower-energy photon, so this is where the electron gains the most. At 0° the photon barely deflects and loses nothing; 90° and 45° give intermediate shifts.

questions.stem: What is the largest number of electrons the $n = 3$ shell can hold?
questions.explanation: The shell has subshells $l = 0, 1, 2$ with $1 + 3 + 5 = 9$ orbitals, each holding two spin states: $2n^2 = 18$. Counting orbitals without spin gives 9. Eight is the number of elements in the third row of the periodic table, which is shorter because 3d fills after 4s. Six is $2n$.

questions.stem: Which values of the orbital quantum number $l$ are allowed when $n = 3$?
questions.explanation: $l$ runs from 0 to $n - 1$, so 0, 1 and 2 (3s, 3p, 3d). Letting $l$ reach $n$ is the common slip. The list from $-2$ to 2 is the set of $m_l$ values for $l = 2$, not values of $l$.

questions.stem: Which statement is the Pauli exclusion principle?
choices: No two electrons in an atom can be in the same shell
No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four quantum numbers
Electrons always fill the highest energy levels first
Each orbital can hold only one electron
questions.explanation: Pauli forbids two electrons sharing all four of $n$, $l$, $m_l$, $m_s$. A shell holds many electrons (up to $2n^2$), and an orbital holds two, one with each spin; one per orbital forgets spin. Electrons fill the lowest available levels first, not the highest.

questions.stem: What is the maximum number of electrons in a d subshell?
questions.explanation: A d subshell has $l = 2$, so $m_l = -2$ to 2 (5 values), each with 2 spins: $2(2l + 1) = 10$. Five forgets spin, 6 is the p subshell, and 14 is the f subshell.

questions.stem: What is the ground-state electron configuration of magnesium ($Z = 12$)?
questions.explanation: After 1s (2), 2s (2) and 2p (6), the last two electrons go into 3s. A p subshell holds at most 6, so $2p^8$ breaks the Pauli principle. 3p lies above 3s, and there is no 2d subshell ($l$ can be at most $n - 1 = 1$).

questions.stem: An X-ray tube operates at 25 kV. What is the shortest wavelength in its spectrum? ($hc = 1240$ eV·nm)
questions.explanation: The most energetic photon takes an electron's full energy, $eV = 25\,000$ eV, so $\lambda_{\min} = 1240/25\,000 = 0.0496$ nm (49.6 pm). Using 25 instead of 25 000 eV gives 49.6 nm. Halving the voltage, as if the energy were $\tfrac12eV$, gives 0.0992 nm, and dividing 25 000 by 1240 gives 20.2.

questions.stem: The voltage on an X-ray tube is increased. What happens to the X-ray spectrum?
choices: The cutoff wavelength and the characteristic lines both shift to shorter wavelengths
Neither the cutoff nor the characteristic lines change
The cutoff wavelength gets shorter, but the characteristic lines stay at the same wavelengths
The characteristic lines shift, but the cutoff wavelength stays the same
questions.explanation: The cutoff $\lambda_{\min} = hc/(eV)$ depends only on the voltage, so it shortens. The characteristic lines come from the target atoms' own inner energy levels, which don't depend on how hard the electrons hit, so they stay put (they may get brighter).

questions.stem: Estimate the energy of the Kα X-ray line of molybdenum ($Z = 42$) using $E \approx 10.2\text{ eV}\,(Z - 1)^2$.
questions.explanation: $E \approx 10.2(41)^2 = 10.2(1681) = 1.71\times10^{4}$ eV $= 17.1$ keV (measured: 17.5 keV). Using $Z^2$ instead of $(Z - 1)^2$ gives 18.0 keV. Using 13.6 eV, which forgets the $(1 - \tfrac14)$ factor for the drop from $n = 2$ to $n = 1$, gives 22.9 keV. Forgetting to square gives 0.42 keV.

questions.stem: A photon whose energy matches an atom's transition passes an atom in the upper state and causes stimulated emission. What comes out?
choices: One photon in a random direction with a random phase
Two photons with the same energy, direction and phase
One photon with twice the original energy
One photon and an ejected electron
questions.explanation: The passing photon continues, and the atom adds an exact copy of it (same energy, direction, phase and polarization). That copying is how a laser amplifies light. A random direction and phase describes spontaneous emission. The atom only releases its transition energy, so no photon of twice the energy appears, and no electron is ejected.

questions.stem: Why must a laser have a population inversion?
choices: To make the emitted light polarized
To make spontaneous emission happen faster
To stop the atoms absorbing the pump energy
So that stimulated emission happens more often than absorption
questions.explanation: A passing photon can either be absorbed by an atom in the lower state or stimulate emission from one in the upper state. Only if more atoms are in the upper state does emission win, so the light grows. Polarization and the speed of spontaneous emission are not what the inversion is for, and the atoms must absorb pump energy to get into the upper state at all.

questions.stem: A laser transition runs from a level 2.10 eV above the ground state to one 0.30 eV above it. What is the laser wavelength? ($hc = 1240$ eV·nm)
questions.explanation: The photon carries the difference, $2.10 - 0.30 = 1.80$ eV, so $\lambda = 1240/1.80 = 689$ nm (red). Using the upper level alone gives 590 nm, adding the two levels gives 517 nm, and using the lower level alone gives 4130 nm.

questions.stem: Why do lithium, sodium and potassium have similar chemical behavior?
choices: They have the same total number of electrons
They have the same number of filled shells
Each has a single s electron outside completely filled subshells
Each has a half-filled p subshell
questions.explanation: Chemistry depends mostly on the outermost electrons. Lithium ($2s^1$), sodium ($3s^1$) and potassium ($4s^1$) each have one loosely held s electron beyond filled subshells, which they give up easily. Their totals (3, 11, 19) and numbers of filled shells differ, and none has an unfilled p subshell in its ground state.

questions.stem: A radioactive sample has a half-life of 3.0 hours. What fraction remains after 12 hours?
questions.explanation: 12 hours is 4 half-lives: $(\tfrac12)^4 = 1/16$. Dividing 12 by 3 and calling it 1/4 confuses the number of half-lives with the fraction.

questions.stem: How many neutrons are in a nucleus of $^{235}_{92}\text{U}$?
$^{226}_{88}\text{Ra}$ undergoes alpha decay. What is the daughter nucleus?
questions.explanation: Alpha emission removes 2 protons and 2 neutrons: $Z = 86$ (radon), $A = 222$. Both $Z$ and $A$ balance: $226 = 222 + 4$, $88 = 86 + 2$.

questions.stem: In beta-minus decay, what happens inside the nucleus?
choices: Two protons and two neutrons are emitted
The nucleus loses energy as a photon
A neutron becomes a proton, emitting an electron and an antineutrino
questions.explanation: β⁻: $n \to p + e^- + \bar\nu$, so $Z$ rises by 1 and $A$ is unchanged (e.g. carbon-14 → nitrogen-14).

questions.stem: A nucleus has a mass defect of 0.100 u. What is its binding energy? (1 u = 931.5 MeV/$c^2$)
Both fission of uranium and fusion of hydrogen release energy because
choices: both increase the total number of nucleons
both move toward nuclei with higher binding energy per nucleon (near iron)
both decrease the binding energy per nucleon
questions.explanation: Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56. Splitting heavy nuclei or fusing light ones both produce more tightly bound products; the mass difference is released as energy.

questions.stem: A sample's activity is 80 kBq. Its half-life is 5.0 days. What is the activity after 20 days?
questions.explanation: 20 days is 4 half-lives: $80/2^4 = 5.0$ kBq. Activity decays with the same half-life as the number of nuclei.

questions.stem: A decay constant is $\lambda = 0.0231$ per day. What is the half-life?
questions.explanation: $T_{1/2} = \ln 2/\lambda = 0.693/0.0231 = 30$ days. 43 days is $1/\lambda$, which leaves out the factor $\ln 2$.

questions.stem: What holds protons together in a nucleus despite their electric repulsion?
choices: The strong nuclear force, which is very strong but short-ranged
questions.explanation: The strong force attracts nucleons strongly over about $10^{-15}$ m, overcoming the Coulomb repulsion between nearby protons.

questions.stem: Which type of radiation is the most penetrating?
questions.explanation: Gamma rays (photons) need thick lead or concrete to stop; beta particles are stopped by millimeters of aluminum; alpha particles by paper or skin.

questions.stem: A bone sample has 25% of the carbon-14 activity of living bone. With $T_{1/2} = 5730$ years, how old is it?
questions.explanation: 25% is $(\tfrac12)^2$: two half-lives, $2(5730) = 11\,460$ years.

questions.stem: Sample A contains twice as many radioactive nuclei as sample B, but A's isotope has a half-life twice as long as B's. How do their activities compare right now?
questions.explanation: Activity is $R = \lambda N = \dfrac{0.693\,N}{T_{1/2}}$. A has twice the $N$ but half the $\lambda$ (twice the half-life), so $R_A = \dfrac{0.693(2N)}{2T} = R_B$. Twice B's comes from counting nuclei only; a longer half-life means each nucleus decays less often.

glossary.definition: The International System of Units, built on seven base units including the meter (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K) and mole (mol).
A unit built from base units by multiplying and dividing, such as the newton ($\text{kg·m/s}^2$) or joule ($\text{kg·m}^2/\text{s}^2$).
Writing a number as $a \times 10^n$ with $1 \le |a| < 10$; every digit of $a$ is significant.
A ratio equal to 1, such as $\tfrac{1000\text{ m}}{1\text{ km}}$, used to change units without changing the quantity.
The digits of a measured value that carry real information: all nonzero digits, zeros between them, and trailing zeros after a decimal point.
How close a measurement is to the true value.
How closely repeated measurements agree with each other, and how finely a value is stated.
The kind of physical quantity something is, written in brackets: length [L], mass [M], time [T]. Speed has dimension [L]/[T].
Checking or deriving relationships by requiring every term of an equation to have the same dimensions.
The power of ten closest to a value; used for quick estimates.
A quantity fully described by a number and a unit, with no direction (mass, time, energy, temperature).
A quantity with both magnitude and direction, such as displacement, velocity, force or momentum.
The vector sum of two or more vectors.
The projections of a vector onto the coordinate axes: $A_x = A\cos\theta$, $A_y = A\sin\theta$ for an angle measured from $+x$.
Vectors of length 1 that mark directions; $\hat\imath$, $\hat\jmath$, $\hat k$ point along $+x$, $+y$, $+z$.
$\vec A\cdot\vec B = AB\cos\phi = A_xB_x + A_yB_y + A_zB_z$, a scalar measuring how much two vectors point the same way.
$\vec A\times\vec B$, a vector of magnitude $AB\sin\phi$ perpendicular to both, with direction given by the right-hand rule.
Point the fingers of your right hand along the first vector, curl them toward the second; the thumb gives the direction of the cross product.
The description of motion (position, velocity, acceleration) without regard to its causes.
An object's coordinate relative to a chosen origin and positive direction.
Change in position, $\Delta x = x_f - x_i$ (a vector; can be negative or zero).
Total length of path traveled; always positive.
Displacement divided by elapsed time, $v_{\text{avg}} = \Delta x/\Delta t$.
Total distance divided by elapsed time.
The velocity at one instant: the slope of the tangent line to the position–time graph at that time.
Rate of change of velocity, $a = \Delta v/\Delta t$ (the slope of the velocity–time graph), in m/s². It is a vector; its sign shows the direction of the change in velocity.
The free-fall acceleration near Earth's surface, $g \approx 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$ directed downward.
Motion under the influence of gravity alone, with acceleration $g$ downward regardless of mass.
The constant speed a falling object reaches when air drag balances its weight.
Two-dimensional motion under gravity alone: constant horizontal velocity plus free fall vertically, giving a parabolic path.
Horizontal distance a projectile travels; on level ground $R = v_0^2\sin 2\theta/g$.
The component of acceleration along the velocity; it changes the speed.
The component of acceleration perpendicular to the velocity, toward the center of curvature; it changes the direction of motion.
A set of coordinate axes attached to some object, from which positions and velocities are measured.
Velocity measured in a particular frame; $\vec v_{AC} = \vec v_{AB} + \vec v_{BC}$.
A reference frame that is not accelerating; Newton's laws hold in it.
A push or pull by one object on another; a vector measured in newtons (N).
SI unit of force: $1\text{ N} = 1\text{ kg·m/s}^2$.
An object keeps a constant velocity (including rest) unless a net force acts on it.
The tendency of an object to keep its velocity; measured by its mass.
The vector sum of all forces acting on an object, $\sum\vec F$.
$\sum\vec F = m\vec a$; equivalently, the net force equals the rate of change of momentum, $\vec F_{\text{net}} = \Delta\vec p/\Delta t$.
The measure of an object's inertia (resistance to acceleration), in kilograms; the same everywhere.
The state of zero net force (and, for extended objects, zero net torque): at rest or moving at constant velocity.
The gravitational force on an object, $W = mg$, directed downward.
The contact force a surface exerts perpendicular to itself; found from Newton's second law, not assumed equal to $mg$.
If A exerts a force on B, B exerts an equal and opposite force on A. The pair acts on different objects.
A sketch of one object showing every force acting on it as an arrow; the starting point of a dynamics problem.
The normal force (scale reading) supporting an object; differs from $mg$ when the object accelerates vertically.
A contact force parallel to surfaces that opposes sliding or the tendency to slide.
Friction between sliding surfaces, $f_k = \mu_k n$, opposite to the sliding velocity.
The dimensionless ratio $\mu_k = f_k/n$ for a pair of sliding surfaces.
Friction between surfaces not sliding; adjusts to prevent motion up to $f_s = \mu_s n$.
The ratio $\mu_s = f_{s,\max}/n$; equals $\tan\theta$ at the angle where an object just starts to slide down an incline.
The pulling force a taut rope, string or cable exerts along its length.
An idealized rope with no mass, which therefore has the same tension throughout.
A massless, frictionless pulley that changes a rope's direction without changing its tension.
Two masses hung over a pulley; $a = \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}g$.
Motion in a circle at constant speed; the acceleration $v^2/r$ points to the center.
The time for one complete cycle (revolution or oscillation), $T = 1/f$.
Number of cycles per second, $f = 1/T$, in hertz (Hz).
The center-directed acceleration of circular motion, $a_c = v^2/r = \omega^2 r$.
The net inward force required for circular motion, $mv^2/r$, supplied by real forces such as tension, friction, gravity or the normal force.
Energy transferred by a force acting through a displacement: $W = Fd\cos\theta$; for a varying force, the area under the force–position graph. A scalar, in joules.
SI unit of work and energy: $1\text{ J} = 1\text{ N·m} = 1\text{ kg·m}^2/\text{s}^2$.
The total work done by all forces on an object; equals its change in kinetic energy.
Energy of motion, $K = \tfrac12mv^2 = p^2/(2m)$.
The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy: $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$.
An ideal spring exerts $F = -kx$, proportional to its stretch or compression and directed back toward equilibrium.
The stiffness $k$ of a spring in N/m: the force per unit stretch.
Stored energy of position or configuration associated with a conservative force; $W_{\text{cons}} = -\Delta U$.
A force whose work between two points is independent of the path (gravity, springs, electrostatic force).
Near Earth's surface, $U_g = mgy$ relative to a chosen zero level; in general $U = -GMm/r$.
Energy stored in a stretched or compressed spring, $U_s = \tfrac12kx^2$.
The sum of kinetic and potential energy, $E = K + U$.
If only conservative forces do work, $K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f$.
A force such as friction or drag whose work depends on the path; its work $W_{\text{nc}}$ changes the mechanical energy.
Rate of doing work or transferring energy: $P = W/\Delta t = \vec F\cdot\vec v$, in watts.
SI unit of power: $1\text{ W} = 1\text{ J/s}$. One horsepower is 746 W.
Ratio of useful output energy (or power) to input, $\eta = P_{\text{out}}/P_{\text{in}}$.
A position where $U(x) = E$, so the kinetic energy is zero and the particle reverses direction.
The product of mass and velocity, $\vec p = m\vec v$ (kg·m/s), a vector.
Force times the time it acts, $\vec J = \vec F_{\text{avg}}\Delta t$ (the area under the force–time graph), in N·s.
The impulse on an object equals its change in momentum: $\vec J = \Delta\vec p$.
With zero net external force, a system's total momentum stays constant.
The mass-weighted average position, $x_{\text{cm}} = \sum m_ix_i/M$; it moves as if all external forces acted on the total mass there.
A collision in which both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved.
A collision in which momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not.
A collision in which the objects stick together; it loses the most kinetic energy allowed by momentum conservation.
Ratio of separation speed to approach speed in a collision: 1 for elastic, 0 for perfectly inelastic.
The angle subtending an arc equal to the radius: $\theta = s/r$. A full turn is $2\pi$ rad.
The change in angular position, $\Delta\theta$, in radians.
Rate of change of angle, $\omega = \Delta\theta/\Delta t$, in rad/s; $\omega = 2\pi f$.
Rate of change of angular velocity, $\alpha = \Delta\omega/\Delta t$, in rad/s².
Revolutions per minute; $1\text{ rpm} = 2\pi/60 \approx 0.1047$ rad/s.
Resistance to angular acceleration about an axis: $I = \sum m_ir_i^2$ (kg·m²); mass farther from the axis counts more.
$I = I_{\text{cm}} + Md^2$ for an axis parallel to one through the center of mass, a distance $d$ away.
Kinetic energy of rotation, $K = \tfrac12I\omega^2$.
The turning effect of a force about an axis: $\tau = rF\sin\theta$, or $\vec\tau = \vec r\times\vec F$ (N·m).
The perpendicular distance from the axis to a force's line of action; $\tau = (\text{lever arm})\times F$.
Rolling in which the contact point is momentarily at rest, so $v_{\text{cm}} = R\omega$.
$L = I\omega$ for a rigid body about a fixed axis; in general $\vec L = \vec r\times\vec p$. Changed only by torque: $\tau = \Delta L/\Delta t$.
With zero net external torque, $L$ is constant: $I_i\omega_i = I_f\omega_f$.
A rapidly spinning wheel whose large angular momentum resists changes in direction; a torque makes it precess.
The slow rotation of a spinning object's axis caused by a torque perpendicular to its angular momentum; rate $\Omega = \tau/L$.
The state of a rigid body at rest with $\sum\vec F = 0$ and $\sum\tau = 0$.
The point where an object's total weight effectively acts; equals the center of mass in uniform gravity.
Force per unit area on a material, $F/A$, in pascals; tensile stress pulls, compressive stress pushes.
The fractional change in length, $\Delta L/L_0$; it has no units.
The ratio of tensile (or compressive) stress to strain in the linear range, $Y = \dfrac{F/A}{\Delta L/L_0}$; about $2.0\times10^{11}$ Pa for steel.
A deformation that disappears completely when the load is removed; stress is proportional to strain.
The largest stress a material can take and still return fully to its original shape.
Permanent deformation that remains after the load is removed, once the stress has exceeded the elastic limit.
The greatest stress a material can withstand before it starts to fail.
Force per unit area applied parallel to a surface, $F/A$.
The sideways displacement of one face relative to the opposite face divided by the distance between them, $\Delta x/L_0$.
The ratio of shear stress to shear strain, $S = \dfrac{F/A}{\Delta x/L_0}$; fluids have none.
The resistance to uniform compression, $B = -\dfrac{\Delta P}{\Delta V/V_0}$; about $2.2\times10^{9}$ Pa for water.
Any two masses attract with $F = Gm_1m_2/r^2$ along the line joining them.
$G = 6.67\times10^{-11}$ N·m²/kg², the constant in Newton's law of gravitation.
A dependence of the form $1/r^2$, as in gravity, Coulomb's law and the intensity of a point source.
An equatorial orbit with a 24-hour period (radius about $4.22\times10^7$ m), so the satellite stays above one point.
(1) Orbits are ellipses with the Sun at a focus; (2) equal areas in equal times; (3) $T^2 \propto a^3$.
Minimum launch speed to coast to infinity: $v_{\text{esc}} = \sqrt{2GM/R}$ (11.2 km/s for Earth).
Oscillation driven by a restoring force proportional to displacement, $F = -kx$; $x = A\cos(\omega t + \phi)$.
The maximum displacement from equilibrium in an oscillation or wave.
$\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi/T$ (rad/s); for a spring, $\omega = \sqrt{k/m}$.
The angle $\phi$ in $x = A\cos(\omega t + \phi)$ that sets where the motion starts in its cycle.
A point mass on a light string; for small swings $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$, independent of mass and amplitude.
A rigid body swinging about a pivot a distance $d$ from its center of mass; $T = 2\pi\sqrt{I/(mgd)}$.
Loss of an oscillator's energy to friction or drag, making its amplitude decay.
Large-amplitude response when a system is driven at its natural frequency.
A traveling disturbance that carries energy through a medium (or through space) without carrying matter along.
A wave that needs a material medium, such as sound or waves on a string.
A wave in which the medium moves perpendicular to the direction of travel.
A wave in which the medium moves parallel to the direction of travel, in compressions and rarefactions (e.g. sound).
The distance over which a wave repeats, crest to crest; $v = f\lambda$.
Mass per unit length of a string, $\mu = m/L$ (kg/m).
Where waves overlap, the net displacement is the sum of the individual displacements.
Overlap of waves in step, so their displacements add (path difference $m\lambda$).
Overlap of waves out of step, so their displacements cancel (path difference $(m + \tfrac12)\lambda$).
The difference in distance traveled by two waves to a point; it determines whether they interfere constructively or destructively.
A stationary oscillation pattern formed by two identical waves traveling in opposite directions.
A point in a standing wave that does not move; adjacent nodes are $\lambda/2$ apart.
A point of maximum oscillation in a standing wave, midway between nodes.
The allowed standing-wave frequencies of a system; for a string fixed at both ends, $f_n = nv/(2L)$.
The lowest standing-wave frequency of a system, $f_1$.
Power per unit area carried by a wave (W/m²); from a point source $I = P/(4\pi r^2)$.
$k = 2\pi/\lambda$ (rad/m), the spatial analog of angular frequency.
The perceived highness or lowness of a sound, determined by its frequency.
Sound below about 20 Hz, too low for humans to hear.
Sound above about 20 kHz, too high for humans to hear; used in medical imaging and sonar.
$\beta = 10\log_{10}(I/I_0)$ in decibels, with $I_0 = 10^{-12}$ W/m².
Unit of sound intensity level; +10 dB is ten times the intensity, +3 dB about twice.
The rate at which loudness throbs when two close frequencies combine: $f_{\text{beat}} = |f_1 - f_2|$.
The change in observed frequency due to relative motion of source and observer: $f' = f\dfrac{v \pm v_o}{v \mp v_s}$.
A cone of piled-up wavefronts from a source moving faster than the wave speed; half-angle $\sin\theta = v/v_s$.
Mass per unit volume, $\rho = m/V$ (kg/m³); water is 1000 kg/m³.
Perpendicular force per unit area, $P = F/A$, in pascals.
SI unit of pressure, $1\text{ Pa} = 1\text{ N/m}^2$; 1 atm $= 1.013\times10^5$ Pa.
Pressure above atmospheric, $P - P_{\text{atm}}$; what tire gauges read.
Total pressure including the atmosphere's contribution.
An instrument measuring atmospheric pressure, classically a mercury column ($P_{\text{atm}} = \rho gh$, 760 mm at sea level).
A pressure change applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout it; basis of hydraulics, $F_1/A_1 = F_2/A_2$.
The net upward force a fluid exerts on an immersed object, equal to the weight of fluid displaced.
$F_B = \rho_{\text{fluid}}V_{\text{displaced}}\,g$.
A model fluid that is incompressible, nonviscous, and flows steadily without rotation.
The path followed by fluid elements in steady flow; streamlines never cross.
Volume passing a point per second, $Q = Av$ (m³/s).
$A_1v_1 = A_2v_2$ for an incompressible fluid: narrower sections flow faster.
Along a streamline of an ideal fluid, $P + \tfrac12\rho v^2 + \rho gy$ is constant.
At equal heights, faster-moving fluid has lower pressure.
Fluid leaves a hole a depth $h$ below the open surface at $v = \sqrt{2gh}$.
Internal friction in a fluid that resists flow between layers.
A measure of hotness tied to the average kinetic energy of particles; equal temperatures mean thermal equilibrium.
The state in which objects in contact no longer exchange net heat because they share the same temperature.
If A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with C, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other.
Temperature scale with water freezing at 0°C and boiling at 100°C (1 atm).
Temperature scale with $T_F = \tfrac95T_C + 32$.
The SI absolute temperature scale, $T = T_C + 273.15$; 0 K is absolute zero.
0 K ($-273.15$°C), the lowest possible temperature.
The fractional change in length per kelvin: $\Delta L = \alpha L\Delta T$.
Energy transferred because of a temperature difference (symbol $Q$, in joules).
Heat needed per kilogram per kelvin, $c$ in $Q = mc\Delta T$; 4186 J/(kg·K) for water.
Heat per kilogram absorbed or released during a phase change at constant temperature, $Q = mL$.
Latent heat for melting or freezing; $3.34\times10^5$ J/kg for water.
Latent heat for boiling or condensing; $2.26\times10^6$ J/kg for water.
Heat transfer through a material by molecular collisions; rate $kA\Delta T/L$.
Material property $k$ (W/(m·K)) setting how readily heat conducts through it.
Heat transfer by bulk motion of a fluid.
Heat transfer by electromagnetic waves; power $P = e\sigma AT^4$ (Stefan–Boltzmann law).
An object loses heat at a rate proportional to its temperature difference from the surroundings, so that difference shrinks exponentially with time.
Amount of substance containing $N_A = 6.022\times10^{23}$ particles.
$N_A = 6.022\times10^{23}$ particles per mole.
$PV = nRT = Nk_BT$, with absolute pressure and temperature.
A gas of point particles that interact only through brief elastic collisions; real gases approach it at low pressure and high temperature.
Standard temperature and pressure: 0°C (273.15 K) and 1 atm; one mole of ideal gas occupies 22.4 L.
$v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\overline{v^2}} = \sqrt{3k_BT/m} = \sqrt{3RT/M}$.
Made of single atoms (He, Ne, Ar); an ideal monatomic gas has $E_{\text{int}} = \tfrac32nRT$.
Each quadratic degree of freedom of a molecule holds on average $\tfrac12k_BT$ of energy.
The distribution of molecular speeds in a gas at temperature $T$, peaked at $\sqrt{2k_BT/m}$ with a high-speed tail.
The total microscopic energy of a system's particles; for an ideal gas it depends only on $T$.
A graph of pressure versus volume; the area under a process curve is the work done by the gas.

$\Delta E_{\text{int}} = Q - W$, with $Q$ heat into the system and $W$ work done by it. (AP Physics 2 writes $\Delta U = Q + W$ with $W$ the work done on the system; same physics, opposite sign for $W$.)
A property that depends only on the current state, not the path (internal energy, entropy, $P$, $V$, $T$).
At constant pressure; $W = P\Delta V$.
At constant volume; $W = 0$ and $Q = \Delta E_{\text{int}}$.
At constant temperature; for an ideal gas $\Delta E_{\text{int}} = 0$ and $Q = W = nRT\ln(V_f/V_i)$.
With no heat exchange ($Q = 0$); for an ideal gas $PV^\gamma$ is constant.
Heat per mole per kelvin; for a monatomic ideal gas $C_V = \tfrac32R$ and $C_P = \tfrac52R$.
A process that returns a system to its initial state, so $\Delta E_{\text{int}} = 0$ and net heat equals net work.
A cyclic device that absorbs heat $Q_H$, does work $W$, and rejects heat $Q_C$ to a colder reservoir.
$e = W/Q_H = 1 - Q_C/Q_H$ for a heat engine.
No cyclic engine converts heat entirely to work; heat does not flow spontaneously from cold to hot; total entropy of an isolated system never decreases.
An idealized process with no friction and only infinitesimal temperature differences, which can be run backward exactly.
The reversible cycle of two isotherms and two adiabats; its efficiency $1 - T_C/T_H$ is the maximum possible.
A device that uses work to move heat from a cold region to a warmer one.
For a refrigerator $K = Q_C/W$; for a heat pump $Q_H/W$. It can exceed 1.
A refrigerator used to deliver heat $Q_H$ to a warm space.
A state variable measuring disorder; $\Delta S = Q/T$ for heat $Q$ added reversibly at constant temperature $T$ (in J/K), and $S = k_B\ln\Omega$.
The property that makes matter exert electric forces; it comes in positive and negative kinds, is quantized in units of $e$, and is conserved.
$e = 1.602\times10^{-19}$ C, the magnitude of the charge on a proton or electron.
SI unit of charge; one coulomb is about $6.24\times10^{18}$ elementary charges.
A material in which some charges (usually electrons) move freely.
A material in which charges cannot move freely.
Separation of charge within a neutral object due to a nearby charge, which lets charged objects attract neutral ones.
Connecting a conductor to Earth, which can supply or absorb any amount of charge.
Charging a conductor without contact by polarizing it near a charged object and grounding it.
$F = k|q_1q_2|/r^2$ with $k = 8.99\times10^9$ N·m²/C², along the line joining two point charges.
$\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}$ C²/(N·m²), with $k = 1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$.
The net force or field from several charges is the vector sum of the individual contributions.
A small positive charge used to probe an electric field without disturbing it.
Force per unit charge, $\vec E = \vec F/q_0$ (N/C = V/m); a point charge makes $E = k|q|/r^2$.
Two equal and opposite charges separated by a small distance.
Curves tangent to $\vec E$, starting on positive and ending on negative charges, denser where the field is stronger; they never cross.
A field with the same magnitude and direction everywhere, as between large parallel plates.
The state of a conductor with no moving charges: $E = 0$ inside, excess charge on the surface, field perpendicular to the surface.
A conducting enclosure that shields its interior from external electric fields.
The amount of field passing through a surface: $\Phi_E = EA\cos\theta$ for a flat area in a uniform field, with $\theta$ measured from the area's normal.
A vector perpendicular to a surface with magnitude equal to its area; outward for closed surfaces.
The total electric flux out of a closed surface equals $Q_{\text{enc}}/\varepsilon_0$. On a symmetric surface where $E$ is constant and perpendicular, $EA = Q_{\text{enc}}/\varepsilon_0$.
An imaginary closed surface chosen to apply Gauss's law, ideally matching the symmetry of the charge.
Energy of a configuration of charges; for two point charges $U = kq_1q_2/r$ (zero at infinity).
Potential energy per unit charge, $V = U/q$, in volts; a point charge gives $V = kq/r$.
SI unit of potential: $1\text{ V} = 1\text{ J/C}$.
The change in potential between two points, $\Delta V$; a charge crossing it gains or loses energy $q\Delta V$.
Energy gained by charge $e$ through 1 V: $1\text{ eV} = 1.602\times10^{-19}$ J.
A surface of constant potential; perpendicular to field lines, and no work is done moving along it.
Two conductors separated by an insulator, storing equal and opposite charges and electric energy.
$C = Q/V$, the charge stored per volt; set by geometry and dielectric.
SI unit of capacitance, $1\text{ F} = 1\text{ C/V}$.
An insulating material placed between capacitor plates; it polarizes, reducing the field and raising the capacitance.
The factor $\kappa$ by which a dielectric multiplies capacitance.
Energy per unit volume stored in a field; for an electric field $u = \tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2$.
Rate of charge flow, $I = \Delta Q/\Delta t$, in amperes; conventional current is the direction positive charge would move.
SI unit of current: $1\text{ A} = 1\text{ C/s}$.
The work per unit charge a source (battery, generator) does moving charge through it, $\mathcal{E}$, in volts.
The slow average velocity of charge carriers along a conductor, $v_d = I/(nqA)$.
$R = V/I$, in ohms: how strongly a component opposes current.
SI unit of resistance: $1\ \Omega = 1$ V/A.
$V = IR$ with constant $R$; obeyed by ohmic materials such as metals at fixed temperature.
Material property $\rho$ (Ω·m) with $R = \rho L/A$.
A material whose resistance drops to exactly zero below a critical temperature.
Conversion of electrical energy to heat in a resistance, at rate $I^2R$.
Current per unit cross-sectional area, $\vec J = nq\vec v_d = \vec E/\rho$.
Resistance $r$ inside a real source, which lowers its terminal voltage when current flows.
Voltage across a source's terminals, $V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$.
Junction rule (currents in = currents out) and loop rule (sum of potential changes around a loop = 0).
The total current into a junction equals the total current out (charge conservation).
The sum of potential changes around any closed loop is zero (energy conservation).
A low-resistance meter connected in series to measure current.
A high-resistance meter connected in parallel to measure potential difference.
Choosing a load resistance equal to the source's internal resistance to transfer maximum power.
The characteristic time of exponential change; $\tau = RC$ for an RC circuit, $L/R$ for an RL circuit.
A circuit that passes slow signal changes and blocks rapid ones; an RC filter has crossover near $1/(2\pi RC)$.
The field $\vec B$ that exerts forces on moving charges and currents; its field lines form closed loops from north to south poles.
SI unit of magnetic field: $1\text{ T} = 1$ N/(A·m). Earth's field is about $5\times10^{-5}$ T.
$\vec F = q\vec v\times\vec B$ on a moving charge (magnitude $|q|vB\sin\theta$); $\vec F = I\vec L\times\vec B$ on a wire.
The frequency $f = |q|B/(2\pi m)$ of a charge circling in a uniform magnetic field, independent of its speed.
A device that separates ions by mass using the radius $r = mv/(qB)$ of their paths in a magnetic field.
$\mu = NIA$ for a current loop; the torque in a field is $\tau = \mu B\sin\phi$.
A device in which magnetic torque on current loops produces rotation; a commutator keeps the torque in one direction.
$\mu_0 \approx 4\pi\times10^{-7} = 1.257\times10^{-6}$ T·m/A, the constant in magnetic field formulas (exactly $4\pi\times10^{-7}$ before the 2019 SI redefinition).
A long coil of wire; inside, $B = \mu_0nI$, nearly uniform and along the axis.
A solenoid with an iron core, giving a strong magnetic field that can be switched on and off.
Describes materials (iron, nickel, cobalt) whose atomic magnetic moments align in domains, producing strong magnetization.
For a closed path along which the field is constant and points along the path, $B\times(\text{path length}) = \mu_0I_{\text{enc}}$; used with symmetry to find the fields of wires and solenoids.
The amount of magnetic field through a loop: $\Phi_B = BA\cos\theta$ for a flat loop in a uniform field ($\theta$ from the loop's normal), in webers.
SI unit of magnetic flux, $1\text{ Wb} = 1\text{ T·m}^2$.
A changing magnetic flux induces an emf: $\mathcal{E} = -N\,\Delta\Phi_B/\Delta t$, $N$ times the slope of the flux–time graph.
An induced current flows in the direction that opposes the change in flux that produced it.
The emf $BLv$ across a conductor of length $L$ moving at speed $v$ perpendicular to a field $B$.
A device that rotates coils in a magnetic field to produce an alternating emf $NBA\omega\sin\omega t$, with peak value $NBA\omega$.
Swirling induced currents in bulk metal exposed to changing flux; they heat the metal and oppose motion.
Two coils on a common core that change AC voltage in the ratio of turns: $V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p$.
$L$ in $\mathcal{E} = -L\,\Delta I/\Delta t$, in henries; for a solenoid $L = \mu_0N^2A/\ell$.
SI unit of inductance: $1\text{ H} = 1$ V·s/A.
A coil used for its inductance; it opposes changes in current and stores energy $\tfrac12LI^2$.
Current (and voltage) that varies sinusoidally, $V = V_0\sin\omega t$; 60 Hz in North America.
Root-mean-square value; for a sinusoid $V_{\text{rms}} = V_0/\sqrt2$, the steady value with the same average power.
Opposition of a capacitor ($X_C = 1/\omega C$) or inductor ($X_L = \omega L$) to AC, in ohms.
Total opposition to AC in a circuit; series RLC: $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$.
A self-sustaining wave of perpendicular oscillating electric and magnetic fields, traveling at $c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}$ in vacuum.
The range of EM waves by wavelength: radio, microwave, infrared, visible (400–700 nm), ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.
$c = 3.00\times10^8$ m/s in vacuum, the same for all EM waves and all inertial observers.
A filter that transmits only the component of the electric field along its axis.
Describes light whose electric field oscillates in a single direction.
Polarized light through a polarizer at angle $\theta$ has $I = I_0\cos^2\theta$.
A line showing the direction light energy travels; the basis of geometric optics.
The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, both measured from the normal.
$n = c/v$, the factor by which light slows in a material.
The bending of light as it crosses a boundary between materials with different speeds of light.
$n_1\sin\theta_1 = n_2\sin\theta_2$, with angles from the normal.
Dependence of the index of refraction on wavelength, which spreads white light into colors.
Complete reflection of light trying to pass into a lower-index medium at more than the critical angle.
The incidence angle with $\sin\theta_c = n_2/n_1$ ($n_1 > n_2$) above which total internal reflection occurs.
Light travels between two points along the path of least time; it implies the laws of reflection and refraction.
An image from which light only appears to come; it cannot be projected on a screen ($d_i < 0$).
An image where light rays actually converge, which can be projected on a screen ($d_i > 0$).
A mirror curved inward that converges parallel rays to a focal point; $f = R/2 > 0$.
The point where rays parallel to the axis converge (or appear to diverge from) after a lens or mirror.
Distance from a lens or mirror to its focal point; positive for converging, negative for diverging optics.
A mirror curved outward; it diverges light, has $f < 0$, and forms virtual, upright, reduced images.
A lens thicker in the middle that brings parallel rays to a focus; $f > 0$.
A lens thinner in the middle that spreads parallel rays; $f < 0$.
$\dfrac1{d_o} + \dfrac1{d_i} = \dfrac1f$, for thin lenses and spherical mirrors.
$m = h_i/h_o = -d_i/d_o$; negative means inverted.
$P = 1/f$ in diopters (m⁻¹).
$\dfrac1f = (n - 1)\left(\dfrac1{R_1} - \dfrac1{R_2}\right)$ for a thin lens.
The curved, transparent front surface of the eye, which does most of its focusing.
The light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye, where the eye forms a real, inverted image.
The eye's ability to change the shape, and so the focal length, of its lens to focus on objects at different distances.
The closest distance at which an eye can focus clearly; 25 cm by convention for a normal eye.
The farthest distance at which an eye can focus; infinity for a normal eye.
Nearsightedness: the eye focuses too strongly, so its far point is closer than infinity; corrected with a diverging lens.
Farsightedness: the eye focuses too weakly, so its near point is farther than 25 cm; corrected with a converging lens.
Loss of accommodation with age as the eye's lens stiffens, so the near point recedes.
The ratio $M = \theta/\theta_0$ of the angle an image subtends through an instrument to the angle the object subtends to the unaided eye at its best viewing distance.
A single converging lens used with the object inside its focal length; angular magnification $25\text{ cm}/f$ (image at infinity) or $1 + 25\text{ cm}/f$ (image at the near point).
Two converging lenses: a short-focal-length objective makes a real, enlarged image that the eyepiece magnifies; $M = m_{\text{obj}}M_{\text{eye}}$.
The lens or mirror of a microscope or telescope nearest the object; it forms the first, real image.
The lens nearest the eye in a microscope or telescope; it acts as a magnifier for the objective's image.
A telescope with a long-focal-length objective lens and a short-focal-length eyepiece; $M = -f_o/f_e$, length about $f_o + f_e$.
A telescope whose objective is a concave mirror; mirrors avoid color fringes and can be made much larger than lenses.
Describes sources with a constant phase relationship, needed for a stable interference pattern.
The spreading of waves through openings or around obstacles comparable in size to the wavelength.
Many equally spaced slits producing sharp maxima at $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$.
Two point sources are just resolved at angular separation $\theta = 1.22\lambda/D$.
The laws of physics are the same in every inertial reference frame.
$\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2} \ge 1$.
Time between two events measured by a clock present at both (at rest relative to them); the shortest measured interval.
Moving clocks run slow: $\Delta t = \gamma\Delta t_0$.
The length of an object measured in its own rest frame; the longest measured length.
Objects are shorter along their direction of motion: $L = L_0/\gamma$.
The energy $E_0 = mc^2$ a particle has by virtue of its mass.
Mass is a form of energy, $E_0 = mc^2$; nuclear reactions convert small mass changes into large energies.
$x' = \gamma(x - vt)$, $t' = \gamma(t - vx/c^2)$: how coordinates change between inertial frames.
A quantum of electromagnetic energy, $E = hf = hc/\lambda$, with momentum $h/\lambda$.
Emission of electrons from a metal by light; explained by photons, with $K_{\max} = hf - \phi$.
The minimum energy $\phi$ needed to free an electron from a metal's surface.
The lowest light frequency, $f_0 = \phi/h$, that can eject photoelectrons.
An ideal object that absorbs all radiation falling on it; it is also the best emitter, and its emission spectrum depends only on its temperature.
The peak wavelength of blackbody radiation is inversely proportional to absolute temperature: $\lambda_{\max}T = 2.898\times10^{-3}$ m·K.

Scattering of an X-ray or gamma-ray photon by a nearly free electron, which lengthens the photon's wavelength by $\Delta\lambda = \dfrac{h}{m_ec}(1 - \cos\theta)$; evidence that photons carry momentum.
The set of discrete wavelengths emitted by an element's atoms, unique to that element.
The allowed energies of a bound system; for hydrogen $E_n = -13.6\text{ eV}/n^2$.
The lowest energy level of an atom or system ($n = 1$ in hydrogen).
The wavelength of a particle, $\lambda = h/p$.
Light and matter both show wave behavior (interference) and particle behavior (discrete quanta), depending on the experiment.
Position and momentum cannot both be sharply defined: $\Delta x\,\Delta p \ge h/(4\pi)$.
A standing-wave state of an electron in an atom, labeled by $n$, $l$ and $m_l$; it holds at most two electrons.
The quantum number $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$ that mainly sets an electron's energy and orbital size.
All the electron states with the same principal quantum number $n$; it holds up to $2n^2$ electrons.
The quantum number $l = 0, 1, \ldots, n - 1$ that sets an orbital's shape and orbital angular momentum $L = \sqrt{l(l+1)}\,h/(2\pi)$; $l = 0, 1, 2, 3$ are called s, p, d, f.
All the electron states with the same $n$ and $l$, such as 2p; it holds up to $2(2l + 1)$ electrons.
The quantum number $m_l = -l, \ldots, l$ that sets an orbital's orientation; the angular momentum component along an axis is $m_l h/(2\pi)$.
The quantum number $m_s = +\tfrac12$ or $-\tfrac12$ that gives the direction of an electron's spin.
The built-in angular momentum (and magnetism) of an electron, which has only two possible settings, up and down.
No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four quantum numbers $n$, $l$, $m_l$, $m_s$.
The list of an atom's occupied subshells with the number of electrons in each, such as $1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^1$ for sodium.
A tube in which electrons accelerated through a high voltage strike a metal target and produce X-rays.
X-rays emitted with a continuous spread of energies as fast electrons are deflected and slowed by nuclei.
The shortest wavelength from an X-ray tube, $\lambda_{\min} = hc/(eV)$, set only by the accelerating voltage.
X-ray lines at wavelengths fixed by the target element, emitted when an electron drops into a vacancy in an inner shell; $E_{K\alpha} \approx 10.2\text{ eV}\,(Z - 1)^2$.
Emission of a photon by an excited atom on its own, at a random moment and in a random direction.
Emission triggered by a passing photon of matching energy; the new photon has the same energy, direction, phase and polarization.
Light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation: a source of monochromatic, coherent, directional light.
A state with more atoms in an upper level than in a lower one, needed for stimulated emission to outpace absorption.
An excited state that lasts unusually long (around a millisecond rather than about 10 ns), letting atoms pile up in it.
A proton or neutron.
The number of protons $Z$ in a nucleus, which identifies the element.
The total number of nucleons $A = Z + N$.
Nuclei with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
The very strong, short-range (~$10^{-15}$ m) attraction between nucleons that holds nuclei together.
$1\text{ u} = 1.6605\times10^{-27}$ kg, equivalent to 931.5 MeV.
The amount by which a nucleus's mass is less than the total mass of its separate nucleons.
Energy needed to separate a nucleus into its nucleons, $E_B = \Delta m\,c^2$.
Splitting of a heavy nucleus into lighter ones, releasing energy (about 200 MeV for uranium-235).
Joining of light nuclei into a heavier one, releasing energy; powers the Sun.
Emission of a helium-4 nucleus; $Z$ drops by 2 and $A$ by 4.
Emission of an electron (β⁻, $Z + 1$) or positron (β⁺, $Z - 1$) as a neutron and proton interconvert.
Emission of a high-energy photon as a nucleus drops to a lower energy state; $Z$ and $A$ unchanged.
Decays per second, $R = \lambda N$, in becquerels.
Time for half of a radioactive sample to decay, $T_{1/2} = \ln 2/\lambda$.
The average lifetime of an unstable nucleus, $\tau = 1/\lambda = T_{1/2}/\ln 2$.

references.title: Electricity, magnetism, optics, and modern physics
references.body:
## Electrostatics

| | |
|---|---|
| Coulomb's law | $F = k\dfrac{\lvert q_1q_2\rvert}{r^2}$ |
| Field | $\vec E = \vec F/q$; point charge $E = kq/r^2$ |
| Flux, Gauss's law | $\Phi_E = EA\cos\theta$; total flux out of a closed surface $= Q_{\text{enc}}/\varepsilon_0$ (symmetric case: $EA = Q_{\text{enc}}/\varepsilon_0$) |
| Line, sheet | $E = \dfrac{2k\lambda}{r}$; $E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$ |
| Potential | $V = kq/r$; $U = kq_1q_2/r$; $\Delta U = q\Delta V$ |
| Field from potential | uniform field: $\Delta V = -Ed$ along the field, $E = \lvert\Delta V\rvert/d$; field points toward lower potential |
| Capacitance | $C = Q/V$; parallel plates $C = \kappa\varepsilon_0A/d$ |
| Capacitor energy | $U = \tfrac12CV^2$; $u = \tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2$ |
| Combinations | parallel $C = \sum C_i$; series $1/C = \sum 1/C_i$ |

## Circuits

| | |
|---|---|
| Current, Ohm's law | $I = \Delta Q/\Delta t$; $V = IR$; $R = \rho L/A$ |
| Power | $P = IV = I^2R = V^2/R$ |
| Resistors | series $R = \sum R_i$; parallel $1/R = \sum 1/R_i$ |
| Real battery | $V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$ |
| Kirchhoff | $\sum I_{\text{in}} = \sum I_{\text{out}}$; $\sum\Delta V = 0$ around a loop |
| RC | $\tau = RC$; charging $q = C\mathcal{E}(1 - e^{-t/\tau})$; discharging $q = Q_0e^{-t/\tau}$ |

## Magnetism and induction

| | |
|---|---|
| Force on charge | $F = \lvert q\rvert vB\sin\theta$; $\vec F = q\vec v\times\vec B$; $r = \dfrac{mv}{\lvert q\rvert B}$ |
| Force on wire | $F = ILB\sin\theta$; loop torque $\tau = NIAB\sin\phi$ |
| Straight wire | $B = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi r}$ |
| Loop center, solenoid | $B = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{2R}$; $B = \mu_0nI$ |
| Parallel wires | $F/L = \dfrac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi d}$ |
| Ampère (symmetric path) | $B\times(\text{path length}) = \mu_0I_{\text{enc}}$ |
| Faraday | $\mathcal{E} = -N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi_B}{\Delta t}$, $\Phi_B = BA\cos\theta$; motional $\mathcal{E} = BLv$; generator peak $NBA\omega$ |
| Transformer | $V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p$; $V_pI_p = V_sI_s$ |
| Inductance | $\mathcal{E} = -L\,\Delta I/\Delta t$; solenoid $L = \mu_0N^2A/\ell$; $U = \tfrac12LI^2$; RL $\tau = L/R$ |
| LC, AC | $f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$; $V_{\text{rms}} = V_0/\sqrt2$; $X_C = \dfrac{1}{\omega C}$, $X_L = \omega L$; $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$ |

## Light and optics

| | |
|---|---|
| EM waves | $c = f\lambda = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}$; $E = cB$ |
| Polarization | $I = I_0\cos^2\theta$ |
| Refraction | $n = c/v$; $n_1\sin\theta_1 = n_2\sin\theta_2$; $\sin\theta_c = n_2/n_1$ |
| Mirrors and lenses | $\dfrac1{d_o} + \dfrac1{d_i} = \dfrac1f$; $m = -\dfrac{d_i}{d_o}$; mirror $f = R/2$; $P = 1/f$ |
| Double slit, grating | $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ (bright); $\Delta y = \lambda L/d$ |
| Single slit | $a\sin\theta = m\lambda$ (dark) |
| Vision | near point 25 cm, far point $\infty$; myopia: $f = -(\text{far point})$; hyperopia: image an object at 25 cm at the near point |
| Angular magnification | $M = \theta/\theta_0$, $\theta_0 = h/(25\text{ cm})$; magnifier $M = 25\text{ cm}/f$ (image at $\infty$) or $1 + 25\text{ cm}/f$ |
| Microscope, telescope | $M = \left(-\dfrac{d_i}{d_o}\right)\dfrac{25\text{ cm}}{f_e}$; $M = -\dfrac{f_o}{f_e}$, length $f_o + f_e$ |
| Resolution | $\theta_{\min} = 1.22\lambda/D$ |
| Thin film | one flip (soap film in air): bright when $2nt = (m + \tfrac12)\lambda$; zero or two flips: bright when $2nt = m\lambda$ |

## Modern physics

| | |
|---|---|
| Relativity | $\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}}$; $\Delta t = \gamma\Delta t_0$; $L = L_0/\gamma$ |
| Velocity addition | $u = \dfrac{u' + v}{1 + u'v/c^2}$ |
| Energy, momentum | $E = \gamma mc^2$, $K = (\gamma - 1)mc^2$, $p = \gamma mv$, $E^2 = (pc)^2 + (mc^2)^2$ |
| Photons | $E = hf = hc/\lambda$; $p = h/\lambda$ |
| Photoelectric effect | $K_{\max} = hf - \phi$ |
| Blackbody, Compton | Wien $\lambda_{\max}T = 2.898\times10^{-3}$ m·K; $\Delta\lambda = \dfrac{h}{m_ec}(1 - \cos\theta)$, $\dfrac{h}{m_ec} = 2.43$ pm |
| Hydrogen | $E_n = -\dfrac{13.6\text{ eV}}{n^2}$ |
| Quantum numbers | $n \ge 1$; $l = 0$ to $n - 1$; $m_l = -l$ to $l$; $m_s = \pm\tfrac12$; subshell $2(2l + 1)$, shell $2n^2$ electrons |
| X-rays | cutoff $\lambda_{\min} = \dfrac{hc}{eV}$; $E_{K\alpha} \approx 10.2\text{ eV}\,(Z - 1)^2$ |
| Matter waves | $\lambda = h/p$; $\Delta x\,\Delta p \ge h/(4\pi)$ |
| Binding energy | $E_B = \Delta m\,c^2$ (1 u ↔ 931.5 MeV) |
| Decay | $N = N_0e^{-\lambda t} = N_0(\tfrac12)^{t/T_{1/2}}$; $T_{1/2} = \ln 2/\lambda$; $R = \lambda N$ |

references.title: Mechanics equations
references.body:
## Vectors

| | |
|---|---|
| Components | $A_x = A\cos\theta$, $A_y = A\sin\theta$ |
| Magnitude, direction | $A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2}$, $\tan\theta = A_y/A_x$ |
| Dot product | $\vec A\cdot\vec B = AB\cos\phi = A_xB_x + A_yB_y + A_zB_z$ |
| Cross product | $\lvert\vec A\times\vec B\rvert = AB\sin\phi$ (right-hand rule) |

## Kinematics

| | |
|---|---|
| Definitions | $v_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$, $a_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$ |
| Graphs | slope of $x$–$t$ = velocity; slope of $v$–$t$ = acceleration; area under $v$–$t$ = displacement; area under $a$–$t$ = change in velocity |
| Constant acceleration | $v = v_0 + at$; $\Delta x = v_0t + \tfrac12at^2$; $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x$; $\Delta x = \tfrac12(v_0 + v)t$ |
| Projectile (level ground) | $R = \dfrac{v_0^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$, $H = \dfrac{v_0^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$, $T = \dfrac{2v_0\sin\theta}{g}$ |
| Relative velocity | $\vec v_{AC} = \vec v_{AB} + \vec v_{BC}$ |
| Circular motion | $v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T}$, $a_c = \dfrac{v^2}{r} = \omega^2r$ |

## Forces

| | |
|---|---|
| Newton's second law | $\sum\vec F = m\vec a = \dfrac{\Delta\vec p}{\Delta t}$ |
| Weight | $W = mg$ |
| Friction | $f_k = \mu_kn$, $f_s \le \mu_sn$ |
| Incline | $mg\sin\theta$ along, $mg\cos\theta$ into the slope |
| Spring | $F = -kx$ |
| Centripetal | $\sum F_{\text{in}} = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$ |
| Atwood machine | $a = \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}g$ |

## Energy and momentum

| | |
|---|---|
| Work | $W = Fd\cos\theta$; varying force: area under the $F$–$x$ graph |
| Kinetic energy | $K = \tfrac12mv^2$; $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$ |
| Potential energy | $U_g = mgy$, $U_s = \tfrac12kx^2$ |
| Energy conservation | $K_i + U_i + W_{\text{nc}} = K_f + U_f$ |
| Power | $P = \dfrac{W}{t} = Fv$ |
| Momentum, impulse | $\vec p = m\vec v$; $\vec J = \vec F_{\text{avg}}\Delta t = \Delta\vec p$ (area under the $F$–$t$ graph) |
| Center of mass | $x_{\text{cm}} = \dfrac{\sum m_ix_i}{M}$ |
| Elastic collision (target at rest) | $v_{1f} = \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}v_{1i}$, $v_{2f} = \dfrac{2m_1}{m_1 + m_2}v_{1i}$ |
| Perfectly inelastic | $v_f = \dfrac{m_1v_1 + m_2v_2}{m_1 + m_2}$ |

## Rotation

| Linear | Rotational |
|---|---|
| $x$, $v$, $a$ | $\theta$, $\omega$, $\alpha$; $v = r\omega$, $a_t = r\alpha$ |
| $m$ | $I = \sum mr^2$; $I = I_{\text{cm}} + Md^2$ |
| $F = ma$ | $\tau = rF\sin\theta = I\alpha$; $\vec\tau = \vec r\times\vec F$ |
| $K = \tfrac12mv^2$ | $K = \tfrac12I\omega^2$ |
| $p = mv$ | $L = I\omega$; point mass $L = mvr_\perp$; $\tau = \Delta L/\Delta t$ |
| $P = Fv$ | $P = \tau\omega$ |

| Shape (mass $M$) | $I$ |
|---|---|
| Hoop, radius $R$ | $MR^2$ |
| Solid disk or cylinder | $\tfrac12MR^2$ |
| Solid sphere | $\tfrac25MR^2$ |
| Thin spherical shell | $\tfrac23MR^2$ |
| Rod about center / end | $\tfrac1{12}ML^2$ / $\tfrac13ML^2$ |

Rolling from height $h$ ($I = cMR^2$): $v = \sqrt{2gh/(1 + c)}$. Static equilibrium: $\sum\vec F = 0$, $\sum\tau = 0$.

## Elasticity

| | |
|---|---|
| Stress, strain | stress $= F/A$ (Pa); strain $= \Delta L/L_0$ |
| Young's modulus | $\dfrac{F}{A} = Y\dfrac{\Delta L}{L_0}$; $\Delta L = \dfrac{FL_0}{YA}$; rod as spring $k = YA/L_0$ |
| Shear | $\dfrac{F}{A} = S\dfrac{\Delta x}{L_0}$ ($A$ = face the force lies along) |
| Bulk | $\Delta P = -B\dfrac{\Delta V}{V_0}$ |

## Gravitation

| | |
|---|---|
| Universal gravitation | $F = \dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$; $g = \dfrac{GM}{R^2}$ |
| Circular orbit | $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$, $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{GM}r^3$ |
| Potential energy | $U = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$ |
| Escape speed | $v_{\text{esc}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$ |
